siting_landscape: Set back on the curving tree-lined streets of the 1926 core around parc Oersted (rues Davy, Deville, Moritz, Hare, Wohler, Oersted, Moissan, Edison, Faraday, boulevard Mellon, rue Lavoisier).
Concrete foundations from the outset ("a symbol of permanence").
massing: Model A1 (documented): a detached house whose roofline includes dormers; plan reorganised under Harold R. Wake so that a kitchen-family room replaces the separate dining and living rooms and adjoins two ground-floor bedrooms.

types.profile_note: Only A1 is documented online (photograph and floor plans reproduced from the company's late-1920s "Townsite Houses" catalogue). Storeys, cladding, window type and the A2–A8 variants await Morisset's album (Part 4b). Do not fill from photographs.
types.source_generation: Ville de Saguenay address→model list (2014); Morisset 2022 (print)
types.blurb_en: The first-phase house: one of the standard models of the summer of 1926, re-drawn by Wake to fit French-Canadian family life (a big kitchen instead of parlour and dining room), varied from house to house by dormers, porches and roof details so that, in the City's phrase, "not a single house was built that resembles its neighbour".
types.origin_en: Brainerd's New York-inspired type plans were "rationalised" on site by the engineer Harold R. Wake, who adapted them to Québec's climate and household size; the CPCQ dossier speaks of "quatre modèles types" enabling the 270 houses of 1926 in 135 days, with variety obtained through dormers, balconies and roofs. The address list is consistent with families A–D being that first set: on the 1926 streets almost every entry is an A, B, C or D code.

siting_landscape: Rue La Traverse carries E01, E04, H01, J01, J02, K01, K02, K03 and G01 — together with B03, B04 and C05, the models that appear nowhere in the 1926 core.
Rue Castner carries G02, G03, G04 and H02; rue Héroult G04; rue Coulomb G01, K01 and L01; rues Montgomery J03 and J04; rues Geoffrion and Neilson H03.

types.profile_note: Grouped stub for the families the public record does not describe; to be split into separate records in Part 4b. The phase attribution is a hypothesis, not a finding: rue La Traverse and rue Castner lie between the 1926 core and the war-era streets, and no online source identifies the 1936–41 Barott houses by letter. Tenure is mixed and read from the civic numbering alone: G02, G03 and G04 are paired (1654-58, 1673-77, 1689-93, 1657-61, 2928-32, 2936-40), as are the single Y (1725-43) and Z (1739-41-43) entries, one H03 (1733-35 rue Neilson) and one N (2816-2820 boulevard du Saguenay); every other entry in these families is a single civic number. Codes are as parsed from the 2014 address list, which carries only E01 and E04 for family E (the Part 4 brief anticipated E01–E05) and bare N, Y and Z with no model number. No canonical form or style is assigned, and nothing has been entered from photographs.

types.blurb_en: The families the catalogue index cannot yet describe: twenty codes clustered on rue La Traverse, rue Castner and rue Coulomb, between the first streets of 1926 and the war-era additions.
types.origin_en: Probably the second construction phase, which opened in early 1936 with houses by the Montréal architect Ernest Isbell Barott; no online source ties Barott's designs to particular model letters, so the attribution stays provisional until Morisset's album is read.

types.phase_title: Sulpician concessions on the chemin du Roy
types.name_en: Stone house of the French tradition
types.name_fr: La maison de pierre de tradition française
types.source_ref: Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec, fiches 93274 (site patrimonial Le Ber-Le Moyne, Lachine), 93440 (maison Rangé-dit-Laviolette, Baie-D'Urfé) et 92796 (maison Hyacinthe-Jamme-dit-Carrière, Pointe-Claire); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissements de Lachine, de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé et de Pointe-Claire (2005)
canonical_names: Urban stone house of French inspiration, one or two levels plus attic, two-slope roof, chimneys in fire-break party walls
types.roofing: cedar shingle at Le Ber-Le Moyne; ribbed copper sheet at Pointe-Claire today, over an original wood shingle

siting_landscape: Each of the three survivors sits on ground that predates the street grid around it. Le Ber-Le Moyne stands on a raised point of land beside lac Saint-Louis at the head of the Lachine rapids, on a slight mound planted with mature trees.

The Baie-D'Urfé house stands at the back of its lot, about a hundred metres from the public road and close to the shore, its main front turned south to the lake and the îles Sainte-Geneviève — RPCQ reads that orientation as evidence that the chemin du Roy once ran between the house and the water.

Pointe-Claire's house stands at the far end of a large treed lot that now isolates it from the postwar subdivision around it, on a censive conceded by the Sulpicians in 1722 along the côte Saint-Jean.
massing: A low stone carré on a near-square or short rectangular plan, one and a half storeys, sitting close to the ground. The Baie-D'Urfé carré measures 9.4 by 9.3 m.

Steep two-slope roof with straight slopes. Eaves are shallow at Lachine, and carried out over a covered gallery at Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire — in both cases a nineteenth-century alteration, not an original feature.
Ancillary buildings belong to the type where they survive - Lachine keeps a stone dépendance of the same date, and an 1781 census records a house, a barn and a stable at Baie-D'Urfé.
articulation: Almost none in the original fabric. What ornament these houses carry — moulded wood chambranles, gable dormers, a neo-Gothic porch, a bell-cast eave — was added between about 1828 and 1874 to bring them up to date.
openings: Openings set out asymmetrically, which RPCQ names as a French-tradition trait at both Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire.
Casement windows with small panes. At Pointe-Claire the south front is opened up for light while the north wall carries only two windows.
materials: Fieldstone throughout, laid up rubble. Pointe-Claire is left bare, and RPCQ names the absence of crépi as a Montréal-region trait; Baie-D'Urfé is whitewashed on three sides.
Two chimney stacks carried up in the line of the gable walls — the trait RPCQ singles out as belonging "plus particulièrement" to the houses of the island of Montréal and its neighbouring regions.

description: « Les deux bâtiments en pierre de plan rectangulaire s'élèvent sur un étage et sont coiffés d'un toit aigu à deux versants droits aux larmiers peu saillants. »
« Fenêtre(s) : Rectangulaire, À battants, à petits carreaux »

« La partie la plus ancienne présente un plan presque carré, comporte des murs en pierre chaulés sur trois côtés et s'élève sur un étage et demi. Elle est couverte d'un toit à deux versants droits aux larmiers débordants couvrant une galerie du côté sud. Deux cheminées s'élèvent dans la continuité des murs pignon. »

« Construite au tournant du XVIIIe siècle, la maison possède des éléments qui se rattachent à la tradition architecturale d'inspiration française, comme le carré en pierre peu dégagé du sol et la disposition asymétrique des ouvertures. Le plan presque carré et les cheminées qui s'élèvent dans la continuité des murs pignon, plus particulièrement associés aux maisons de l'île de Montréal et des régions environnantes, sont aussi des caractéristiques de l'architecture de cette époque. »
contexte: « La maison LeBer-LeMoyne, dont l'importance patrimoniale est exceptionnelle, a été reconnue par un classement en vertu de la Loi sur les biens culturels en 2001. Elle date du Régime français et est l'une des plus anciennes au Canada. Avec son site, elle rappelle la vocation agricole et commerciale des débuts de Lachine. » (Lachine, 19.E.4)

« Le chemin du Lakeshore regroupe la plus grande densité de bâtiments d'intérêt patrimonial de l'arrondissement. Son parcours comprend d'anciennes maisons de ferme, des maisons bourgeoises et des villas d'été de la fin du XIXe siècle et du début du XXe siècle qui nous sont parvenues avec des degrés d'authenticité divers. » (Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé, 4.I.1)

« … le moulin banal (1709-1710), classé bien archéologique en 1983, la maison Hyacinthe-Jamme dit Carrière (vers 1780), classée monument historique en 1964 par le ministère des Affaires culturelles, ainsi que d'autres maisons des XVIIIe et XIXe siècles. » (Pointe-Claire, 3.1)
elements_caracteristiques: « Elle illustre ce type par son corps de logis bas en pierre, son élévation d'un étage et demi, son toit aigu à deux versants, ses deux cheminées logées dans les murs pignons, ses ouvertures disposées de manière asymétrique et ses fenêtres à battants à petits carreaux. »
« Le plan presque carré et l'absence de crépi sont des éléments fréquemment associés à la maison d'inspiration française de la région de Montréal. »
« Elle est l'une des rares maisons de ferme datant de la fin du XVIIIe siècle à subsister à l'intérieur des terres de Pointe-Claire. »

types.profile_note: A thin record by design, and honest about it. None of the six West Island places has a per-type typology document — no inventory, no thesaurus, no per-type table — so this record is built from the three individual houses that do carry statutory records, plus the three 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers, which characterise sectors and not building types. What that leaves empty: `window_proportion` is null because all three RPCQ fiches describe the windows as casements with small panes and none gives a proportion; `roof.pitch_deg` is null because the fiches say "aigu" and "à pente moyenne" and never a figure; `lot_width_m`, `setback_front_m`, `setback_side_m` and `front_yard_green_pct` are null because no source measures a lot or a setback anywhere in the West Island; `sectors` is null because a shared record cannot carry sector codes that exist in only one of its places. `storeys` is entered as 1.5 from the RPCQ "Nombre d'étages" field, which reads 1½ for all three — note that the Le Ber-Le Moyne description text contradicts its own data field, saying the buildings "s'élèvent sur un étage". The canonical is `french-urban-house-stone` rather than `french-rural-house-1st-hip` even though all three are farm or trading-post houses in open country: the discriminant in this vocabulary is fabric and roof, not siting, and all three are stone under a straight two-slope roof with stacks in the gable walls, where the rural canonical is pièce-sur-pièce timber under a hip carried to the wall head with no cellar. RPCQ says as much itself, calling the nearby Sainte-Anne example « la maison rurale d'inspiration urbaine, fréquente dans la région de Montréal et les régions avoisinantes ». The phase is p1 and marked provisional: Lachine's house is 1669–71 and Baie-D'Urfé's about 1700, both inside p1, but Pointe-Claire's classed survivor was built between 1769 and 1791, inside p2 — RPCQ states plainly that this building tradition « se poursuit au-delà de la Conquête (1760) », so the type is filed at its origin and the reader is told the fabric outlives it.
conservation: All three houses are protected individually, and none of the three village or shore ensembles around them is. Lachine's is a classed site patrimonial (2001) covering the exteriors and the land; Pointe-Claire's is a classed immeuble patrimonial (1964-08-12) covering exterior, interior and land; Baie-D'Urfé's is a municipal citation (2001) covering only the exterior envelope of the oldest, eastern section.
types.source_generation: three RPCQ statements of heritage value (valeur patrimoniale + éléments caractéristiques) read against three sector-characterisation cahiers; no source publishes a per-type table for any West Island place, so the five columns are assembled from the three classed or cited houses themselves
types.blurb_en: A low fieldstone box of one and a half storeys under a steep two-slope roof, stacks rising inside the gable walls, openings placed where they were wanted rather than where symmetry asked for them. Three of them survive across three of the six West Island places — a trading post of 1669–71 at Lachine, a farm house of about 1700 at Baie-D'Urfé, and one of 1769–91 at Pointe-Claire — and all three are protected individually while nothing around them is. One record, three municipalities: the photograph on this card is Lachine's, and Baie-D'Urfé's and Pointe-Claire's stand beside it on the type page.
types.origin_en: The Sulpicians became seigneurs of the island of Montréal in 1663 and conceded the côtes that run out to its western end; the houses built on those concessions were stone because stone was what the fields gave up and because fire and raiding made anything else a poor bet. What survives is very little. Lachine's is the oldest and least altered: two rectangular stone buildings put up in 1669–71 as a fur-trade post for Charles Le Moyne and Jacques Le Ber, restored in the 1980s toward their seventeenth-century appearance and now the Musée de Lachine. Baie-D'Urfé's was built about 1700 by Hubert Rangé dit Laviolette on a concession he bought in 1695, and then quietly rebuilt by the Pilon family between 1839 and 1874 — the walls raised, the roof pitch eased off, moulded chambranles and projecting eaves added in what RPCQ calls a taste imported after the Conquest. Pointe-Claire's went up between 1769 and 1791 on a censive conceded in 1722, and was altered again in 1828. Read together the three make the point the West Island pages keep making: the form is one form across three municipalities, the protection is three separate individual instruments granted in 1964, 2001 and 2001, and not one of them protects an ensemble.

photo.credit: « Maison Rangé, 20122, chemin Lakeshore (Baie-D'Urfé) », photo Anne-Marie Dufour, 2010-12-03, Flickr stream *Parcours riverain — Ville de Montréal*; Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0, Flickr licence review passed (verified through the Commons API).
photo.note: Inspected before use, and used with a caveat. The photograph is taken from the drive on the north side and shows the L-shaped ensemble of three volumes; the low stone wing at the left is the protected eastern section, but the covered south gallery, the three dormers and the whitewash that the citation describes are on the lake front and are not visible from this angle.
photo.alt: Photograph of Stone house of the French tradition houses in Baie-D'Urfé, from Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec

types.phase_title: The population quintuples, and the merger
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), § 1.2.2 « Les ensembles urbains d'intérêt » et secteurs 7.U.1 à 7.U.8 (Dorval), 5.U.2 et 5.U.3 (Pointe-Claire), 19.U.2 (Lachine), 2.U.2 et 2.U.4 (Pierrefonds-Senneville) et 2.E.4 (Senneville), avec le § 2 Historique de l'arrondissement de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé
canonical_names: One-storey horizontal house, ≤30° roof, integrated garage

siting_landscape: Detached on its own lot, set back from the street with side margins, and with parking in the front yard — the Lachine cahier's description of the same wave, and the one place any West Island source describes the siting rule rather than the building.

Cul-de-sac and crescent street patterns recur, sometimes with a planted median down a wide avenue, and Dorval's cahier ties the effect of every one of these sectors to mature trees on the properties rather than to the houses.

Built in small series from a short catalogue of models. Dorval's 7.U.5 is praised for using « un nombre relativement restreint de modèles » while letting the materials vary house to house; Lachine's 19.U.2 calls the catalogue of types on its territory « particulièrement impressionnant ». In Lachine the dominant form of that catalogue is not this one but the taller contractor's box known locally as the maison « Gameroff », which carries its own record on that page; what belongs here is the alignment of Californian-inspired bungalows the cahier singles out at the end of the 51e Avenue.
massing: One storey, plain-pied. The Dorval cahier repeats the phrase « bungalows de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique » for two separate sectors, 7.U.1 and 7.U.4, and treats it as the norm for the municipality from the 1940s–50s onward.
A hipped roof is the commonest form. Lachine records more variety in the same years — pitched, hipped, or hipped combined with a false mansard.
Split-level versions appear in the same wave and the same decade; Dorval's 7.U.5 dates a whole quadrilateral of them to the 1950s.
articulation: Almost none, and what there is varies within a single street rather than between streets. Dorval's Model Homes are described as houses that look alike until you look closely, at which point the window types, the roofs, the use of artificial stone and clapboard and the handling of the brick are all different.
openings: Not described by any West Island source beyond the note that window types differ between otherwise identical Dorval houses.
materials: Brick dominant, with artificial stone and clapboard used as accent — the three materials Dorval's cahier names on avenue Dahlia.
Red brick at Pointe-Claire's Magil project, built 1953–55.

description: « Ce petit secteur adjacent au parc Dorval, près de l'extrémité est de l'arrondissement, se caractérise par l'uniformité du bâti : bungalows de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique comme matériau dominant, garage, rue en cul-de-sac, aménagement paysager relativement simple. L'époque approximative de construction serait les années 1950. » (7.U.1)

« Cette rue résidentielle est bordée de bungalows qui se ressemblent mais qui, en y regardant de près, affichent certaines différences dans le type de fenêtres, de toiture, l'emploi de pierre artificielle et de planche à clin, ou encore dans le traitement de la brique. Ce projet qui a débuté en 1951 comprenait 28 unités de logement réparties entre 12 bungalows détachés et 16 semi-détachés; il incluait aussi les deux édifices d'appartements situés au coin du chemin du Bord-du-Lac. » (7.U.2, Dorval Model Homes – avenue Dalhia)

« Ce développement résidentiel est semblable à celui du secteur 7.U.1 – rue en cul-de-sac, bungalows similaires de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique, carport, terrain bien aménagé et présence d'arbres matures. La construction remonte approximativement aux années 1950. » (7.U.4, place Décary)
« L'ambiance de ce secteur est celle d'une banlieue de type californien des années 1950, avec ses bungalows bas intégrant un carport. » (7.U.6, avenues Claude et Allard)
« Les bâtiments de ce secteur précèdent ceux de la période des années 1940-1950, où la construction de bungalows devient la norme à Dorval. » (7.I.1)

« Ce secteur de Lakeside Heights se compose de maisonnettes d'un étage et demi et de bungalows en brique rouge construits entre 1953 et 1955. Il présente des qualités d'ensemble remarquables avec un couvert végétal à maturité et des maisons typiques des constructions d'après-guerre, peu transformées. » (5.U.2, projet Magil)

« Ce secteur est composé de maisons construites autour de 1947 sur le modèle des maisons de la Wartime Housing Limited. … Aujourd'hui, même s'il y reste bien peu de ces maisons de vétérans, le secteur continue de se démarquer par le tracé particulier des rues et le lotissement. » (5.U.3, secteur des vétérans)

« Ce vaste secteur est très homogène et regroupe une grande variété d'habitations unifamiliales détachées d'un ou deux étages construites en petites séries, implantées avec marges de recul sur les côtés et en retrait de la rue, et possédant un espace de stationnement en cour avant. Elles ont le plus souvent un plan carré ou rectangulaire, une volumétrie simple, un revêtement de brique avec éléments de décor en bois et des formes de toit variables (en pente, pavillon, ou combinaison pavillon fausse mansarde). Ces habitations sont issues de l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970. » (19.U.2, Victoria – Sir-George-Simpson)

« Notons toutefois l'intérêt particulier que présente la 51e Avenue, qui se termine, à l'intersection de la rue Sherbrooke, par un alignement de bungalows d'inspiration californienne particulièrement bien conservés. » (19.U.2)

« Bien que la plupart des édifices les plus imposants ont été construits en fonction d'une utilisation saisonnière, le secteur comprend aussi des résidences de l'après-guerre et des demeures contemporaines qui lui donnent un caractère suburbain mais qui poursuivent la tradition d'intégration du bâti au paysage. » (2.E.4, grandes propriétés de Senneville)

« On y trouve une grande variété de bungalows d'intérêt architectural (des petites séries et des exemplaires uniques) en excellente condition. La végétation mature, les grandes marges de recul avant bien paysagées des propriétés et l'absence de trottoirs contribuent à la grande homogénéité du secteur. » (2.U.2, Belvédère — in the Pierrefonds half of that arrondissement, not in Senneville)
contexte: « Le Plan d'urbanisme reconnaît l'intérêt de certains développements résidentiels d'après-guerre, qui composent une part importante du patrimoine des anciennes banlieues, en créant une catégorie appelée Ensembles urbains d'intérêt. On y retrouve, entre autres, des ensembles homogènes de bungalows, des secteurs de maisons qui adoptent le modèle développé par la Wartime Housing Limited ou des exemples des premières coopératives d'habitation. Leur repérage est exploratoire … » (the same paragraph in all twenty-seven cahiers)

« Dans les années 1950-1960, grâce à la construction de l'autoroute Métropolitaine et au boom démographique de l'après-guerre, le développement de cette banlieue essentiellement résidentielle s'accélère et l'urbanisation gagne alors le nord de la voie ferrée. Même si le caractère rural disparaît, les rues bordées d'arbres maintiennent une apparence champêtre. » (§ 2, Historique)

types.profile_note: Better evidenced than the other four shared records, and still not evidenced everywhere. The 2005 Ville de Montréal series created a category — Ensembles urbains d'intérêt — expressly to catch postwar suburban housing, and Dorval's cahier alone gives it eight sectors with real building description, so the columns here are unusually well supported for a place with no typology document. But the support is not even across the six places, and that is the thing to know before trusting this record. Dorval and Pointe-Claire are described in detail. Lachine is well described too, but most of what its sector 19.U.2 describes is the one- or two-storey contractor's box that Lachine's own page records as the maison « Gameroff »; only the Californian bungalow alignment at the 51e Avenue is unambiguously this type, and that is what is claimed here. Senneville is attested by one clause in sector 2.E.4, which records postwar houses inside the estate belt and says they continue its tradition of setting buildings into the landscape — no bungalow sector of its own is named, and the well described bungalow sector in the same cahier, 2.U.2 Belvédère, is in the Pierrefonds half of that arrondissement and not in Senneville. Baie-D'Urfé is attested only by its cahier's historique, which dates the acceleration of its suburban growth to the 1950s–60s and to the Métropolitaine, and names no postwar sector; the postwar ensembles in that cahier, 4.U.1 Devon-York with its « bâtiments de l'après-guerre … rappelant le "ranch" californien », 4.U.2 Sunny Acres and 4.U.3 Lakeview-Morgan, are introduced under a paragraph about the territory of Beaconsfield. Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue is the one membership no retrieved source attests at all: its cahier, once found, names no postwar sector and its single ensemble urbain d'intérêt, 1.U.1, is the Garden City Press ensemble of J.-J. Harpell, which is not this type. It is kept in `places` because the record is the shared West Island postwar record and because a later source may supply what this one does not, and it is flagged here rather than asserted quietly. Fields left null and why: `roofing` — no source names a roof covering anywhere in the six places; `roof.pitch_deg` — « toit pavillon » with no figure; `lot_width_m`, `setback_front_m`, `setback_side_m`, `front_yard_green_pct` — the cahiers describe setbacks, front-yard parking and landscaping at length and measure none of it; `sectors` — a shared record cannot carry sector codes that exist in only one of its places, and here they would run 7.U.x, 5.U.x, 19.U.x and 2.U.x at once. `window_proportion: horizontal` is the weakest entry in the record: it is read from the form and from the Dorval note that window types vary between otherwise identical houses, not from any stated proportion, and it should be the first field to correct. `styles: [minimal-traditional]` is a classification made here, not a style any West Island source names; the nearest a source comes is Dorval's « banlieue de type californien » and Lachine's « bungalows d'inspiration californienne ».
conservation: This is the only wave in the West Island whose recognition is explicitly experimental. The 2005 series says its own identification of these sectors « est exploratoire » and aims to link them to conservation concerns « pour une première fois ».

Where the cahiers return to it, they say the same thing twice - the value lies in the plan, the planting and the consistency of the materials rather than in any individual house, and personalisation is what erodes it. Lachine's 19.U.2 records that practically every building in its sector has been modified, and lists how: raising, building to the lot line, added upper storeys or a garage, changed cladding, changed openings, changed roof form.

Pointe-Claire's veterans' sector is the sharpest case: the cahier says few of the wartime houses are left and that what still marks the sector is the street layout and the subdivision, not the buildings.
types.source_generation: five sector-characterisation cahiers of the same 2005 series, read together; the series created a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, expressly to catch postwar suburban housing, and that category is the only per-type writing any West Island source does
types.blurb_en: One storey, hipped roof, brick with artificial stone and clapboard for variety, a carport or a garage, a cul-de-sac and mature trees. Built from a short catalogue of models across all six West Island places from the late 1940s, and the only twentieth-century housing the 2005 evaluation series took seriously enough to invent a category for.
types.origin_en: The wave arrives at different moments and for different reasons. At Dorval it is the airport: the aerodrome opened in 1941, air traffic grew fast after the war, the rest of the territory was opened to subdivision and the population went from under 3,000 in the 1940s to more than 20,000 by 1971. At Pointe-Claire it is a straight housing shortage — a veterans' sector on the Wartime Housing Limited model about 1947, then the Magil project of 1953–55. At Lachine it is what the cahier calls « l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970 », running east across the last open ground and producing a catalogue of contractors' types so consistent that the dominant one is still known locally by its builder's name. At Baie-D'Urfé it is the Métropolitaine and the demographic boom together, pushing settlement north across the railway for the first time. What the 2005 cahiers do with all of it is the interesting part. The series invented a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, to hold postwar suburbs, said openly that the exercise was exploratory, and then valued these places for their street layouts, their planting and the consistency of their materials rather than for their architecture — while recording, in the same paragraphs, that almost every house had already been raised, extended, re-clad or re-roofed. It is the one wave on these six pages that the source treats as heritage-in-progress rather than as heritage.

photo.credit: The only photographs of West Island postwar bungalows located during this research are the 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers' own — Dorval, p. 30–31, captioned « 7.U.1 165, rue McNicoll », « 7.U.2 1, avenue Dalhia », « 7.U.3 70, avenue des Lilas », « 7.U.4 Vue d'ensemble » and « 7.U.6 Avenue Claude »; Pointe-Claire, p. 34, « 5.U.2 Le 105 de l'avenue de Windward Crescent »; Lachine, p. 40, « 19.U.2 La 53e Avenue » and « 19.U.2 Une maison "Gameroff" typique au 3, 40e avenue ». © Ville de Montréal; not reproduced here. Wikimedia Commons was searched for a freely licensed photograph of a postwar bungalow in any of the six places and none was found. The one candidate that looked promising by its address — « Quatre-Vents, 12, avenue Dahlia (Dorval) », on the Model Homes street itself — was downloaded and inspected and is not a bungalow at all but a two-and-a-half-storey stuccoed house with a tiled coping and an arcaded loggia, so it was rejected. The Cité de Dorval's own heritage study of that address (LEMAYMICHAUD + Réal Paul architecte, « Expertise historique et étude patrimoniale, 12, avenue Dahlia, Dorval ») confirms the rejection and dates the house to 1803, enlarged 1874–85 in a neo-Gothic manner and wholly remade 1927–37 into the Italianate it wears now — one of the first stone houses in the district, standing on the street the bungalows were later built along, and not one of them. The same study independently repeats the cahier's figures for the 1951 project - 28 dwellings, 12 detached and 16 semi-detached bungalows, and two apartment buildings.
photo.alt: Photograph of Postwar bungalow houses in Baie-D'Urfé, from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: The radial bourg and the French-inspired farmhouse
types.source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 48
canonical_names: One-storey rural house of French inspiration, pièce-sur-pièce walls, hipped roof without eaves, no cellar

siting_landscape: Generally set without regard to the public road, its principal façade turned south for the most sunlight — the sharpest siting rule in this part, and the opposite of Île d'Orléans, where the chemin Royal governs.
The oldest dwelling type in the site. Survivors stand mainly on the ceinture, the old farm lots outside the Trait-Carré.
massing: Almost square or rectangular plan, of modest dimensions, one and a half storeys.
Barely raised off the ground, with squat proportions.
Two straight steeply pitched slopes, covered in wood shingle.
articulation: The plan lists no ornament for this type at all — the whole description is plan, roof, walls, openings and chimneys.
openings: Asymmetrically disposed; wood casement windows with small panes.
materials: Walls of pièce-sur-pièce or of stone, the stone usually rendered and whitewashed.
One or two chimney stacks emerging from the roof.

description: La maison rurale d'inspiration française est le plus ancien type d'habitation que l'on trouve sur le territoire du site patrimonial. Ce type s'est adapté aux conditions locales particulières, telles que le climat, les savoir-faire et les matériaux disponibles.
implantation: Ce type de bâtiment est généralement implanté sans égard à la voie publique et sa façade principale est orientée vers le sud pour bénéficier d'un maximum d'ensoleillement.
volumetrie: un plan presque carré ou rectangulaire. Des dimensions modestes et un volume d'un étage et demi. La maison est peu exhaussée du sol et ses proportions sont trapues
toiture: un toit à deux versants droits à forte pente, couvert en bardeaux de bois
materiaux: des murs en pièce sur pièce ou en pierre (habituellement recouverte d'un crépi et chaulée)
une ou deux souches de cheminées émergent de sa toiture
ouvertures: des ouvertures disposées de façon asymétrique. Ces fenêtres en bois sont à battants à petits carreaux

types.profile_note: Transcribed from the plan de conservation's printed p. 48. The French under each column is the plan's own wording, unedited: the five bullets of « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type » plus the two sentences of the introductory paragraph, which carry the siting rule and the type's position in the sequence. The plan supplies no ornament, no window proportion and no roof pitch in degrees for this type, so those cells stay empty rather than being filled by inference.
types.source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
types.blurb_en: The oldest house in the site and the only one that ignores the road: a low, squat, one-and-a-half storey box of pièce-sur-pièce or whitewashed rendered stone, under two straight steep slopes of wood shingle, with one or two stacks and small-paned casements set wherever the inside wanted them. Its façade faces south for the sun, whatever direction the Trait-Carré happens to run.
types.origin_en: The house of the Régime français, built on the trapezoidal farm lots the Jesuits conceded from 1665 and, under the règle du tiers, always in the first third of the lot against the Trait-Carré. The plan de conservation warns that this type is easier to see than to date: several 18th-century houses were altered so heavily that their apparent age is nothing like their real one — 8180-8182 Le Trait-Carré Est was built about 1724 and given a mansard roof in 1931 — while the maison Éphraïm-Bédard looks like a French-inspired farmhouse and was built about a century later.

photo.credit: "House in Charlesbourg, Quebec City 03" by Wilfredor, 9 February 2021, Wikimedia Commons, released CC0 (Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication) — licence read on the Commons API before download. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:House_in_Charlesbourg,_Quebec_City_03.jpg
photo.match_note: Matched on form, not on address. The photograph shows the type's diagnostic set — one and a half storeys barely raised off the ground, squat proportions, two straight steep slopes in wood shingle, gable dormers, a central stack, vertical plank cladding. The plan records that the two houses converted to cultural spaces, maison Éphraïm-Bédard and maison Pierre-Lefebvre, are the ones clad « en planches verticales », and the building in the photograph carries a cultural society's banner; which of the two it is has not been confirmed, so it is not named.
photo.alt: Photograph of Rural house of French inspiration houses in Charlesbourg (Trait-Carré), from MCC

types.phase_title: The neoclassical village and Baillairgé's church
types.source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 49
canonical_names: One-and-a-half-storey rectangular house, steep two-slope roof (straight or bell-cast), full-width gallery under the eaves, stone or wood
types.roofing: bardeaux de cèdre ou tôle traditionnelle à la canadienne ou à baguettes

siting_landscape: The type that marks the whole 19th century in the site, and the one that fills the Trait-Carré on both sides.
massing: Rectangular plan, raised off the ground to give a rudimentary cellar.
Two-slope roof with overhanging larmiers, sometimes upturned.
A summer kitchen sometimes repeats the volume of the house at reduced scale, set back against the north-east wall or perpendicular at the rear.
articulation: A gallery running along the façade, sheltered by the overhanging larmier — a transitional space between inside and out, often decorated with ornamental woodwork.
Openings framed by moulded wood chambranles.
openings: Many wood casement windows with large panes, rectangular and vertically proportioned, usually set symmetrically about the door at the centre of the façade.
materials: Pièce-sur-pièce or madrier-sur-madrier structure.
Vertical or horizontal plank cladding, or fieldstone rendered and whitewashed. In wood or in masonry alike, these houses are white.

description: Après la Conquête, les Britanniques introduisent de nouveaux savoir-faire qui, couplés à l'évolution des techniques de construction et des manières d'habiter, favorisent l'émergence d'un nouveau type architectural qui marque tout le XIXe siècle : la maison québécoise d'inspiration néoclassique. Ce type reprend certaines caractéristiques du modèle français, dont le plan rectangulaire et le toit à versants.
volumetrie: un plan rectangulaire surélevé du sol afin d'aménager une cave rudimentaire
toiture: un toit à deux versants à larmiers débordants, parfois recourbés, couvert de bardeaux de cèdre ou de tôle traditionnelle à la canadienne ou à baguettes
saillies: une galerie longeant la façade, protégée par le larmier débordant du toit, espace de transition entre l'intérieur et l'extérieur, souvent décorée de boiseries ornementales
une cuisine d'été reprenant parfois le volume de la maison à une échelle réduite, généralement implantée en recul contre le mur nord-est ou perpendiculairement à l'arrière
materiaux: une structure construite en pièce sur pièce ou en madrier sur madrier
un parement de planches verticales ou horizontales, ou en maçonnerie de pierres des champs recouverte d'un crépi et chaulée. En bois ou en maçonnerie, ces maisons sont de couleur blanche
ouvertures: de nombreuses fenêtres en bois à battants à grands carreaux, de forme rectangulaire aux proportions verticales. Ces fenêtres sont souvent disposées symétriquement autour de la porte occupant le centre de la façade. Les ouvertures sont encadrées de chambranles moulurés en bois

types.profile_note: Transcribed from the plan de conservation's printed p. 49. The seven bullets of « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type » are split across the columns: plan and roof make up massing, the gallery and the summer kitchen sit under saillies, structure and cladding are materials, and the ornamental woodwork of the gallery and the moulded chambranles are the only ornament the plan names, so they carry articulation. The plan gives no storey count and no roof pitch for this type. The colour statement is unusual and worth keeping verbatim: the plan does not say these houses are often white, it says they are white.
types.source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
types.blurb_en: The 19th-century village house, and the one the Trait-Carré is mostly made of: a rectangular white box raised just enough for a rough cellar, with the roof's larmiers reaching out past the wall — often curving up as they go — to shelter a gallery running the whole width of the façade. Large-paned casements sit symmetrically either side of a central door in moulded frames, and a summer kitchen often repeats the house in miniature at the back.
types.origin_en: The plan makes it an explicitly post-Conquest form: British know-how, changing construction technique and changing ways of living produce a new type that "marque tout le XIXe siècle", while keeping the rectangular plan and the sloped roof of the French model. It is the same house Saint-Lambert, Terrebonne, Lévis, Québec City and Île d'Orléans each catalogue under their own names, and the Charlesbourg description is the one that insists on the colour.

photo.credit: "Old house in Charlesbourg" by Wilfredor, 10 February 2021, Wikimedia Commons, released CC0 (Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication) — licence read on the Commons API before download. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Old_house_in_Charlesbourg.jpg
photo.match_note: Matched on form, not on address. White walls, a two-slope roof whose larmier overhangs and turns up over a gallery running the length of the façade, turned posts, a balustrade and bracket woodwork, an end stack, and a long low rear extension in the position the plan describes for the cuisine d'été.
photo.alt: Photograph of Québec house of neoclassical inspiration houses in Charlesbourg (Trait-Carré), from MCC

types.phase_title: Mansards and the institutional build-out
types.source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), pp. 49–50
canonical_names: Two-storey house under a two- or four-slope mansard roof, dormers in the brisis, wood gallery under its own awning
types.roofing: as the neoclassical type — cedar shingle or traditional tin

siting_landscape: Appears in the last quarter of the 19th century, and the plan's statistics show how far it spread — 27 of the site's 138 principal buildings, about 19 %, carry a mansard roof.
Its earliest examples here favour the four-slope mansard, as on the former couvent des Soeurs du Bon-Pasteur; the two-slope version is used more from the turn of the 20th century.
massing: Rectangular plan, tending to lengthen relative to the individual houses of the preceding types.
A mansard roof of gently pitched terrasson over a nearly vertical brisis, generally of two slopes, with four-slope and hipped variants.
articulation: Sometimes elaborate ornament — decorative woodwork on galleries, on dormers and around the openings.
openings: Symmetrically disposed, sometimes arched, of vertical proportion; often wood casements with large panes.
materials: Made of the same materials as the Québec house of neoclassical inspiration.

description: Dans le dernier quart du XIXe siècle, un nouveau type de maison fait son apparition dans les paysages traditionnels, soit la maison mansardée issue du style Second Empire. Cette architecture trouve sa source dans l'architecture monumentale développée à Paris sous le règne de Napoléon III et qui réintroduit une forme de toit associée à la période classique française. D'abord réservé à l'architecture monumentale – bâtiments institutionnels et maisons bourgeoises –, le style Second Empire est ensuite popularisé dans l'architecture des couvents et des presbytères puis, rapidement, dans l'architecture domestique du milieu rural québécois. Le toit mansardé constitue la principale caractéristique de la maison mansardée ainsi que son plus grand avantage.
volumetrie: un plan rectangulaire qui tend à s'allonger par rapport aux maisons individuelles des types précédents
toiture: un toit mansardé constitué d'un terrasson à pente douce et d'un brisis presque vertical. Ce toit est généralement à deux versants, mais il existe des variantes à quatre versants ou à croupes
materiaux: Elle est faite des mêmes matériaux que la maison québécoise d'inspiration néoclassique.
ouvertures: des ouvertures disposées symétriquement, parfois cintrées, aux proportions verticales. Ces fenêtres en bois sont souvent à battants à grands carreaux
ornementation: une ornementation parfois élaborée, constituée notamment de boiseries décoratives sur les galeries, les lucarnes et autour des ouvertures

types.profile_note: Transcribed from the plan de conservation's printed pp. 49–50. Materials are not itemised for this type: the plan simply refers them back to the neoclassical house, and the cladding list here repeats that record's rather than inventing one. The plan gives no storey count and no pitch. The siting column carries the plan's own built-fabric statistics for mansard roofs from printed pp. 45–46, which are counts for the whole site rather than for this residential type alone.
types.source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
types.blurb_en: A rectangular plan that stretches longer than the houses before it, under a roof of gentle terrasson over an almost vertical brisis — two slopes usually, four or hipped sometimes. Symmetrical, vertically proportioned openings, occasionally arched, and ornament that can turn elaborate: decorative woodwork on the galleries, on the dormers and round the windows. Its materials are simply those of the neoclassical house it succeeds.
types.origin_en: The plan traces the route explicitly: monumental Paris under Napoleon III, reintroducing a roof form of the French classical period; then Québec's institutional buildings and bourgeois houses; then convents and presbyteries; then, quickly, rural domestic architecture. Charlesbourg shows the whole chain in one place — the presbytery of 1875, the convent of 1883 and the sacristy of 1887 are all Second Empire, and the houses follow. The plan is also candid that some mansards here are retro-fits: a few old houses got one to make the attic habitable.

photo.match_note: Matched on form, not on address, though the civic number 7960 is legible on the façade. It carries the plan's description almost item for item: a two-slope mansard of gently pitched terrasson over a near-vertical brisis, here in traditional tin; two dormers set in the brisis; symmetrical, vertically proportioned openings; and decorative woodwork on the gallery and around the dormers, which is the "ornementation parfois élaborée" the plan names.

types.phase_title: Vernaculaire industriel
types.source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 51
canonical_names: Boomtown house or shop-house, balloon frame, flat or low-pitch roof behind a raised crown
types.style_label: Boomtown (false front) / Vernaculaire industriel (Québec industrial vernacular)

siting_landscape: Flat roofs account for 31 of the site's 138 principal buildings, about 22 %, and the plan says most of them date from the 20th century.
The oldest flat roof in the site is not a house at all but a former forge at 7821 Le Trait-Carré Est, built between 1863 and 1886.
massing: Distinguished by its flat or low-pitched roof, concealed behind a parapet.
articulation: Inherited from the parent type — standardised architectural elements, doors and windows. The parapet is the type's defining articulation.
openings: Rectangular openings of vertical proportion; wood windows, casement or sash.
materials: Machined materials; the parent type's beams, boards and asbestos-cement tile.

sous_variantes: le bâtiment « Boomtown » se distingue par son toit plat ou à faible pente dissimulé derrière un parapet

types.profile_note: The sub-variant bullet is transcribed verbatim from printed p. 51 and is a single line — the shortest type definition in this part. The volumetrie, ouvertures and materiaux entries are the parent type's shared bullets, repeated so the child record stands on its own. The siting column carries the plan's flat-roof statistics from printed p. 45, which count the whole site rather than this sub-variant alone. The plan also notes that the salle Pierre-Garon of 1925, an institutional building, carries a parapet « évoquant l'architecture "Boomtown" » — the vocabulary travelling from the shopfront to the parish hall.

types.blurb_en: One line in the plan and nothing more: a flat or barely sloping roof hidden behind a parapet. It is the shopkeeper's end of the industrial vernacular, and at Charlesbourg it belongs with the fourteen buildings that put a shop on the ground floor and a dwelling above it.
types.origin_en: Boomtown is now the most widely distributed form on this site, catalogued at Saint-Lambert, Gatineau, Québec City, Trois-Rivières, Lévis, Île d'Orléans and here. Charlesbourg is the case where it is filed as a sub-variant rather than a type, and where the plan shows the parapet jumping category: the salle paroissiale of 1925, now the salle Pierre-Garon, borrows it for a parish hall.

Low-pitched pavilion roof, sometimes with a dormer on the front slope.

types.blurb_en: A square plan two storeys high under a shallow pavilion roof, sometimes with a single dormer on the front slope, clad in horizontal boards or brick. The plan gives it three lines and no more — which is itself the point: the whole appeal of the industrial vernacular was that it needed no more than three lines to describe.
types.origin_en: The same American Foursquare that Saint-Lambert, Gatineau, Québec City, Trois-Rivières, Lévis and Île d'Orléans all catalogue. What differs at Charlesbourg is its rank: here it is a sub-variant inside the maison vernaculaire industrielle rather than a courant of its own, and the plan's built-fabric survey confirms it arrived with the century, putting most of the site's pavilion roofs on two-storey cubic houses of the first decades of the 20th century.

types.phase_title: Vernaculaire industriel
types.source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), pp. 50–51
canonical_names: Maison vernaculaire industrielle (group — cubique, cottage vernaculaire, Boomtown)

siting_landscape: From the end of the 19th century until the Second World War, this is the type that dominates new building in the site — the plan's words are "le type qui domine les nouvelles constructions".
massing: A simplified volume. A light frame, also called "Balloon Frame".
Suits the single-family dwelling but can also hold two.
articulation: Standardised architectural elements, such as doors and windows.
openings: Rectangular openings of vertical proportion; wood windows, casement or sash.
materials: Machined materials — beams and boards. New materials appearing at the start of the 20th century, such as asbestos-cement tile.

description: De la fin du XIXe siècle jusqu'à la Seconde Guerre mondiale, l'architecture vernaculaire industrielle est le type qui domine les nouvelles constructions érigées dans le site patrimonial. Les phénomènes de la standardisation des matériaux, de la mécanisation du travail et de la diffusion à grande échelle de plans au moyen de catalogues et de revues à travers l'Amérique du Nord ont donné naissance à cette architecture aux États-Unis. Elle est ensuite introduite au Canada et devient populaire grâce à la simplicité et au faible coût de sa construction. La maison vernaculaire se décline en de multiples variantes adaptées à des besoins spécifiques. Elle convient à l'habitation unifamiliale, mais peut aussi abriter deux logements. Elle comprend, notamment, la maison cubique (ou « Four Square »), le cottage vernaculaire et les bâtiments de type « Boomtown ».
volumetrie: un volume simplifié. Une charpente claire, aussi appelée « Balloon Frame »
materiaux: des matériaux usinés, tels que les poutres et les planches. Des nouveaux matériaux faisant leur apparition au début du XXe siècle, comme la tuile d'amiante-ciment. Des éléments architecturaux standardisés, tels que les portes et les fenêtres
ouvertures: des ouvertures de forme rectangulaire aux proportions verticales. Ces fenêtres en bois sont à battants ou à guillotine
sous_variantes: la maison cubique se distingue par un plan carré à deux étages. Sur son toit en pavillon à faible pente, on trouve parfois une lucarne sur le versant avant. Son parement est souvent en planches horizontales ou en brique

le cottage vernaculaire se compare à la maison québécoise d'inspiration néoclassique par sa forme générale, mais son avant-toit diffère par le larmier sans coyaux et sa pente légèrement plus faible. Il existe une variante où la façade est aménagée sur le mur pignon

types.profile_note: Transcribed from the plan de conservation's printed pp. 50–51. This is a parent record: the plan sets out three shared characteristics for the type as a whole and then three further bullets, each defining one sub-variant, and those three are reproduced here in full under Sous-variantes and again on the child records. The roof form and storey count are deliberately null on the parent, because the plan gives a different roof to each child — pavilion for the cubique, gabled for the cottage vernaculaire, flat behind a parapet for the Boomtown. This nesting is the plan's own reading; the Île d'Orléans inventory and the Lévis catalogue treat the same three forms as three top-level courants instead, which is why the canonical layer carries both.
types.source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim. The last three bullets each define one sub-variant and are carried on the three child records.
types.blurb_en: The type that took over. From the 1890s to the Second World War it is what got built here: a simplified volume on a balloon frame, machined beams and boards, catalogue doors and windows, asbestos-cement tile, rectangular vertically proportioned casements or sashes — cheap, simple and adaptable enough to hold one household or two. The plan then splits it three ways: cubique, cottage vernaculaire, Boomtown.
types.origin_en: Standardised materials, mechanised labour and plans distributed at continental scale through catalogues and magazines produced this architecture in the United States; it came to Canada and spread on the strength of how simple and cheap it was to build. Charlesbourg's plan de conservation is one of the two Québec sources on this site that treat the three forms as one family with a parent — the Ville de Québec thésaurus is the other — while the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans and the Ville de Lévis list them as separate courants of equal rank. Nothing in the buildings changes; the disagreement is entirely about the level of the category.

types.phase_title: Vernaculaire industriel
types.source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 51
canonical_names: Industrial-vernacular cottage, 1½–2½ storeys, rectangular/L/T plan, straight two-slope roof

siting_landscape: Reads at a glance as the traditional Québec house it stands beside on the Trait-Carré; the difference is in the eave.
massing: Compares to the Québec house of neoclassical inspiration in its general form.
But its eave differs — the larmier has no coyaux, and its pitch is slightly shallower.
A variant sets the façade on the gable wall.
articulation: Inherited from the parent type — standardised architectural elements, doors and windows.
openings: Rectangular openings of vertical proportion; wood windows, casement or sash.
materials: Machined materials; the parent type's beams, boards and asbestos-cement tile.

sous_variantes: le cottage vernaculaire se compare à la maison québécoise d'inspiration néoclassique par sa forme générale, mais son avant-toit diffère par le larmier sans coyaux et sa pente légèrement plus faible. Il existe une variante où la façade est aménagée sur le mur pignon
volumetrie: un volume simplifié. Une charpente claire, aussi appelée « Balloon Frame »
ouvertures: des ouvertures de forme rectangulaire aux proportions verticales. Ces fenêtres en bois sont à battants ou à guillotine
materiaux: des matériaux usinés, tels que les poutres et les planches. Des nouveaux matériaux faisant leur apparition au début du XXe siècle, comme la tuile d'amiante-ciment. Des éléments architecturaux standardisés, tels que les portes et les fenêtres

types.profile_note: The sub-variant bullet is transcribed verbatim and in full from printed p. 51, because it is the clearest published statement anywhere in the sources this site draws on of how the industrial vernacular differs from the traditional type it imitates. The distinction turns on one word: a coyau is the short piece fixed at the foot of a rafter that lifts and curves the eave outward, producing the larmier retroussé of the traditional Québec roof. The cottage vernaculaire keeps the silhouette and drops the coyau, so the eave runs straight out instead of flaring — and the pitch slackens slightly with it. The plan's own built-fabric survey gives the arithmetic of that distinction across the site: of 56 two-slope roofs, 26 have larmiers retroussés and 30 do not. The volumetrie, ouvertures and materiaux entries are the parent type's shared bullets, repeated so the child record stands on its own.
types.source_generation: Plan de conservation, the sub-variant bullet inside « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type » for the maison vernaculaire industrielle, transcribed verbatim
types.blurb_en: The industrial vernacular wearing the traditional house's clothes. In general form it is the Québec house of neoclassical inspiration; what gives it away is the eave, where the larmier runs out straight because there is no coyau under it, on a pitch that is slightly shallower. One variant turns the façade onto the gable wall.
types.origin_en: The plan's sentence on this form is the most useful in the whole part, because it is the only place in these sources where a document says plainly what separates a mass-produced house from the handbuilt one it copies — and the answer is a single missing piece of carpentry. The coyau is fiddly work; the balloon frame and the catalogue plan dispensed with it. This is the same form the Île d'Orléans inventory calls the cottage vernaculaire américain, Lévis calls the vernaculaire américain, and Québec City catalogues as the cottage vernaculaire industriel.

types.phase_title: Suburbanisation, cité, merger
types.source_ref: MCC, Plan de conservation du site patrimonial de Charlesbourg (2016), p. 51
canonical_names: One-storey horizontal house, ≤30° roof, integrated garage

siting_landscape: Arrives at the turn of the 1950s, when sprawl subdivides the farm lots and bungalows go up across the site.

The plan counts 26 buildings of one storey, "majoritairement des bungalows érigés après la Deuxième Guerre mondiale", and 15 buildings clad in the non-traditional brick-and-artificial-stone combination, "principalement des bungalows".
massing: Rectangular or rather square plan.
Generally one storey.
Low-profile pavilion roof, or hipped.
articulation: The plan names no ornament for this type.
openings: The plan gives no opening description for this type.
materials: Mixed cladding of brick and artificial stone.

description: Au tournant des années 1950, l'étalement urbain amène le lotissement de plusieurs terres agricoles et la construction de bungalows à travers le site patrimonial de Charlesbourg.
volumetrie: un plan rectangulaire ou plutôt carré
un volume généralement d'un étage
toiture: un toit à pavillon à profil bas ou à croupes
materiaux: un parement mixte en brique et en pierre artificielle

types.profile_note: Transcribed from the plan de conservation's printed p. 51. This is the shortest of the five type descriptions — four bullets, covering plan, volume, roof and cladding only. The plan supplies no openings and no ornament for it, and those cells are left saying so rather than being filled from the general literature on the Québec bungalow. The siting column carries the plan's own built-fabric counts from printed pp. 45–46, which are counts for the whole site.
types.source_generation: Plan de conservation narrative typology, the paragraph plus the bulleted list headed « Voici les principales caractéristiques de ce type », transcribed verbatim
types.blurb_en: A rectangular or nearly square plan, one storey, a low pavilion or hipped roof, and brick mixed with artificial stone. Four lines is all the plan gives it — and yet more than a third of everything standing inside this declared site went up between 1925 and 1975.
types.origin_en: The bungalow is what the declaration of 1965 was reacting to. Sprawl reached Charlesbourg at the turn of the 1950s and cut up the farm lots; the plan records that 65 buildings, 48.5 % of the site, date from 1925–1975, and that most of the site's 26 single-storey buildings are post-war bungalows. The 2005 Étude de caractérisation makes the same point from the other side: by 1963 urban sprawl had already reached the ceinture, much of the agricultural heritage had gone, and the perimeter drawn in 1965 enclosed "le produit (la zone d'occupation villageoise) plutôt que la source (ce qu'il restait des terres agricoles à l'origine du village)".
