Casement windows with large panes, casement with transom, or sash.
materials: Wood-plank or brick cladding.
Few projections beyond a gallery under an awning, sometimes with a balcony above on the central third.

elements_caracteristiques: Volume cubique ou rectangulaire de deux étages, peu dégagé du sol
Toiture plate ou à faible pente vers l’arrière
Saillies peu présentes à l’exception d’une galerie protégée d’un auvent, parfois avec un balcon à l’étage
Parement de planches de bois ou de brique
Distribution régulière des ouvertures, composition généralement symétrique
Fenêtres à battants à grands carreaux, à battants avec imposte ou à guillotine

Ornementation concentrée dans la partie supérieure de la façade : corniche à modillons ou à consoles, parapet en gradins ou jeux de briques. Autres éléments d’ornementation discrets : chambranles, planches cornières, platebandes en brique, etc.
repartition: Sur le territoire du site patrimonial de l'Île-d'Orléans, on retrouve quelques exemplaires de maisons Boomtown dans toutes les municipalités.

types.source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
types.blurb_en: A flat-topped two-storey box that spends all its ornament in one place — the top of the front wall, where a bracketed cornice or a stepped parapet makes the building look taller and squarer than it is. Everything below that is plain boards or brick and a gallery.
types.origin_en: The balloon frame, "qualifiée d'American Boomtown", arrived with the fast growth of American cities and spread especially after the economic crisis of 1870 as a cheap, quick way to build in boom towns. In Québec it coexists with the traditional and mansard houses before supplanting them at the turn of the 20th century. On this island it never supplanted anything, but there are examples in all six municipalities.

photo.credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 41 — six captioned examples, including stepped-parapet houses at 504 and 1913 chemin Royal and a shop-house at 148 chemin du Bout-de-l'Île. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.
photo.alt: Photograph of Boomtown house houses in Île d'Orléans, from MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch

types.phase_title: Catalogue types — vernaculaire américain, cubique, Boomtown, Arts and Crafts
types.source_ref: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 38
canonical_names: Two-storey square or rectangular block under a pyramidal or hipped roof, brick, gallery or porch

siting_landscape: "La maison cubique est assez peu représentée dans le site patrimonial de l'Île-d'Orléans."
A rural echo of an urban phenomenon: standardisation drove growth in the towns first, "ce phénomène se répercutera ensuite dans les milieux ruraux".
massing: Cubic volume on a square plan of two full storeys, raised slightly off the ground.
Low-pitch pavilion (four-slope) roof, sometimes flat; usually a dormer on the front slope.
articulation: "Ornementation variable selon le statut social du propriétaire" — the one type whose decoration the inventory ties explicitly to the owner's standing.
Picturesque influences show up on some models: aisseliers, ornamental woodwork, cornices.
openings: Regular distribution of openings.
Casement windows with large panes, casement with transom, or sash; hipped, gable, triangular or lean-to dormers, sometimes replaced by gables.
materials: Brick, or light cladding: wood boards, cedar shingle, embossed tin, asbestos-cement tile.
Gallery under an independent awning across the front, sometimes with a balcony above.

elements_caracteristiques: Volumétrie cubique, plan carré de deux étages légèrement surhaussé du sol
Toit en pavillon (quatre versants) à faibles pentes, revêtu de tôle traditionnelle, ou parfois toit plat
Revêtement extérieur en brique ou en matériau léger (planches de bois, bardeaux de cèdre, tôle embossée, tuiles d’amiante-ciment)
Galerie couverte d’un auvent indépendant, aménagée en façade avant avec parfois un balcon à l’étage
Distribution régulière des ouvertures
Fenêtres à battants à grands carreaux, à battants avec imposte ou à guillotine
Lucarnes à croupe, à pignon, triangulaire ou en appentis, parfois remplacées par des pignons
Ornementation variable selon le statut social du propriétaire.
repartition: La maison cubique est assez peu représentée dans le site patrimonial de l’Île-d’Orléans.

types.source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
types.blurb_en: Two entire floors under a shallow pavilion roof, on a square plan — a shape whose whole point is interior volume. The inventory says as much: its interest "réside dans les dimensions de son espace habitable", giving an ordinary family the room of a bourgeois house. How much ornament it carries depended on who was paying.
types.origin_en: An American model, "conçu par l'architecte Frank Kidder en 1891" and commonly called the Four Square house, spread through catalogues and trade journals across North America. It reached Québec's towns on the back of cheap standardised materials and falling construction costs, then reached the countryside. On Île d'Orléans it stayed rare.

photo.credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 39 — six captioned examples at Saint-Pierre, Saint-François, Saint-Jean and Sainte-Famille, including a brick example at 1634 chemin Royal. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.
photo.alt: Photograph of Cubic house (Four Square) houses in Île d'Orléans, from MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch

types.phase_title: The bridge, régionalisme and modernisme
types.source_ref: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 46
canonical_names: Detached modern house — free plan, flat or sculptural roof, ribbon or large glazed openings

siting_landscape: "À l'île d'Orléans, nous n'avons répertorié qu'une résidence issue de l'architecture moderne." One house, out of 659.
The inventory names it: the maison Paul-Brunet, 37 chemin de l'Église, "témoigne de l'architecture moderne. Son architecture s'inspire notamment d'un paquebot."
massing: Simple volume, stripped of ornament.
Free plans producing very varied forms.
Flat roofs, or roofs of sculptural form.
articulation: No applied ornament: "l'expressivité des matériaux remplace les éléments d'ornementation".
openings: Large glazed surfaces, including horizontal ribbon windows.
materials: Modern materials — concrete and steel.

elements_caracteristiques: Volumétrie simple et dépouillée d’ornements
Plans libres qui créent des formes très variées
Toits plats ou de formes sculpturales
Matériaux modernes tels que le béton et l’acier, alors que l’expressivité des matériaux remplace les éléments d’ornementation.
Grandes surfaces vitrées dont des fenêtres en bandeau horizontal
repartition: À l’île d’Orléans, nous n’avons répertorié qu’une résidence issue de l’architecture moderne.

types.profile_note: The one courant of the eleven with a known population of exactly one: the synthesis states « À l'île d'Orléans, nous n'avons répertorié qu'une résidence issue de l'architecture moderne. » The English columns above translate the five bullets on p. 46; there is no five-column table behind them beyond that. The brief provisionally filed this courant under the postwar slab-and-tower form pending the parse; the parse rules that out, since the island's single example is a detached house. It carries the detached modern house form instead, added for it and for the other single-family modern records that had been filed under the slab.
types.source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
types.blurb_en: The island's single modern house. The courant is a real one — free plan, flat or sculptural roof, concrete and steel, ribbon glazing, no ornament at all because the materials are the ornament — but on Île d'Orléans the inventory found exactly one example of it, and even that one is a ship: the maison Paul-Brunet at 37 chemin de l'Église, modelled on an ocean liner.
types.origin_en: Born of the European modern movement (Art nouveau, the Bauhaus) and American rationalism (the Chicago School), modernism breaks with inherited form more completely than any style before it — practical and functionalist, sober, refusing ornament, and putting aluminium, concrete, steel and large sheets of glass at the front of the design. It divides into several currents more or less faithful to the movement that produced them. Almost none of that reached this island.

photo.credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 46 — one captioned example, printed inline below the characteristics list: the maison Paul-Brunet at 37 chemin de l'Église. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.
photo.alt: Photograph of Modernism houses in Île d'Orléans, from MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch

types.phase_title: The bridge, régionalisme and modernisme
types.source_ref: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 44
canonical_names: Régionalisme québécois house — a 1910–1945 revival of French-regime and Norman rural forms, steep shingled roof, fire-break gable walls

siting_landscape: "On ne retrouve que quelques cas de régionalisme québécois dans l'inventaire, surtout situé à Sainte-Pétronille, car cette architecture s'allie bien à celle de la villégiature."
The inventory warns that these houses are easy to misdate: "ces maisons peuvent souvent se confondre avec des constructions plus anciennes vue l'intention de les imiter".
massing: Rectangular volume, more or less imposing, with annexes.
High pitched roof, its slopes generally straight or slightly upturned, covered in wood or asphalt shingle.
articulation: Ornament often limited to the frames of the openings: chambranles, faux volets.
Sheltered outdoor spaces — perrons, galleries.
openings: Sash or casement windows with small panes, and generously sized gable dormers.
materials: Wood cladding — shingle or boards — or asbestos-cement.
Chimneys of massive appearance.

elements_caracteristiques: Volume rectangulaire plus ou moins imposant pourvu d’annexes
Haute toiture en pente aux versants généralement droits ou légèrement recourbés recouverts de bardeau de bois ou d’asphalte
Espaces extérieurs protégés (perrons, galeries)
Cheminées à l’aspect massif
Revêtement de bois (bardeaux ou planches) ou d’amiante-ciment
Fenêtres à guillotine ou à battants munies de carreaux et lucarnes à pignon de bonnes dimensions
Ornements souvent limités aux encadrements d’ouvertures (chambranles, faux volets).
repartition: On ne retrouve que quelques cas de régionalisme québécois dans l’inventaire, surtout situé à Sainte-Pétronille, car cette architecture s’allie bien à celle de la villégiature.

types.source_generation: Patri-Arch inventory synthesis (cover Août 2014, fieldwork 2013–14, reissued 2025 as …maj2025.pdf), "Principaux éléments caractéristiques"
types.blurb_en: A 1930s house built to look like a 1730s one. Québec's own version of Arts and Crafts went back to the buildings of the French regime for its vocabulary — high shingled roof, fire-break gable walls, stone or stucco standing in for lime — and copied them as faithfully as it could. On this island the results sit among the resort houses at Sainte-Pétronille, and the inventory dates the individual examples: 1939, 1940, 1944, 1945.
types.origin_en: "Le Québec possède une version du courant Arts and Crafts qui lui est propre, soit le régionalisme québécois", running from 1910 to the end of the Second World War. It began in the research of the McGill architecture professors Percy Erskine Nobbs and Ramsay Traquair, who wanted an authentically regional style, and spread through their students. It fed on the identity politics of the 1920s onward, which glorified New France, and found fertile ground under Duplessis; Gérard Morisset, the abbé Jean-Thomas Nadeau and Marius Barbeau argued for the same rediscovery of tradition.

photo.credit: MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch, rapport de synthèse, p. 45 — six captioned and dated examples — 1939, c. 1940, 1940, 1944 and 1945 — four of them at Sainte-Pétronille. © Patri-Arch; rights ceded to the MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans. Not reproduced here.
photo.alt: Photograph of Québec regionalism houses in Île d'Orléans, from MRC de L'Île-d'Orléans / Patri-Arch

types.phase_title: Seigneurial côtes and the fur-trade posts
types.name_en: Stone house of the French tradition
types.name_fr: La maison de pierre de tradition française
types.source_ref: Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec, fiches 93274 (site patrimonial Le Ber-Le Moyne, Lachine), 93440 (maison Rangé-dit-Laviolette, Baie-D'Urfé) et 92796 (maison Hyacinthe-Jamme-dit-Carrière, Pointe-Claire); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissements de Lachine, de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé et de Pointe-Claire (2005)
canonical_names: Urban stone house of French inspiration, one or two levels plus attic, two-slope roof, chimneys in fire-break party walls
types.roofing: cedar shingle at Le Ber-Le Moyne; ribbed copper sheet at Pointe-Claire today, over an original wood shingle

siting_landscape: Each of the three survivors sits on ground that predates the street grid around it. Le Ber-Le Moyne stands on a raised point of land beside lac Saint-Louis at the head of the Lachine rapids, on a slight mound planted with mature trees.

The Baie-D'Urfé house stands at the back of its lot, about a hundred metres from the public road and close to the shore, its main front turned south to the lake and the îles Sainte-Geneviève — RPCQ reads that orientation as evidence that the chemin du Roy once ran between the house and the water.

Pointe-Claire's house stands at the far end of a large treed lot that now isolates it from the postwar subdivision around it, on a censive conceded by the Sulpicians in 1722 along the côte Saint-Jean.
massing: A low stone carré on a near-square or short rectangular plan, one and a half storeys, sitting close to the ground. The Baie-D'Urfé carré measures 9.4 by 9.3 m.

Steep two-slope roof with straight slopes. Eaves are shallow at Lachine, and carried out over a covered gallery at Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire — in both cases a nineteenth-century alteration, not an original feature.
Ancillary buildings belong to the type where they survive - Lachine keeps a stone dépendance of the same date, and an 1781 census records a house, a barn and a stable at Baie-D'Urfé.
articulation: Almost none in the original fabric. What ornament these houses carry — moulded wood chambranles, gable dormers, a neo-Gothic porch, a bell-cast eave — was added between about 1828 and 1874 to bring them up to date.
openings: Openings set out asymmetrically, which RPCQ names as a French-tradition trait at both Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire.
Casement windows with small panes. At Pointe-Claire the south front is opened up for light while the north wall carries only two windows.
materials: Fieldstone throughout, laid up rubble. Pointe-Claire is left bare, and RPCQ names the absence of crépi as a Montréal-region trait; Baie-D'Urfé is whitewashed on three sides.
Two chimney stacks carried up in the line of the gable walls — the trait RPCQ singles out as belonging "plus particulièrement" to the houses of the island of Montréal and its neighbouring regions.

description: « Les deux bâtiments en pierre de plan rectangulaire s'élèvent sur un étage et sont coiffés d'un toit aigu à deux versants droits aux larmiers peu saillants. »
« Fenêtre(s) : Rectangulaire, À battants, à petits carreaux »

« La partie la plus ancienne présente un plan presque carré, comporte des murs en pierre chaulés sur trois côtés et s'élève sur un étage et demi. Elle est couverte d'un toit à deux versants droits aux larmiers débordants couvrant une galerie du côté sud. Deux cheminées s'élèvent dans la continuité des murs pignon. »

« Construite au tournant du XVIIIe siècle, la maison possède des éléments qui se rattachent à la tradition architecturale d'inspiration française, comme le carré en pierre peu dégagé du sol et la disposition asymétrique des ouvertures. Le plan presque carré et les cheminées qui s'élèvent dans la continuité des murs pignon, plus particulièrement associés aux maisons de l'île de Montréal et des régions environnantes, sont aussi des caractéristiques de l'architecture de cette époque. »
contexte: « La maison LeBer-LeMoyne, dont l'importance patrimoniale est exceptionnelle, a été reconnue par un classement en vertu de la Loi sur les biens culturels en 2001. Elle date du Régime français et est l'une des plus anciennes au Canada. Avec son site, elle rappelle la vocation agricole et commerciale des débuts de Lachine. » (Lachine, 19.E.4)

« Le chemin du Lakeshore regroupe la plus grande densité de bâtiments d'intérêt patrimonial de l'arrondissement. Son parcours comprend d'anciennes maisons de ferme, des maisons bourgeoises et des villas d'été de la fin du XIXe siècle et du début du XXe siècle qui nous sont parvenues avec des degrés d'authenticité divers. » (Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé, 4.I.1)

« … le moulin banal (1709-1710), classé bien archéologique en 1983, la maison Hyacinthe-Jamme dit Carrière (vers 1780), classée monument historique en 1964 par le ministère des Affaires culturelles, ainsi que d'autres maisons des XVIIIe et XIXe siècles. » (Pointe-Claire, 3.1)
elements_caracteristiques: « Elle illustre ce type par son corps de logis bas en pierre, son élévation d'un étage et demi, son toit aigu à deux versants, ses deux cheminées logées dans les murs pignons, ses ouvertures disposées de manière asymétrique et ses fenêtres à battants à petits carreaux. »
« Le plan presque carré et l'absence de crépi sont des éléments fréquemment associés à la maison d'inspiration française de la région de Montréal. »
« Elle est l'une des rares maisons de ferme datant de la fin du XVIIIe siècle à subsister à l'intérieur des terres de Pointe-Claire. »

types.profile_note: A thin record by design, and honest about it. None of the six West Island places has a per-type typology document — no inventory, no thesaurus, no per-type table — so this record is built from the three individual houses that do carry statutory records, plus the three 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers, which characterise sectors and not building types. What that leaves empty: `window_proportion` is null because all three RPCQ fiches describe the windows as casements with small panes and none gives a proportion; `roof.pitch_deg` is null because the fiches say "aigu" and "à pente moyenne" and never a figure; `lot_width_m`, `setback_front_m`, `setback_side_m` and `front_yard_green_pct` are null because no source measures a lot or a setback anywhere in the West Island; `sectors` is null because a shared record cannot carry sector codes that exist in only one of its places. `storeys` is entered as 1.5 from the RPCQ "Nombre d'étages" field, which reads 1½ for all three — note that the Le Ber-Le Moyne description text contradicts its own data field, saying the buildings "s'élèvent sur un étage". The canonical is `french-urban-house-stone` rather than `french-rural-house-1st-hip` even though all three are farm or trading-post houses in open country: the discriminant in this vocabulary is fabric and roof, not siting, and all three are stone under a straight two-slope roof with stacks in the gable walls, where the rural canonical is pièce-sur-pièce timber under a hip carried to the wall head with no cellar. RPCQ says as much itself, calling the nearby Sainte-Anne example « la maison rurale d'inspiration urbaine, fréquente dans la région de Montréal et les régions avoisinantes ». The phase is p1 and marked provisional: Lachine's house is 1669–71 and Baie-D'Urfé's about 1700, both inside p1, but Pointe-Claire's classed survivor was built between 1769 and 1791, inside p2 — RPCQ states plainly that this building tradition « se poursuit au-delà de la Conquête (1760) », so the type is filed at its origin and the reader is told the fabric outlives it.
conservation: All three houses are protected individually, and none of the three village or shore ensembles around them is. Lachine's is a classed site patrimonial (2001) covering the exteriors and the land; Pointe-Claire's is a classed immeuble patrimonial (1964-08-12) covering exterior, interior and land; Baie-D'Urfé's is a municipal citation (2001) covering only the exterior envelope of the oldest, eastern section.
types.source_generation: three RPCQ statements of heritage value (valeur patrimoniale + éléments caractéristiques) read against three sector-characterisation cahiers; no source publishes a per-type table for any West Island place, so the five columns are assembled from the three classed or cited houses themselves
types.blurb_en: A low fieldstone box of one and a half storeys under a steep two-slope roof, stacks rising inside the gable walls, openings placed where they were wanted rather than where symmetry asked for them. Three of them survive across three of the six West Island places — a trading post of 1669–71 at Lachine, a farm house of about 1700 at Baie-D'Urfé, and one of 1769–91 at Pointe-Claire — and all three are protected individually while nothing around them is. One record, three municipalities: the photograph on this card is Lachine's, and Baie-D'Urfé's and Pointe-Claire's stand beside it on the type page.
types.origin_en: The Sulpicians became seigneurs of the island of Montréal in 1663 and conceded the côtes that run out to its western end; the houses built on those concessions were stone because stone was what the fields gave up and because fire and raiding made anything else a poor bet. What survives is very little. Lachine's is the oldest and least altered: two rectangular stone buildings put up in 1669–71 as a fur-trade post for Charles Le Moyne and Jacques Le Ber, restored in the 1980s toward their seventeenth-century appearance and now the Musée de Lachine. Baie-D'Urfé's was built about 1700 by Hubert Rangé dit Laviolette on a concession he bought in 1695, and then quietly rebuilt by the Pilon family between 1839 and 1874 — the walls raised, the roof pitch eased off, moulded chambranles and projecting eaves added in what RPCQ calls a taste imported after the Conquest. Pointe-Claire's went up between 1769 and 1791 on a censive conceded in 1722, and was altered again in 1828. Read together the three make the point the West Island pages keep making: the form is one form across three municipalities, the protection is three separate individual instruments granted in 1964, 2001 and 2001, and not one of them protects an ensemble.

photo.credit: « Site historique Le Ber-Le Moyne, 1, chemin du Musée (Lachine) », photo Denis Tremblay, 2012-12-03, from the Flickr stream *Parcours riverain — Ville de Montréal*. Licence verified on Wikimedia Commons via the API and the file's own wikitext, which carries {{cc-by-2.0}} and a passed FlickreviewR check (reviewer FlickreviewR 2, 2024-04-30, reviewlicense cc-by-2.0). Author of record on Commons is "Parcours riverain - Ville de Montréal"; the photographer named in the file description is Denis Tremblay, not Anne-Marie Dufour.
photo.note: Inspected before use. Shows what the RPCQ fiche describes — rubble fieldstone walls, a steep two-slope roof in cedar shingle, a stone stack in the line of each gable wall, shuttered small openings, and the contemporary stone dépendance standing separately to the left.
photo.alt: Photograph of Stone house of the French tradition houses in Lachine (borough of Montréal), from Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec

types.phase_title: Suburbanisation and the merger
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), § 1.2.2 « Les ensembles urbains d'intérêt » et secteurs 7.U.1 à 7.U.8 (Dorval), 5.U.2 et 5.U.3 (Pointe-Claire), 19.U.2 (Lachine), 2.U.2 et 2.U.4 (Pierrefonds-Senneville) et 2.E.4 (Senneville), avec le § 2 Historique de l'arrondissement de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé
canonical_names: One-storey horizontal house, ≤30° roof, integrated garage

siting_landscape: Detached on its own lot, set back from the street with side margins, and with parking in the front yard — the Lachine cahier's description of the same wave, and the one place any West Island source describes the siting rule rather than the building.

Cul-de-sac and crescent street patterns recur, sometimes with a planted median down a wide avenue, and Dorval's cahier ties the effect of every one of these sectors to mature trees on the properties rather than to the houses.

Built in small series from a short catalogue of models. Dorval's 7.U.5 is praised for using « un nombre relativement restreint de modèles » while letting the materials vary house to house; Lachine's 19.U.2 calls the catalogue of types on its territory « particulièrement impressionnant ». In Lachine the dominant form of that catalogue is not this one but the taller contractor's box known locally as the maison « Gameroff », which carries its own record on that page; what belongs here is the alignment of Californian-inspired bungalows the cahier singles out at the end of the 51e Avenue.
massing: One storey, plain-pied. The Dorval cahier repeats the phrase « bungalows de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique » for two separate sectors, 7.U.1 and 7.U.4, and treats it as the norm for the municipality from the 1940s–50s onward.
A hipped roof is the commonest form. Lachine records more variety in the same years — pitched, hipped, or hipped combined with a false mansard.
Split-level versions appear in the same wave and the same decade; Dorval's 7.U.5 dates a whole quadrilateral of them to the 1950s.
articulation: Almost none, and what there is varies within a single street rather than between streets. Dorval's Model Homes are described as houses that look alike until you look closely, at which point the window types, the roofs, the use of artificial stone and clapboard and the handling of the brick are all different.
openings: Not described by any West Island source beyond the note that window types differ between otherwise identical Dorval houses.
materials: Brick dominant, with artificial stone and clapboard used as accent — the three materials Dorval's cahier names on avenue Dahlia.
Red brick at Pointe-Claire's Magil project, built 1953–55.

description: « Ce petit secteur adjacent au parc Dorval, près de l'extrémité est de l'arrondissement, se caractérise par l'uniformité du bâti : bungalows de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique comme matériau dominant, garage, rue en cul-de-sac, aménagement paysager relativement simple. L'époque approximative de construction serait les années 1950. » (7.U.1)

« Cette rue résidentielle est bordée de bungalows qui se ressemblent mais qui, en y regardant de près, affichent certaines différences dans le type de fenêtres, de toiture, l'emploi de pierre artificielle et de planche à clin, ou encore dans le traitement de la brique. Ce projet qui a débuté en 1951 comprenait 28 unités de logement réparties entre 12 bungalows détachés et 16 semi-détachés; il incluait aussi les deux édifices d'appartements situés au coin du chemin du Bord-du-Lac. » (7.U.2, Dorval Model Homes – avenue Dalhia)

« Ce développement résidentiel est semblable à celui du secteur 7.U.1 – rue en cul-de-sac, bungalows similaires de type plain-pied, toit pavillon, brique, carport, terrain bien aménagé et présence d'arbres matures. La construction remonte approximativement aux années 1950. » (7.U.4, place Décary)
« L'ambiance de ce secteur est celle d'une banlieue de type californien des années 1950, avec ses bungalows bas intégrant un carport. » (7.U.6, avenues Claude et Allard)
« Les bâtiments de ce secteur précèdent ceux de la période des années 1940-1950, où la construction de bungalows devient la norme à Dorval. » (7.I.1)

« Ce secteur de Lakeside Heights se compose de maisonnettes d'un étage et demi et de bungalows en brique rouge construits entre 1953 et 1955. Il présente des qualités d'ensemble remarquables avec un couvert végétal à maturité et des maisons typiques des constructions d'après-guerre, peu transformées. » (5.U.2, projet Magil)

« Ce secteur est composé de maisons construites autour de 1947 sur le modèle des maisons de la Wartime Housing Limited. … Aujourd'hui, même s'il y reste bien peu de ces maisons de vétérans, le secteur continue de se démarquer par le tracé particulier des rues et le lotissement. » (5.U.3, secteur des vétérans)

« Ce vaste secteur est très homogène et regroupe une grande variété d'habitations unifamiliales détachées d'un ou deux étages construites en petites séries, implantées avec marges de recul sur les côtés et en retrait de la rue, et possédant un espace de stationnement en cour avant. Elles ont le plus souvent un plan carré ou rectangulaire, une volumétrie simple, un revêtement de brique avec éléments de décor en bois et des formes de toit variables (en pente, pavillon, ou combinaison pavillon fausse mansarde). Ces habitations sont issues de l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970. » (19.U.2, Victoria – Sir-George-Simpson)

« Notons toutefois l'intérêt particulier que présente la 51e Avenue, qui se termine, à l'intersection de la rue Sherbrooke, par un alignement de bungalows d'inspiration californienne particulièrement bien conservés. » (19.U.2)

« Bien que la plupart des édifices les plus imposants ont été construits en fonction d'une utilisation saisonnière, le secteur comprend aussi des résidences de l'après-guerre et des demeures contemporaines qui lui donnent un caractère suburbain mais qui poursuivent la tradition d'intégration du bâti au paysage. » (2.E.4, grandes propriétés de Senneville)

« On y trouve une grande variété de bungalows d'intérêt architectural (des petites séries et des exemplaires uniques) en excellente condition. La végétation mature, les grandes marges de recul avant bien paysagées des propriétés et l'absence de trottoirs contribuent à la grande homogénéité du secteur. » (2.U.2, Belvédère — in the Pierrefonds half of that arrondissement, not in Senneville)
contexte: « Le Plan d'urbanisme reconnaît l'intérêt de certains développements résidentiels d'après-guerre, qui composent une part importante du patrimoine des anciennes banlieues, en créant une catégorie appelée Ensembles urbains d'intérêt. On y retrouve, entre autres, des ensembles homogènes de bungalows, des secteurs de maisons qui adoptent le modèle développé par la Wartime Housing Limited ou des exemples des premières coopératives d'habitation. Leur repérage est exploratoire … » (the same paragraph in all twenty-seven cahiers)

« Dans les années 1950-1960, grâce à la construction de l'autoroute Métropolitaine et au boom démographique de l'après-guerre, le développement de cette banlieue essentiellement résidentielle s'accélère et l'urbanisation gagne alors le nord de la voie ferrée. Même si le caractère rural disparaît, les rues bordées d'arbres maintiennent une apparence champêtre. » (§ 2, Historique)

types.profile_note: Better evidenced than the other four shared records, and still not evidenced everywhere. The 2005 Ville de Montréal series created a category — Ensembles urbains d'intérêt — expressly to catch postwar suburban housing, and Dorval's cahier alone gives it eight sectors with real building description, so the columns here are unusually well supported for a place with no typology document. But the support is not even across the six places, and that is the thing to know before trusting this record. Dorval and Pointe-Claire are described in detail. Lachine is well described too, but most of what its sector 19.U.2 describes is the one- or two-storey contractor's box that Lachine's own page records as the maison « Gameroff »; only the Californian bungalow alignment at the 51e Avenue is unambiguously this type, and that is what is claimed here. Senneville is attested by one clause in sector 2.E.4, which records postwar houses inside the estate belt and says they continue its tradition of setting buildings into the landscape — no bungalow sector of its own is named, and the well described bungalow sector in the same cahier, 2.U.2 Belvédère, is in the Pierrefonds half of that arrondissement and not in Senneville. Baie-D'Urfé is attested only by its cahier's historique, which dates the acceleration of its suburban growth to the 1950s–60s and to the Métropolitaine, and names no postwar sector; the postwar ensembles in that cahier, 4.U.1 Devon-York with its « bâtiments de l'après-guerre … rappelant le "ranch" californien », 4.U.2 Sunny Acres and 4.U.3 Lakeview-Morgan, are introduced under a paragraph about the territory of Beaconsfield. Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue is the one membership no retrieved source attests at all: its cahier, once found, names no postwar sector and its single ensemble urbain d'intérêt, 1.U.1, is the Garden City Press ensemble of J.-J. Harpell, which is not this type. It is kept in `places` because the record is the shared West Island postwar record and because a later source may supply what this one does not, and it is flagged here rather than asserted quietly. Fields left null and why: `roofing` — no source names a roof covering anywhere in the six places; `roof.pitch_deg` — « toit pavillon » with no figure; `lot_width_m`, `setback_front_m`, `setback_side_m`, `front_yard_green_pct` — the cahiers describe setbacks, front-yard parking and landscaping at length and measure none of it; `sectors` — a shared record cannot carry sector codes that exist in only one of its places, and here they would run 7.U.x, 5.U.x, 19.U.x and 2.U.x at once. `window_proportion: horizontal` is the weakest entry in the record: it is read from the form and from the Dorval note that window types vary between otherwise identical houses, not from any stated proportion, and it should be the first field to correct. `styles: [minimal-traditional]` is a classification made here, not a style any West Island source names; the nearest a source comes is Dorval's « banlieue de type californien » and Lachine's « bungalows d'inspiration californienne ».
conservation: This is the only wave in the West Island whose recognition is explicitly experimental. The 2005 series says its own identification of these sectors « est exploratoire » and aims to link them to conservation concerns « pour une première fois ».

Where the cahiers return to it, they say the same thing twice - the value lies in the plan, the planting and the consistency of the materials rather than in any individual house, and personalisation is what erodes it. Lachine's 19.U.2 records that practically every building in its sector has been modified, and lists how: raising, building to the lot line, added upper storeys or a garage, changed cladding, changed openings, changed roof form.

Pointe-Claire's veterans' sector is the sharpest case: the cahier says few of the wartime houses are left and that what still marks the sector is the street layout and the subdivision, not the buildings.
types.source_generation: five sector-characterisation cahiers of the same 2005 series, read together; the series created a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, expressly to catch postwar suburban housing, and that category is the only per-type writing any West Island source does
types.blurb_en: One storey, hipped roof, brick with artificial stone and clapboard for variety, a carport or a garage, a cul-de-sac and mature trees. Built from a short catalogue of models across all six West Island places from the late 1940s, and the only twentieth-century housing the 2005 evaluation series took seriously enough to invent a category for.
types.origin_en: The wave arrives at different moments and for different reasons. At Dorval it is the airport: the aerodrome opened in 1941, air traffic grew fast after the war, the rest of the territory was opened to subdivision and the population went from under 3,000 in the 1940s to more than 20,000 by 1971. At Pointe-Claire it is a straight housing shortage — a veterans' sector on the Wartime Housing Limited model about 1947, then the Magil project of 1953–55. At Lachine it is what the cahier calls « l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970 », running east across the last open ground and producing a catalogue of contractors' types so consistent that the dominant one is still known locally by its builder's name. At Baie-D'Urfé it is the Métropolitaine and the demographic boom together, pushing settlement north across the railway for the first time. What the 2005 cahiers do with all of it is the interesting part. The series invented a category, Ensembles urbains d'intérêt, to hold postwar suburbs, said openly that the exercise was exploratory, and then valued these places for their street layouts, their planting and the consistency of their materials rather than for their architecture — while recording, in the same paragraphs, that almost every house had already been raised, extended, re-clad or re-roofed. It is the one wave on these six pages that the source treats as heritage-in-progress rather than as heritage.

photo.credit: The only photographs of West Island postwar bungalows located during this research are the 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers' own — Dorval, p. 30–31, captioned « 7.U.1 165, rue McNicoll », « 7.U.2 1, avenue Dalhia », « 7.U.3 70, avenue des Lilas », « 7.U.4 Vue d'ensemble » and « 7.U.6 Avenue Claude »; Pointe-Claire, p. 34, « 5.U.2 Le 105 de l'avenue de Windward Crescent »; Lachine, p. 40, « 19.U.2 La 53e Avenue » and « 19.U.2 Une maison "Gameroff" typique au 3, 40e avenue ». © Ville de Montréal; not reproduced here. Wikimedia Commons was searched for a freely licensed photograph of a postwar bungalow in any of the six places and none was found. The one candidate that looked promising by its address — « Quatre-Vents, 12, avenue Dahlia (Dorval) », on the Model Homes street itself — was downloaded and inspected and is not a bungalow at all but a two-and-a-half-storey stuccoed house with a tiled coping and an arcaded loggia, so it was rejected. The Cité de Dorval's own heritage study of that address (LEMAYMICHAUD + Réal Paul architecte, « Expertise historique et étude patrimoniale, 12, avenue Dahlia, Dorval ») confirms the rejection and dates the house to 1803, enlarged 1874–85 in a neo-Gothic manner and wholly remade 1927–37 into the Italianate it wears now — one of the first stone houses in the district, standing on the street the bungalows were later built along, and not one of them. The same study independently repeats the cahier's figures for the 1951 project - 28 dwellings, 12 detached and 16 semi-detached bungalows, and two apartment buildings.
photo.alt: Photograph of Postwar bungalow houses in Lachine (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: The railway, the resorts and the country estates
types.name_en: Bourgeois brick house in the Victorian taste
types.name_fr: Maison bourgeoise en brique au goût victorien
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Lachine (2005), sectors 19.I.2, 19.I.6, 19.I.7
canonical_names: 2½-storey house of irregular plan, medium-pitched roofs, towers/turrets/oriels/gables, asymmetrical
Opulent village house (maison cossue) in stone or brick with elaborate ornamentation, deep setback and ornamental fence

siting_landscape: On the boulevard Saint-Joseph between the 18th and 34th Avenues, where the cahier says the finest examples stand.

On the chemin de LaSalle and rue McLaughlin, in a sector the cahier reads as having a village atmosphere produced by low density and regular siting, with back gardens giving directly onto Lac Saint-Louis and open views between the buildings.
In the Saint-Antoine – Remembrance sector, where mature vegetation harmonises a mix of domestic and institutional building.
massing: The cahier gives no storey count. In Saint-Antoine – Remembrance it speaks of « belles séries d'habitations à la volumétrie plus ou moins complexe » — runs of houses of more or less complex massing — and that is the whole of what it says about volume.
Semi-detached as well as detached: « de belles maisons en brique jumelées d'inspiration victorienne ».
articulation: The word the cahier repeats is « cossues » — opulent — set against the modest small-gabarit architecture around them.
openings: The cahier states nothing about the openings of this type.
materials: Brick, in all three sectors.

description: Entre la 18e et la 34e Avenue, le boulevard Saint-Joseph regroupe de beaux exemples de maisons bourgeoises en brique au goût victorien
Ce secteur comprend en outre de belles maisons en brique jumelées d'inspiration victorienne et de belles séries d'habitations à la volumétrie plus ou moins complexe.
L'architecture, de petit gabarit, est modeste, mais on trouve aussi des maisons d'inspiration victorienne plus cossues.

types.profile_note: This is a thin record and it is thin because the source is. The cahier names the type three times in three sectors and never describes it: no storeys, no roof, no openings, no ornament, no dates, no addresses. Only the material — brick — and the two attributes "victorian-inspired" and "opulent" are stated, plus the observation that some are semi-detached and that the massing of the runs is more or less complex. Every other column is null. The canonical forms and the styles are this site's reading of those words and of the photograph below; the cahier attributes no style and this record should be revisited if a per-building inventory of Lachine ever becomes available.
types.source_generation: Sector characterisation. Three separate sector paragraphs name the same class of house; the record is their intersection and nothing more.
types.blurb_en: The house of the people who did well out of the canal and the works: brick, opulent, Victorian in taste, detached or semi-detached, standing among much plainer neighbours on the boulevard Saint- Joseph, on the chemin de LaSalle and in the Saint-Antoine sector. The cahier calls it out three times and describes it none of them.
types.origin_en: The firms that came to the canal at the end of the 19th century employed more than labourers. "Outre les ouvriers," the cahier says, "les entreprises emploient des gens de métiers spécialisés ainsi que des professionnels qui éliront domicile surtout dans le secteur ouest de Lachine" — skilled tradesmen and professionals, who chose the west end. What they built there is the beginning of the gradient this page is really about: worker housing east of the institutional core, bourgeois houses in the middle, and beyond the 32nd Avenue the summer-resort houses of Summerlea on their large treed lots, which belong to the shared West Island record for the villa anglaise de villégiature rather than here.

photo.credit: Rue McLaughlin, Lachine — sector 19.I.7, where the cahier notes modest small-gabarit architecture alongside "des maisons d'inspiration victorienne plus cossues". In the frame: a red-brick house with a round corner turret under a conical slate roof, gabled and dormered neighbours, and a lower stuccoed house with a columned porch. Photograph by Anne-Marie Dufour for « Parcours riverain - Ville de Montréal », 12 November 2010, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rue_McLaughlin_(Lachine)_(8551544881).jpg
photo.match_note: Matched on street and on form. The photograph is of rue McLaughlin, which is named in the description of sector 19.I.7, and the corner turret, irregular plan and asymmetrical front are what put the record under the Queen Anne canonical form. No civic number, date or architect is known for any building in the frame, and none is claimed.
photo.alt: Photograph of Bourgeois brick house in the Victorian taste houses in Lachine (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: The railway, the resorts and the country estates
types.name_en: Brick duplex and triplex, detached or in continuous alignment
types.name_fr: Duplex et triplex en brique, détachés ou en alignement continu
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Lachine (2005), sectors 19.I.1, 19.I.2, 19.I.8
canonical_names: Two-storey, two-dwelling brick box, flat roof, superposed units, cornice or parapet
Three-storey, three-dwelling brick building with exterior stair to upper units, flat roof

siting_landscape: Detached, party-walled or in continuous alignment — the cahier records all three, sometimes in the same sentence.
In Vieux-Lachine the grid is orthogonal, the blocks rectangular and regular, and there are no back lanes; siting varies from hard on the street line to a setback deep enough for an exterior stair.
In the low part of Ville Saint-Pierre siting and setbacks are generally constant within a zone but change from one zone to the next.
massing: Two to three superposed dwellings on one lot.
In Dawes the same fabric runs up to large brick buildings of two or three storeys with mansard or false-mansard roofs and dormers.
articulation: Exterior stairs on the façade, in the Ville Saint-Pierre examples.
Sometimes a porte cochère — the carriage arch that leads to the back of the lot, the same device the Centre-Sud of Ville-Marie uses on its own worker housing.

The cahier records what has been lost as carefully as what survives: in Ville Saint-Pierre the wood cladding has usually been replaced by vinyl, and the cornices, crowns and railings have often disappeared.
openings: The cahier states nothing about the openings of this type.
materials: Brick, « le plus souvent ».
Wood, on the ornament that survives: the cahier notes decorative elements in wood on the two-storey houses of the upper part of Ville Saint-Pierre.

description: duplex et triplex détachés ou en alignement continu, le plus souvent en brique, avec parfois des portes cochères
des duplex ou triplex en brique avec des escaliers en façade
implantation: Les implantations et les marges de recul des bâtiments, généralement constantes, varient d'une zone à l'autre.
materiaux: Les parements de bois ont la plupart du temps été remplacés par des parements de vinyle. Les éléments de décor tels que les corniches, les couronnements et les garde-corps ont souvent disparu.

types.profile_note: Built from three sector paragraphs that name the same form in three parts of the borough, and from nothing else. The cahier gives no storey count for the duplex as against the triplex, no roof pitch, no window type, no lot width and no setback figure, so those are null; the flat roof is inferred from the crowns and cornices the same paragraphs describe as lost, and from the canonical forms this record is filed under, not from a statement in the source. The tenure plan is recorded as duplex because that is the smaller of the two the cahier names; the triplex is the same record.
types.source_generation: Sector characterisation. Three sector descriptions naming the same form, transcribed and set side by side; nothing added.
types.blurb_en: The worker housing the canal and the factories produced: two or three dwellings stacked on one lot, in brick more often than not, sometimes standing free, sometimes party-walled, sometimes running the length of a block in one alignment. Ville Saint-Pierre's have their stairs on the façade. Vieux- Lachine's sometimes have a carriage gate through to the back of the lot.
types.origin_en: Lachine's east end densified around work. The canal opened in 1825 and the first railway on the island reached the Lachine quay in 1847; Dominion Bridge settled near the locks in 1883 and other firms followed, and the cahier says workers arrived in numbers, settled in the eastern sectors, and pushed the built-up area across the railway. Companies and promoters, in its words, "construisent une multiplicité de types d'habitation et déclinent souvent leurs variantes en alignement continu, en série, jumelées ou individuelles" to house the factory hands and the men working on the canal. The porte cochère puts this record beside the Centre-Sud worker housing of Ville-Marie, where the carriage gate leads to houses at the back of the yard; and the exterior stair puts it beside every other plex on this site.

photo.credit: Boulevard Saint-Joseph, Lachine — brick and painted-brick buildings of two and three storeys in continuous alignment, with balconies, moulded cornices, a false-mansard turret and, mid-block, an exterior stair; the dome of the Sœurs de Sainte-Anne mother house closes the view. Photograph by Anne-Marie Dufour for « Parcours riverain - Ville de Montréal », 12 November 2010, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Boulevard_Saint-Joseph_(Lachine)_(8551449525).jpg
photo.match_note: Matched on form and on street, not on civic number. The boulevard Saint-Joseph is sector 19.E.2 and runs through 19.I.1 and 19.I.2, all three of which describe this fabric.
photo.alt: Photograph of Brick duplex and triplex, detached or in continuous alignment houses in Lachine (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: The railway, the resorts and the country estates
types.name_en: Small one-storey brick house, wider than deep, with a crown
types.name_fr: Petite maison unifamiliale d'un étage en brique à couronnement
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Lachine (2005), sector 19.I.1
canonical_names: Maison shoebox — one-storey flat-roofed rectangular house set perpendicular to the street, built to be extended upward

siting_landscape: In the orthogonal grid of Vieux-Lachine: regular rectangular blocks with no back lanes, and buildings sited variably — sometimes directly on the street line, sometimes set back far enough for an exterior stair or a short path to the front door.
massing: One storey, and small.
Wider than deep — the cahier's own words, « plus larges que profondes », and the point on which this type parts company with the Montréal shoebox it otherwise resembles.
articulation: Crowned. The cahier names the crown as the one architectural feature of the type, which implies a flat or barely sloping roof behind it.
openings: The cahier states nothing about the openings of this type.
materials: Brick.

description: petites maisons unifamiliales d'un étage en brique, plus larges que profondes et avec des couronnements
implantation: La grille orthogonale du tissu urbain, avec ses îlots rectangulaires réguliers et sans ruelles, accueille un bâti qui s'installe selon des modes d'implantation variables, parfois directement sur la ligne de rue, parfois avec un recul pouvant accommoder des escaliers extérieurs ou une petite allée menant à la porte principale.

types.profile_note: The whole documented content of this type is one clause of one sentence in a sector description: « petites maisons unifamiliales d'un étage en brique, plus larges que profondes et avec des couronnements ». The cahier gives no date, no roof form in words, no window type, no ornament beyond the crown, no lot dimension and no setback, so all of those are null. The phase is provisional: the type sits inside a sector whose growth the cahier ties to the consolidation of Lachine's industrial vocation, which is p3, but no year is printed for the houses themselves. The style attribution is this site's reading and not the cahier's, which attributes none. The canonical link needs a warning. The Montréal shoebox is defined by being narrow and set end-on to the street, built to be built over later; Lachine's version is explicitly the other way round — wider than deep. It is filed with the shoebox because it is the same one-storey, flat-roofed, crowned, single-family small brick house, and because the divergence is the useful thing to see.
types.source_generation: Sector characterisation. One clause of the typological sentence inside the description of Vieux-Lachine, transcribed and not extended.
types.blurb_en: A small single-family house of one storey in brick, wider across the front than it is deep, finished at the top with a crown. It is the plainest thing in the old town and the cahier gives it eleven words; what those words describe is a house that is the mirror image of the Montréal shoebox, which turns its narrow end to the street and grows upward. This one turns its long side to the street and does not.
types.origin_en: It belongs to the dense grid of Vieux-Lachine, which grew along the boulevard Saint-Joseph and then reached rue Saint-Louis and rue Victoria as the arrival of firms like Dominion Bridge consolidated Lachine's industrial vocation. The cahier sets it in a list beside the wooden village houses, the attached and terraced houses under mansards and false mansards, and the brick duplexes and triplexes — four kinds of small dwelling on the same street grid, housing the workforce that the canal and the factories drew in.

photo.credit: 26e Avenue, Lachine — the faubourg fabric of sector 19.I.2, where the cahier says the suburb character is felt best, "à l'architecture modeste en bois et en brique". The building in the middle of the frame is a one-storey red-brick house, wider than deep, under a flat roof behind a plain crown; at the left is a wood-clad village house with a bell-cast roof and gable dormers, and at the right a two-storey brick house with a front gallery. Photograph by Anne-Marie Dufour for « Parcours riverain - Ville de Montréal », 18 November 2010, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:26e_Avenue_(Lachine)_(8552634536).jpg
photo.match_note: Matched on form, not on address. The photograph is of the 26th Avenue, inside sector 19.I.2 and not 19.I.1, and the cahier's typological sentence belongs to 19.I.1; but 19.I.2's own description names the same modest brick-and-wood fabric, and the centre building carries the three attributes the sentence gives — one storey, brick, wider than deep, crowned. Neither the civic number nor the date of the building is known.
photo.alt: Photograph of Small one-storey brick house, wider than deep, with a crown houses in Lachine (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: Suburbanisation and the merger
types.name_en: The maison « Gameroff » — contractor-built house of the 1950s–1970s quarters
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Lachine (2005), sector 19.U.2
canonical_names: Two-storey box, low hip roof, integrated garage, marquise

siting_landscape: Detached, set back from the street, with side yards and a parking space in the front yard.
Built in small series rather than one at a time.
The quality of the public and private landscaping across the sector is called remarkable; two modern schools sit in wide green enclaves within it.
massing: One or two storeys.
Square or rectangular plan, simple massing.
Roof forms vary: pitched, hipped, or a hipped-and-false-mansard combination.
articulation: Decorative elements in wood on a brick wall, and nothing else the cahier records.

Practically every building in the sector has been modified and personalised: raised, built out to the lot line, given extra storeys or a garage, re-clad, re-fenestrated, re-roofed. The cahier says the further east one goes the more the standard models have been altered.
openings: The cahier states nothing about the openings, except that they are among the things later owners changed.
materials: Brick cladding with wooden decorative elements.

description: Ce vaste secteur est très homogène et regroupe une grande variété d'habitations unifamiliales détachées d'un ou deux étages construites en petites séries, implantées avec marges de recul sur les côtés et en retrait de la rue, et possédant un espace de stationnement en cour avant.

Elles ont le plus souvent un plan carré ou rectangulaire, une volumétrie simple, un revêtement de brique avec éléments de décor en bois et des formes de toit variables (en pente, pavillon, ou combinaison pavillon fausse mansarde). Ces habitations sont issues de l'urbanisation massive des années 1950-1970.

Le « catalogue » des typologies implantées sur ce territoire est particulièrement impressionnant. On y trouve des maisons boom-town, des bungalows et une variété de maisons construites par des entrepreneurs, dont le plus connu localement a laissé au type architectural dominant son appellation familière de maison « Gameroff ».

types.profile_note: Everything above is transcribed from one sector description. The cahier gives the plan, the massing, the storeys, the siting, the cladding, the ornament and the roof-form range, and gives nothing else: no dimensions, no window proportion, no roof pitch, no garage rule, no dates for individual houses beyond the 1950–1970 range for the wave that produced them. It also gives nothing at all about the contractor — no first name, no firm, no number of houses built, no years — so none of that is asserted here. The type carries no style attribution because the cahier makes none and because the form is defined by a builder rather than by an idiom.
types.source_generation: Sector characterisation. The description of the Victoria – Sir-George-Simpson ensemble, transcribed in full; the caption of its illustrated example supplies the one address.
types.blurb_en: A detached one- or two-storey house on a square or rectangular plan, simple in massing, clad in brick with wooden trim, under a roof that might be pitched, hipped, or hipped with a false mansard; set back from the street with side yards and a car parked in front, and built in small series. What makes it worth a card is its name. The cahier records that among the contractors who built the 1950s–1970s quarters of Lachine, the best known locally gave the dominant house type its familiar name — the maison « Gameroff » — and that is a piece of purely local vernacular naming that made it into a municipal heritage document.
types.origin_en: Lachine answered the postwar boom the way other towns did, by turning its unbuilt sectors into dormitory quarters, and the sector called Victoria – Sir-George-Simpson is what came out: a vast, very homogeneous stretch of detached houses that the cahier says testify to the emergence of a middle class, to individual ownership, and to a way of living made possible by the car. It also says the catalogue of types deployed there is "particulièrement impressionnant" and lists three at once — Boomtown houses, bungalows, and the contractors' houses of which the Gameroff is the dominant one. That is the note this record should end on: a document written to identify heritage found a 1950s–1970s tract worth naming as an ensemble, and named its houses after the man who built them.

types.blurb_en: The house that gives Lévis its street picture: one and a half to two and a half storeys, raised a little off the ground, under a medium-pitched two-slope roof whose curved base carries out over a covered veranda. Clapboard or shingle walls, four- and six-pane casements set symmetrically, gabled dormers, and carpentered trim on the surrounds, corner boards and veranda.
types.origin_en: At about seven hundred buildings this is the second most numerous current in the catalogue, and the one the City's own walking-tour brochure uses to explain how the Norman house of the colonists became something Québécois. The brochure reads the maison Lefrançois at 39 rue Wolfe as exactly that evolution — dormers cut into the roof and clapboard on the walls — and the maison Pampalon at 40 rue Wolfe as its later stage, where the ground floor lifts far enough to make the basement usable.

types.blurb_en: Steep two-slope roofs over an irregular plan, with pointed-arch openings and vertical windows of varied pattern. The City's own line drawing for this current is a chapel, and its projections — bell tower, buttresses, pinnacles — are ecclesiastical; the domestic version reads through the same steep gables and decorative bargeboards.
types.origin_en: Lévis's best-known Neo-Gothic building is a house: the maison Alphonse-Desjardins of 1882–1884, where the first caisse populaire was founded in 1900. The RPCQ describes it as « une habitation de style néogothique… de plan asymétrique en forme de « L », à un étage et demi… coiffée d'un toit à deux versants ponctué de deux pignons en façade », and it was classed an immeuble patrimonial on 21 March 1983. The City's fiche spans 1830 to 1940, a reach of over a century, so the phase placement here follows the opening date and is marked provisional.

types.blurb_en: Two to three storeys under a straight two-slope or hipped tin roof, faced in brick or cut stone at the front and clapboard down the sides — a distinction of expense that the fiche records plainly. types.blurb_en: The main-street block of the côte du Passage and the avenue Bégin: two or three storeys of brick, flat-roofed or shallow-gabled, with shop windows and transomed commercial doors below and a signage cornice, signs and retractable awnings above.
types.origin_en: The second of the catalogue's two « Autre type » entries, and one of only two of the twenty carrying no « Nombre à Lévis » figure. All seven of its fields describe the commercial ground floor — vitrines, portes commerciales, corniche d'affichage, enseignes, auvents rétractables — and none describes the dwellings above, which is how a mixed-use fiche is normally written: the shopfront is what distinguishes the type, the flats over it are what it has in common with everything else on the street. The City's walking-tour brochure says of the édifice Laurentien on rue Guenette that it « jumelle aujourd'hui les vocations commerciale et résidentielle », which is the mixed use the name promises.

types.blurb_en: Two or three storeys, square or rectangular, flat-roofed, finished at the top by a cornice or parapet and at the front by a covered veranda — the superposed-dwelling form of the industrial faubourgs, and at about 600 buildings the third most numerous current in the catalogue.
types.origin_en: Where Boomtown hides a shallow slope behind a parapet, this current has no slope to hide: the flat roof is the type. It is the Lévis relative of the Montréal plex and of Gatineau's flat-roofed brick and wood houses, and the City's ornament list — modillion cornice, patterned brickwork, veranda trim — is the richest of the three flat-roofed currents it publishes.

types.origin_en: Wartime Housing Limited's standard dwelling, built for shipyard and munitions workers and kept in production into the 1960s; the City dates the current 1940–1970 and counts about 200. It is the first current in the catalogue whose materials are all industrial products rather than wood, stone or tin, and the ornamental ironwork on the veranda is the period's signature.

types.phase_title: Wartime housing and modernism
types.source_ref: Ville de Lévis, « Styles architecturaux », fiche 19 « Modernisme », 1950-1975
canonical_names: One-storey horizontal house, ≤30° roof, integrated garage
Postwar modernist residential tower or slab

siting_landscape: The City counts about 30 buildings of this current across the merged territory of Lévis (fiche, « Nombre à Lévis »).
massing: Varied, according to use.
Rectangular or complex plan.
Flat roof.
Annexe volumes.
articulation: Sober.
openings: Varied and repetitive, in horizontal bands.
materials: Brick, concrete, metal cladding.

volumetrie: diversifiée selon l'usage
toiture: plate
saillies: volumes annexes
ornementation: sobre
ouvertures: variées et répétitives, en bandeau horizontal
revetements: brique, béton, revêtement métallique

types.profile_note: Encoded by sources/levis/parse.py from the City's fiche for this courant. The five columns follow the fiche's own seven fields: Volumétrie, Plan, Toiture and Saillies together make up massing, Ornementation is articulation, Ouvertures is openings and Revêtements is materials. The French under each English list is the fiche's wording verbatim, unedited. Siting has no counterpart in the fiche, so it carries the catalogue's own « Nombre à Lévis » distribution figure instead, and no French. Phase follows the opening year of the index's period range (1950-1975).
types.source_generation: Ville de Lévis « Styles architecturaux » online catalogue (crawled 16 August 2026)
types.blurb_en: Flat-roofed, brick, concrete or metal-clad, with openings set in repeating horizontal bands. The one current in the catalogue whose massing the City declines to fix at all — « diversifiée selon l'usage » — because the same language served houses, schools and offices.
types.origin_en: The last of the twenty currents, dated 1950–1975 and counted at about thirty buildings. Lévis published a separate Inventaire du patrimoine moderne in 2016 covering 79 buildings put up between 1946 and 1975 (RPCQ inventory 1313), and a guide, L'architecture moderne, un héritage du 20e siècle à démystifier. The City's line drawing for the current is an office block, and the fiche's own volumetry row concedes the range, so both a low ranch house and a slab are cross-linked here.

types.phase_title: Longue-Pointe — the côtes, the redoubt and the village
types.name_fr: La maison villageoise de Longue-Pointe (maison en carré de bois)
types.source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sector 27.I.3 Longue-Pointe and ch. 2
canonical_names: Small-gabarit village house of an 18th–19th-century bourg, wood or brick, tin roof, minimal setback

siting_landscape: Along the old chemin du Roy — the present rue Notre-Dame Est — and the village streets running off it, around the parish church of Saint-François-d'Assise on the river bank; the church itself has been demolished.
The village core was « largement amputé » when the Louis-Hippolyte-Lafontaine bridge-tunnel was built in the early 1960s, so what survives is a fragment, not a continuous frontage.
massing: Small village gabarit, one to one-and-a-half occupied levels.
materials: Squared-timber walls — « maisons en carré de bois » — most often sheathed in wood boards or wood shingles, and sometimes in clay brick.

types.profile_note: The entire documentary basis for this record is one sentence of sector fiche 27.I.3: « il présente encore aujourd'hui un bâti villageois typique : maisons en carré de bois, souvent recouvertes de planches ou de bardeaux de bois et parfois de brique d'argile. » That sentence gives wall construction and cladding and nothing else, so roof form, storey count beyond the small village gabarit, articulation and openings are left null or empty rather than inferred from the photograph. Sector 27.I.3 is not encoded in this page's sectors.yaml, which carries only the five E sectors; the I, U, N and AP sectors of arrondissement 27 are Part 10b work, and the sector reference is therefore made in this note instead of in the `sectors` field. One building in the photographed street carries a raised and ornamented parapet with a 1898 date panel — a boomtown crown, and this borough's only observed instance — but the cahier does not name the form, so it is recorded here and not encoded as a type.
types.blurb_en: What was on the ground before any of the rest of it. Small squared-timber houses sheathed in board, shingle or brick, strung along the old chemin du Roy around a parish founded in 1722 — the oldest settlement layer in the borough, and the one most thoroughly cut apart, first by the tramway that reached the end of the island in 1897 and then by the bridge-tunnel approaches of the early 1960s.
types.origin_en: Longue-Pointe is the borough's French-regime layer. A wooden redoubt went up on the shore about 1670 in the chain of forts protecting Ville-Marie; a chapel and presbytery followed at the turn of the eighteenth century; Saint-François-d'Assise de la Longue Pointe became, in 1722, one of the few parishes erected on the island under the French regime, and the territory became a municipality in 1845. In 1825 the parish counted 67 houses, holding « de nombreux artisans, des aubergistes, des rentiers, des journaliers mais surtout des agriculteurs ». Its urbanisation came late precisely because it was far from Montréal's economy, and the cahier says so: development « se fera plus tardivement que celui des municipalités voisines (Hochelaga et Maisonneuve) puisqu'elle est située assez loin du centre des activités économiques de Montréal ». Longue-Pointe, Beaurivage and Tétraultville were all annexed to Montréal in 1910.

photo.credit: "Lepailleur street in Mercier neighbourhood, Montreal, Quebec, Canada" by Félix Mathieu-Bégin (User:Webfil), 6 January 2014, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — licence read on the Commons API before download. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mercier,_rue_Lepailleur.jpg
photo.match_note: Same street as the cahier's own illustration for this sector, which is captioned « 27.I.3 La rue Lepailleur dans Longue-Pointe », but a different and later frame, so the match is visual rather than documentary. The frame shows the mixed village fabric the fiche describes — small two-storey volumes clad in painted wood boards and in red brick, standing close to the sidewalk — together with the 1898 date panel on the raised parapet of the corner building at the right.
photo.alt: Photograph of Village house of Longue-Pointe houses in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (borough of Montréal), from Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005)

types.phase_title: Hochelaga industrialises and is annexed
types.name_en: Company workers' house of the Hudon mill, rue Saint-Germain
types.name_fr: La maison ouvrière de la filature Hudon, rue Saint-Germain
types.source_ref: MEM, « Les maisons ouvrières de la rue Saint-Germain » (2017); Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sector 27.E.1
canonical_names: Duplex with interior stair, flat roof

siting_landscape: Built at the sidewalk edge with no setback, and set in an unbroken run — « disposées en enfilade et en bordure du trottoir ».
Rue Saint-Germain between rues Rouville and Adam, civic numbers 1451 to 1544; one of the three streets sector 27.E.1 names as the first ground of Hochelaga's workers' housing.
massing: Square-ish two-storey volumes — « cubes de bois revêtus de briques ».

Two dwellings, one on the ground floor and one above, reached by a stair inside the building. No exterior stair; this is 1881, nearly twenty years before the outside stair becomes standard in Montréal.
materials: Wood frame faced in brick.

types.profile_note: Siting, massing and materials are quoted from the MEM (Mémoires des Montréalais / Centre des mémoires montréalaises, Ville de Montréal) article of 8 November 2017 by the Atelier d'histoire Mercier-Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, which is the only account of these houses found in an institutional source; the Évaluation names rue Saint-Germain as a first street of workers' housing but gives no fiche and does not list these buildings individually. Articulation and openings are left empty rather than inferred — no photograph of the row could be verified on Commons, and the houses were renovated in 1981, so present appearance is not evidence of 1881 detailing. The interior stair is the article's own statement, « L'escalier est à l'intérieur », and it is the reason this record attaches to duplex-interior-stair rather than to the exterior-stair members of the plex family.
types.blurb_en: The corporate counterpart to Maisonneuve, built two years before Maisonneuve existed. Brick-faced wooden cubes running unbroken along the sidewalk on rue Saint-Germain, two dwellings each with the stair inside, put up in 1881 by the V. Hudon cotton mill for its own workers — and, according to the Ville's MEM, the only surviving nineteenth-century company-built housing in Montréal.
types.origin_en: Hochelaga industrialised faster than it could house anyone. Four large works arrived between 1871 and 1881 — the W.C. McDonald tobacco factory, the Abattoirs de l'Est, the Compagnie des moulins à coton V. Hudon and the Filature Sainte-Anne, the last two merging in 1905 into Dominion Textile, which then held half of the Canadian textile industry — and, in the Évaluation's words, « les terrains sont lotis sans réglementation particulière ». The Hudon mill announced its own workers' housing in early December 1881 and built this row; it was renovated in 1981, exactly a century later. Read this record against the plex on the next page and against Arvida and Témiscaming: an employer housing its workforce directly is what a company town does, and it is precisely what Maisonneuve two years later did not do. Maisonneuve's promoters sold lots and built civic monuments instead, and left the housing to the ordinary speculative builder.
