photo.alt: Photograph of Company workers' house of the Hudon mill, rue Saint-Germain houses in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (borough of Montréal), from MEM

types.phase_title: The cité de Maisonneuve
types.name_en: Bourgeois residence of the cité, Beaux-Arts
types.source_ref: RPCQ fiche 92740, Château Dufresne; Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), ch. 2 and sector 27.E.3
canonical_names: Opulent village house (maison cossue) in stone or brick with elaborate ornamentation, deep setback and ornamental fence

siting_landscape: Set on a large landscaped ground behind a cast-iron fence, on one of the two thoroughfares laid out for prestige — rue Sherbrooke Est, or boulevard Pie-IX, whose subdivision « privilégiait de riches constructions sur des terrains plus grands que ce que l'on retrouve dans les environs ».
Garages and other service space put underground at the rear rather than on the street front.
massing: Rectangular two-storey corps de logis under a flat roof ringed by a balustrade.
Two paired houses composed as one unified block, with lateral wings set back from the main façade and rising only to half height, and a rear annex holding a winter garden.
articulation: Symmetry and frontality — two avant-corps framing a central section carried on three pairs of coupled Ionic columns.

Classical ornament — column capitals, entablature and the terrace roof edged with a balustrade. The RPCQ names this house, with the Maisonneuve bain public et gymnase and the Saint-Sulpice library, as an illustration of Beaux-Arts composition applied in Québec.
openings: Vertical rectangular and round-headed openings, disposed symmetrically about the central bay.
materials: Indiana limestone facing.
Structure and twenty massive piers in reinforced concrete.

types.profile_note: Every line here is read off one building, the Château Dufresne (Maisons Marius et Oscar Dufresne, 4040 rue Sherbrooke Est, 1915–1918, Marius Dufresne with the French architect Jules Renard), because it is the only house of this class in the borough with a fiche of its own; the Évaluation says as much — « Des demeures somptueuses sont également construites pour la bourgeoisie canadienne-française, mais elles constituent l'exception. Le meilleur exemple en est le château Dufresne. » Sector 27.E.3 establishes that a whole street of such houses was intended on boulevard Pie-IX and that « plusieurs bâtiments témoignent encore du faste qu'avait autrefois cette voie », but it names none of them, so the siting line is the sector's and the rest is the Château's. ONE CORRECTION TO THE PART 10 MEMO. The RPCQ does not say this was the first reinforced-concrete private residence in Montréal. Its wording is « l'une des premières utilisations de ce matériau pour la construction résidentielle à Montréal, voire au Québec », and again « il s'agit de l'une des premières résidences à structure en béton armé à Montréal » — one of the first, not the first. The superlative is not in the source and is not published here. On the style tags: beaux-arts is the RPCQ's own word for this building, repeated four times in its fiche. city-beautiful is attached deliberately and is the only house record on this site that carries it, because this is the house the author of Maisonneuve's City Beautiful plan built for himself while executing it, and because the RPCQ ties the two together explicitly — Beaux-Arts is a current « fréquemment associé aux projets urbains d'inspiration City Beautiful ». The tag belongs to the designer and the moment, not to a set of formal features that could be found in another house.
types.blurb_en: The exception the record keeps insisting on. Two houses for two brothers built as one Beaux-Arts block in Indiana limestone — Marius Dufresne, who as municipal engineer designed Maisonneuve's public buildings, on one side, and Oscar Dufresne, who ran the family shoe factory, on the other — standing on twenty reinforced-concrete piers at a moment when almost no house in Montréal did. Forty rooms, a winter garden, garages underground.
types.origin_en: Maisonneuve was 80 % francophone and, in the Évaluation's phrase, « composée surtout de travailleurs et de locataires »; its promoters had founded the place in 1883 to be, as the RPCQ puts it, « la "Westmount des francophones" ». The bourgeois house is where that ambition became a building. The Dufresne brothers were both instruments of it: Oscar sat as échevin and ran Dufresne et Locke, the shoe manufactory established at Maisonneuve about 1900 and one of its largest employers; Marius was municipal engineer from 1910 to 1918 and drew the market (1912–1914), the fire station (1914–1915) and the public bath and gymnasium (1914–1916). They began their own house in 1915, the year the civic building programme was breaking the city's finances, and finished it in 1918, the year the province annexed Maisonneuve to Montréal. It was classé in 1976; the civic buildings had to wait until 2022.

photo.credit: "North facade of the Château Dufresne, 4040 Sherbrooke East, Montreal, Quebec, Canada" by Thomas1313, 18 April 2012, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — licence read on the Commons API before download. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Façade_avant_-_Château_Dufresne.JPG
photo.match_note: The building itself, at the address the RPCQ fiche gives. Visible in the frame and named in the fiche's éléments caractéristiques: the two-storey limestone block, the flat roof ringed by its stone balustrade, the three pairs of coupled Ionic columns in the central section, the two avant-corps framing them, the half-height lateral wings set back, and the cast-iron fence, which the classement covers along with the building and its underground spaces but not the grounds.
photo.alt: Photograph of Bourgeois residence of the cité, Beaux-Arts houses in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (borough of Montréal), from RPCQ fiche 92740

types.phase_title: The cité de Maisonneuve
types.name_en: Shop-and-dwellings block on the commercial artery
types.name_fr: L'immeuble commercial avec logements, rues Ontario et Sainte-Catherine
types.source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sectors 27.E.2 and 27.I.1; Guide patrimonial de MHM
canonical_names: Mixed commercial-residential block, flat roof, shops below and dwellings above

siting_landscape: Built to the lot lines with no setback, on the corner of a commercial artery and a residential street — rue Ontario Est and rue Sainte-Catherine Est are the two the Évaluation identifies as the axes of urban development once the tramway reached the east end.
The corner is chamfered so the shop entrance faces the crossing.
massing: Three storeys under a flat roof, shop at street level and dwellings above.
A projecting oriel rides the chamfered corner through the upper storeys.
articulation: Ground floor read as its own register — the borough's Guide patrimonial defines « entablement » precisely as « partie supérieure d'un rez-de-chaussée (commercial) prenant la forme d'un bandeau ».
Crown gathered into a bold projecting cornice of worked painted metal, ornamented across the whole frontage and returning around the chamfer.
openings: Vertical rectangular upper windows in regular bays; glazed shopfront below, here with glass-block infill of a later phase.
materials: Rock-faced grey limestone above, brick at the shopfront piers; the Guide's palette for significant sectors allows grey limestone, smooth or rock-faced, and clay brick in red, brown, beige, orange, polychrome or glazed.

types.profile_note: A weaker record than the others on this page, and marked as such. The Évaluation gives this form no fiche; it names commercial buildings only inside its list of what makes the sectors' fabric — « Industries, banques, édifices commerciaux, écoles et églises composent un paysage bâti riche et diversifié » — and its individual listings for rue Ontario Est are banks, not shop-houses. The articulation and materials lines are drawn from the borough's Guide patrimonial, which regulates the commercial ground-floor entablature and the crown as their own categories in the secteurs significatifs; the massing and siting lines are read from the photographed example and are labelled visual, not documentary. The type is included because it is the one thing Maisonneuve's own zoning by-law was written to keep off the residential streets: the cahier records that the city « instaure un règlement de zonage qui est une nouveauté à l'époque. Celui-ci interdit la construction de commerces ou d'industries sur certaines rues, consacrées uniquement au développement résidentiel. » The plex streets and this corner are two halves of one rule.
types.blurb_en: The other half of Maisonneuve's zoning experiment. Where the by-law let commerce go — rue Ontario Est, rue Sainte-Catherine Est — the block turns its corner on a chamfer, puts a shop under three storeys of flats, runs an oriel up the angle and finishes the whole thing with an ornamented metal cornice. The streets the by-law reserved for housing got the plex instead, and no shop at all.
types.origin_en: The tramway is the cause. The Évaluation dates Hochelaga's commercial axes to the moment the streetcar arrived — rue Sainte-Catherine and the new Montreal Street Railway viaduct of 1892 « pour desservir les populations de l'est montréalais » — and dates Maisonneuve's own growth from the same year: « à partir de 1892, les tramways favorisent le développement rapide de Maisonneuve et placent la municipalité dans la zone d'influence de Montréal ». Shops followed the rails, and the corner block is what a builder puts on a lot that has to earn from both a shopfront and a stack of flats.

photo.credit: "4239, Ontario Street East, Montreal, Quebec, Canada, H1V 1K2" by Thomas1313, 7 November 2014, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — licence read on the Commons API before download. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:4239,_Ontario_Street_East,_Montreal.jpg
photo.match_note: Matched on address and form, but to a building the Évaluation does not list, so the confidence is visual rather than documentary. The frame shows the whole of the description: three storeys of rock-faced grey limestone on a chamfered corner, an oriel on the chamfer, a shop at street level behind brick piers with later glass block, and a heavy star-ornamented metal cornice carried right round the crown. The address places it inside sector 27.E.2, a block from the ancien hôtel de ville.
photo.alt: Photograph of Shop-and-dwellings block on the commercial artery houses in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (borough of Montréal), from Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005)

types.phase_title: The cité de Maisonneuve
types.name_fr: L'habitation ouvrière de trois étages (« plex »)
types.source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sector 27.E.2 and § 3.1; Guide patrimonial de MHM
canonical_names: Plex — the Montréal family of two to six stacked dwellings on a narrow lot

siting_landscape: Continuous alignments along tree-lined streets — the Évaluation names the trees twice, in the sector fiche (« le long de rues bordées d'arbres ») and in its overview of the borough's residential heritage.

In Hochelaga the first such streets are Moreau, Dézéry and Saint-Germain, settled directly around the deep-water port and the Notre-Dame rail lines; in Maisonneuve the sector runs east to Viauville, between rues Sicard and Viau.
massing: Three storeys, one dwelling to a floor, under a flat roof.
Front balcony at each upper level, and an exterior stair climbing to the upper doors so that every dwelling keeps its own entrance from the street.
articulation: Crown treated as a distinct element — the borough's conservation guide governs « couronnement » as its own category, in worked and painted wood, worked painted metal, or brick laid in a distinctive bond, plus false mansards and dômes in natural slate, fish-scale metal or tôle à la canadienne.
Openings framed by a lintel of brick laid as a shallow-arched soldier course, of stone, or of concrete with a moulded relief, over a stone or concrete sill 5 to 6 inches high.
openings: Vertical openings; for pre-1940 buildings the guide prescribes double-hung sashes at 1/2–1/2 or 2/5–3/5, or casements at 1/3–2/3 or 2/5–3/5 with a fixed upper light, glazed in uniform clear or frosted glass without muntins or patterns.
Principal door with a glazed panel 42 to 54 inches high, and a secondary balcony door glazed 36 to 42 inches, which may carry the traditional Montréal muntin pattern.
materials: The Évaluation's own words for the borough's residential heritage — « plex » en pierre ou en brique. Grey limestone, smooth-faced or rock-faced, and clay brick in red, brown, beige, orange or polychrome, plus glazed brick.

Stair, balcony guard and stringer in steel, wrought iron or welded aluminium, painted; natural galvanised steel is prohibited as a non-original component. Balcony floors in tongue-and-groove wood or composite board, boards no wider than 6 inches, on a bipartite wooden fascia with a slatted wooden soffit.

types.profile_note: This is the record the brief's warning is about, so it says plainly what the documents say and what they do not. NO DISTINCT « MAISON-MODÈLE » FOR MAISONNEUVE IS DOCUMENTED. The word « modèle » does occur in the cahier, but not of a house: sector 27.E.2 calls the municipality itself « la cité-modèle de Maisonneuve », and the only model house named anywhere in the document is « le modèle des maisons de la Wartime Housing Limited » in sector 27.U.1, which is a 1950 federal type in Mercier and has nothing to do with the cité. What the cité's workers lived in is the ordinary Montréal plex — three storeys and a rangée of them, one dwelling to a floor, and the Évaluation's whole description of it is a single clause: « les habitations ouvrières de trois étages le long de rues bordées d'arbres », supported by its overview line, « un patrimoine résidentiel composé de "plex" en pierre ou en brique le long de rues bordées d'arbres ». Neither document gives dwelling counts or stair positions per building, so this record attaches to the canonical family rather than to one of its seven members: the same street can hold a duplex, a triplex and a multiplex without the fiches distinguishing them. The exterior stair is not named in the Évaluation at all; it is carried here from the borough's own Guide patrimonial, which regulates « escalier courbe » and adds the note « les escaliers traditionnels (typiquement montréalais) doivent être conservés et maintenus en bon état », and it is visible along the whole photographed alignment on rue Dézéry. Every articulation, opening and material line likewise comes from the Guide's prescriptive tables for « secteur significatif » and « immeuble significatif » — that is, from what the borough will today allow to be rebuilt, which is its reading of what was originally there.
types.blurb_en: What Maisonneuve's workers actually lived in. Three storeys of grey limestone or clay brick under a flat roof, one dwelling to a floor, each with its own door off the street and the upper doors reached by an iron stair curving up out of the front yard — repeated down both sides of a street planted with trees. The Évaluation gives it one clause and no fiche, which is the point: the ambition at Maisonneuve went into the civic buildings and the boulevard, and the housing was the standard Montréal product.
types.origin_en: The form arrives with the industry. Hochelaga's mills — the W.C. McDonald tobacco works, the Abattoirs de l'Est, the V. Hudon cotton mills and the Filature Sainte-Anne, all established between 1871 and 1881 — drew what the cahier calls « une main-d'œuvre bon marché issue des populations agricoles qui convergent vers la ville », and « les terrains sont lotis sans réglementation particulière ». At Maisonneuve after 1883 the promoters offered huge cheap lots and tax exemptions to industry, and the population went from about 350 at the founding to 2,000 in 1896 and roughly 18,000 in 1911 — 80 % francophone and « composée surtout de travailleurs et de locataires ». Renters in a boom is what the plex is for. Maisonneuve also enacted a zoning by-law that the cahier calls « une nouveauté à l'époque », barring shops and industry from certain streets reserved for housing alone — one of the earliest use-separation controls in Québec, and the reason these streets read as purely residential while rue Ontario Est a block away does not.

photo.credit: "La rue Dézéry à Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (entre la rue De Rouen et la rue Ontario), Montréal" by Atilin, 11 February 2006, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — licence read on the Commons API before download. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HochMais.JPG
photo.match_note: Matched on street name and on form, not on a listed address. Rue Dézéry is one of the three streets sector 27.E.1 names as the first ground of Hochelaga's workers' housing; the frame shows the alignment the fiche describes — three storeys of rock-faced grey limestone and red brick under flat roofs, one balcony to a level, curving iron stairs climbing to the upper doors, and the street trees. The photographed stretch is between De Rouen and Ontario, north of parc Dézéry.
photo.alt: Photograph of Three-storey workers' plex houses in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (borough of Montréal), from Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005)

types.phase_title: Suburban Mercier — veterans' houses, bungalows, the Olympic Park
types.name_en: Brick bungalow of the 1950s Mercier developments
types.name_fr: Le bungalow de brique des lotissements de Mercier
types.source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sectors 27.U.2, 27.U.3 and 27.U.5
canonical_names: One-storey horizontal house, ≤30° roof, integrated garage

siting_landscape: Whole developments built to one plan, with rows of trees along the sidewalk that the cahier reads as deliberate — « les alignements d'arbres matures en bordure du trottoir, découlant d'un plan d'ensemble organisé, ajoutent à l'harmonie des rues ».
In the 1955 ensemble the streets run in loops, « le type de lotissement qui est popularisé dans les nouvelles banlieues développées après la guerre ».
massing: One storey. In the earliest ensemble (rues Honoré-Beaugrand to Cirier, early 1950s) a square plan with no door on the principal façade at all, only a band of windows set either to the left or to the right.
In the 1955 ensemble (rues Honoré-Beaugrand and Chénier), detached or semi-detached, rectangular or L-plan, hipped or gabled roofs, with or without a carport.
openings: A horizontal window band as the whole of the principal façade's composition, in the earliest ensemble.
materials: Brick throughout, and it stays dominant — in the 1955 ensemble most houses have taken on individuality through changed cladding or windows, « cependant, la plupart respectent leur volume et leur composition d'origine et la brique reste le matériau dominant ».

types.profile_note: Composed from three sector fiches of the Évaluation — 27.U.2 (rues Honoré-Beaugrand to Cirier, early 1950s), 27.U.3 (rue Gustave-Bleau to place Lepailleur, early 1950s, « des bungalows en brique tous identiques ») and 27.U.5 (rues Honoré-Beaugrand and Chénier, 1955) — which describe three different developments rather than one type, and are treated here as one record because the cahier itself groups them under the same category and describes them in the same terms. Where they disagree, both readings are kept: the square doorless plan belongs to 27.U.2 only, the loop streets and the plan variety to 27.U.5 only. Articulation is left empty; none of the three fiches describes ornament. These three sectors are not in this page's sectors.yaml, which holds the five E sectors only.
types.blurb_en: The other post-war Mercier, and the odder one. Identical brick bungalows put up in whole streets in the early 1950s — in one development with no front door at all on the street face, just a band of windows pushed to one side — laid out with rows of trees along the sidewalk that the Ville's surveyors could still recognise fifty years later as part of the original plan.
types.origin_en: Mercier is where the borough turned suburban. The Évaluation notes that the criteria it used to find heritage sectors « n'a pas permis d'identifier beaucoup de secteurs dans la partie est du territoire », and answers itself: « cela ne signifie pas pour autant que cette partie de l'arrondissement ne présente pas d'intérêt. Les qualités d'ensemble de plusieurs rues devraient être maintenues. » That is why these four developments are recorded as ensembles urbains d'intérêt rather than as heritage sectors — the value is in the coherence of a whole street, not in any single house, and the document's own recommendation is to study such territories, « recenser les typologies des ensembles qui présentent une grande homogénéité », and build public awareness of them. It is a recommendation for exactly the kind of record this page is.

types.phase_title: Suburban Mercier — veterans' houses, bungalows, the Olympic Park
types.name_en: Veterans' house, to the Wartime Housing Limited model
types.source_ref: Évaluation du patrimoine urbain (2005), sectors 27.U.1 and 27.U.4; Guide patrimonial de MHM, « Maison des vétérans » types I–III
canonical_names: Wartime or veterans' house, 1½ storeys, to Wartime Housing Limited or NHA plans

siting_landscape: Grouped as whole developments rather than as single houses, laid out to one plan; the borough's ensembles are north of rue de Rouen and along rue Curatteau.
massing: Detached houses of closely similar volume across the whole ensemble — « ces maisons présentent une volumétrie semblable, apportant une harmonie certaine à l'ensemble ».
Two-slope gabled roof.
The borough's Guide distinguishes three variants and notes that type II carries an entrance vestibule (« tambour d'entrée ») and therefore has no columns.
articulation: Guard rails 36 inches high; simple painted metal fascia; painted or natural wooden slat soffits; painted untreated wooden columns where there are any.
Wooden surround mouldings, painted and untreated, around the cladding.
openings: Double-hung windows in a 1/2–1/2 ratio, glazed in uniform clear or frosted glass without patterns, muntins permitted.
Door carrying one glazed panel, optionally divided into nine lights, the glass clear and plain, 91.4 to 124.5 cm high.
materials: Light horizontal wood clapboard in a pale, low-contrast tone harmonised with its surroundings; brick with a two-slope roof in the rue Curatteau ensemble.
Original roof covering is asphalt shingle — stated as such by the Guide for both the maisons des vétérans and the Village Champlain houses.

types.profile_note: Massing and context come from the Évaluation's sector fiches 27.U.1 and 27.U.4; everything under articulation, openings and materials comes from the borough's Guide patrimonial, whose prescriptive tables carry a « Maison des vétérans » column beside the secteur significatif and immeuble significatif columns, with three lettered types. The Guide is a conservation manual, so those lines describe what may be rebuilt today, which is the borough's reading of the original. Sectors 27.U.1 and 27.U.4 are not encoded in this page's sectors.yaml, which carries only the five E sectors of arrondissement 27; the U-sector enumeration is recorded in the header of that file and is Part 10b work. Note the date: the cahier puts these ensembles « autour de 1950 » and the rue Curatteau one in 1953, so they are post-war builders' adoptions of the wartime model rather than Wartime Housing Limited's own construction — « ce modèle fut adopté par la suite par plusieurs promoteurs ».
types.blurb_en: The federal minimal house, arriving in Mercier after the war it was invented for. A detached one-and-a-half-storey box under a two-slope roof, clad in pale clapboard or brick, built in whole streets to one volume so that the ensemble reads as a single gesture — around 1950 north of rue de Rouen, in 1953 on rue Curatteau.
types.origin_en: The Évaluation states the lineage exactly: these ensembles were built « autour de 1950 sur le modèle des maisons de la Wartime Housing Limited. Ce modèle a été développé durant la Deuxième Guerre mondiale pour répondre à la crise du logement qui sévissait alors et pour loger les ouvriers à proximité des entreprises consacrées à l'industrie de guerre. Le modèle fut adopté par la suite par plusieurs promoteurs qui cherchaient à rejoindre un segment de marché composé de personnes désirant habiter une maison individuelle à prix abordable. » That last clause is the whole post-war housing shift in one sentence: a state emergency type turned into a market product. The same object appears on this site at Lévis, in the Sud-Ouest, in Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension, in Parc-Extension and at Verdun's Crawford Park; this is its eastern Montréal instance, and it is the one place in this borough where the cahier uses the word « modèle » of a house at all.

types.blurb_en: The founding house type of TMR. When Frederick Todd laid out the town in 1912 he was borrowing directly from Ebenezer Howard's Garden City movement, and the first houses near the station borrowed the movement's architecture too: the English Arts-and-Crafts cottage of Letchworth and Hampstead Garden Suburb. Look for steep 45° gables, a brick ground floor with stucco or half-timbering above, small-paned windows, and a deliberately picturesque, asymmetrical silhouette that reads as a cottage in a garden rather than a house on a street.
types.origin_en: The Garden City movement's architecture as well as its planning. Ebenezer Howard's 1898 tract produced Letchworth (Parker & Unwin, 1903) and Hampstead Garden Suburb (1907), and their house vocabulary, itself drawn from Voysey, Baillie Scott and the English cottage, travelled with the idea: steep gables, roughcast or half-timbered upper storeys over brick, small-paned casements, picturesque asymmetry, the house read as a cottage in a garden. The by-law's Garden City House is this, with the 45° roof, stucco-and-timber upper floor and small brick module written out as criteria.

types.blurb_en: “Faubourien” refers to the vernacular of Montreal's old inner suburbs (the faubourgs): a plain two-storey brick box, flat or hipped roof, sometimes a false mansard, and a front verandah on wooden columns. In TMR the type is what the Plateau or Rosemont row house becomes when it is given its own lot, a side driveway and a lawn. Its virtue is restraint: symmetry, aligned windows, one material.
types.origin_en: Faubourien points to the maison de faubourg, the plain brick house of Québec's nineteenth-century inner suburbs: two or three storeys, flat or false-mansard roof, aligned openings, minimal ornament, a front gallery on wooden posts. Montreal's Plateau PIIA uses the same term for its own housing stock. In TMR the type is what that urban house becomes on a detached or semi-detached lot with a side driveway; several examples take on the cubic mass and hipped roof of the American Foursquare, which was being built across Canada in the same years.

types.blurb_en: The interwar Montreal walk-up, three storeys of red brick under a flat roof, with a decorated parapet, a stone base, patterned brickwork and a prominent entrance portico. Balconies with iron or stone railings give the façade its rhythm. These sit on the town's few multi-family lots and are the collective sibling of the faubourg house.
types.origin_en: Three-storey brick apartment houses of the 1920s and 30s, Montreal's standard multi-family building of the period. This is where Art Deco actually lives in TMR: stepped and decorated parapets, geometric brick panels, artificial-stone entrance surrounds, iron balcony rails with angular motifs. Héritage Montréal describes the same repertoire on 1920s Montreal plexes (dark brick, artificial-stone insertions around doors and windows, appliqués with geometric forms). The by-law absorbs it as "distinctive brick motifs and bonds" and "a body crowned by a brick motif and a parapet" rather than naming the style.

types.blurb_en: A 1930s–50s revival of the 18th-century Quebec farmhouse: a steep roof whose eaves flare out into “larmiers” that shelter the front door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, and a calm symmetrical front. It was the domestic face of a broader interwar interest in Québécois heritage. The distinctive move is the roof, which is asked to express the base of the house through its overhang.
types.origin_en: A regionalist revival of the eighteenth-century Laurentian farmhouse: bell-cast roof whose eaves flare into larmiers sheltering the door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, a calm symmetrical front. The Canadian Encyclopedia locates its source in the anglophone rediscovery of pre-industrial Québec during the 1920s–30s, stimulated by Clarence Gagnon's paintings and encouraged by Percy Nobbs and Ramsay Traquair at McGill, whose surveys of old Québec buildings fed a fashion for fieldstone and pitched roofs among the province's leading domestic architects. TMR's Canadian houses are the suburban, builder-scale version of that fashion.

types.blurb_en: Colonial Revival as it arrived from the American Northeast: a long, simple gabled rectangle with its broad side to the street, symmetrical windows, dormers set halfway up the roof, and a discreet canopy over the front door. Brick or stone below, clapboard or stucco above. It is quieter than the Georgian house, and the by-law wants it kept quiet: bay windows are the only projections allowed.
types.origin_en: A long side-gabled rectangle with its broad face to the street, symmetrical openings, dormers half-way up the roof, a discreet door canopy; brick or stone below and clapboard or stucco above. It is the New England colonial house as codified in 1920s–40s pattern books and builders' plan services, the quieter cousin of Georgian Revival. The by-law keeps it quiet: bay windows are the only projections it allows.

types.blurb_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment courts arranged in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. A stone base and stone string courses tie them to the collegiate-Tudor mood of the interwar decades. Entrances are marked by a distinct architectural element rather than a big portico.
types.origin_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment blocks in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with stone bases, stone string courses, steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. The idiom is the residential cousin of interwar school and college architecture, and of the "garden apartment" courts built across North America in the 1930s–40s. The by-law's "New England (collective)" label is looser than the architecture: these blocks are more Tudor than New England.

types.blurb_en: Georgian Revival: the most formal of TMR's houses. A red-brick box of two full storeys, three or five bays wide, with a central door flanked by pilasters and topped by an elaborate crown, sash windows with small panes, and a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gabled roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law lets you emphasise the central bay with a slight projection and a pediment, and nothing more.
types.origin_en: The formal wing of Colonial Revival. Two full storeys of red brick, three or five bays, a central door with pilasters and an entablature or pediment, sash windows with small panes, a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gable roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law permits one flourish, a slightly projected central bay under a pediment, and nothing else. In Canada the style carried an Imperial-loyalist inflection that made it a natural fit for a town founded and first settled by anglophones.

types.blurb_en: Tudor Revival, TMR's most romantic type: steep 45° roofs broken into several gables, a natural-stone ground floor with brick or half-timbered stucco above, patterned brickwork (herringbone, Dutch bond), small-paned casements, sometimes a round turret at the entrance. Where the Georgian house is symmetrical, the manor is deliberately picturesque, and its garage is meant to hide.
types.origin_en: The by-law's "English manor" is Tudor Revival by any other name: stone ground floor with brick or stucco-and-timber above, patterned brick (herringbone, Dutch bond), 45° multi-gabled roofs, small-paned casements, sometimes a round entrance turret. In North America the style peaked in the 1920s–30s and lingered into the 1940s; its Montreal fashion was strongest in the anglophone west end and suburbs. Tudor detailing also surfaces on some Phase 1 Garden City houses, which is why the two types share the half-timbered gable.

types.blurb_en: The postwar ranch bungalow: one storey, long and low, with a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, and big undivided windows wider than they are tall. Buff (“chamois”) brick or stone, black shingles, a wide driveway. The type that arrived with the car and the last empty lots of the 1950s and 60s.
types.origin_en: One storey, long and low, a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, big undivided windows wider than tall, buff ("chamois") brick or stone, a wide driveway. In Québec usage bungalow simply means the postwar single-family suburban house; the form is the Ranch house that spread from the American Southwest after 1945 and became the default Canadian suburban dwelling of the 1950s–60s.

Black asphalt shingles, or a tone matched to the cladding colour

types.blurb_en: In Quebec usage a “cottage” is simply a two-storey detached house, and this is its postwar version: a plain box under a low hip roof, stone or brick on the ground floor with stucco or siding above, garage built into the front, and a flat marquise over the door. A visible line at the ground-floor lintels or the upper sills divides base from body.
types.origin_en: In Québec real-estate usage a cottage is a two-storey detached house, as opposed to the one-storey bungalow; the OQLF notes the word's British origin and its earlier sense of an elegant, English-inspired country house. TMR's postwar cottage is a plain box: stone or brick base, stucco or siding above, low hip roof, integrated garage, flat marquise over the door, a horizontal line at the ground-floor lintels or upper sills dividing base from body. Some examples keep vestigial colonial detailing (Minimal Traditional); others, in cut stone with flat roofs and rounded or banded corners, are the town's clearest echo of Streamline Moderne.

types.blurb_en: Two volumes offset by half a storey: a one-storey wing beside a one-and-a-half-storey wing, with the garage tucked under the bedrooms and pushed forward, and a recessed entrance under the eaves. Salmon, buff or brown stone with wood or metal infill panels; both roofs share one low-pitched material. The interior stair does the work the façade shows.
types.origin_en: A plan type more than a style, dominant across North American suburbs from the mid-1950s: two volumes offset by half a storey, the garage under the bedrooms and pushed forward, a recessed entrance under the eaves. TMR's are dressed in Ranch and Contemporary materials, salmon, buff or brown stone with wood or metal infill panels, under one shared low-pitched roof.

types.blurb_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom, filtered through 1960s Montreal: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked right under the eaves and running around the corners as ribbons, long “Roman” brick or long-cut stone, and one-storey wings (garage, porch, solarium) that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical, and the most architect-driven of the phase-3 types.
types.origin_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom of 1900–1915, revived and simplified in the 1950s–60s Contemporary house: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked under the eaves and wrapping the corners as ribbons, long "Roman" brick or long-cut stone, one-storey wings that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical and the most architect-driven of the Phase 3 types; the by-law's insistence on the Roman brick module is the tell.

types.blurb_en: The 1950s–70s modernist apartment building: flat roof finished with a horizontal coping band, a set-back penthouse floor on top, balconies grouped into recessed loggias, wide undivided windows and a marquise over the door. Sand or red brick, often several brick colours on one façade. Parking goes underground; the front yard stays almost entirely green.
types.origin_en: Flat-roofed brick slabs of the 1950s–70s with a horizontal coping band, a set-back penthouse floor, loggia balconies and wide undivided windows, in sand or red brick and often several brick colours on one façade. The town's share of the postwar Modernism that lines Côte-des-Neiges and Sherbrooke; the earliest examples, with brick-and-stone banding, still carry a Streamline accent.

Set on carefully landscaped grounds; the mature trees on the parcels are counted as part of the sector's quality.
massing: Paired under one roofline, each half a single dwelling with its own independent entrance.
articulation: A restricted choice of materials and colours holds the street together, though the houses themselves are stylistically very diverse.
materials: Noble materials — stone and brick — characterise the sector.

types.origin_en: The dominant form of the 1903–1920 build-out. The 2005 evaluation reads the sector's homogeneity as an effect of speed — most of the stock went up inside seventeen years — and of a narrow palette of materials, not of a repeated plan; the houses vary stylistically while the street reads as one thing.

types.origin_en: Outremont's version of the Montréal duplex, and the point where it separates from the Plateau's. The 2005 text describes « des duplex jumelés aux accès indépendants » — the pairing is with the adjoining house and the second dwelling is reached from inside the front door, so the exterior stair that defines the Plateau plex is absent here. Both sit under the same canonical form; the difference is exactly what that page is for.

siting_landscape: The mountain flank, the steepest ground in the borough; lots vary in size because the streets are winding, sometimes switchbacking to avoid the steepest slopes.
The houses along chemin de la Côte-Sainte-Catherine are perched on the upper part of their lots and reached by long staircases.
Streets lined with numerous trees, which the evaluation reads as the source of the sector's picturesque character.
The part south of boulevard du Mont-Royal falls inside the Mount Royal heritage and natural district.
massing: Detached, on large irregular lots; the topography « a favorisé les prouesses architecturales et paysagères ».
articulation: A sampling of styles evocative of the past, alongside the new twentieth-century ones.
materials: Noble materials — stone and brick.

types.blurb_en: The bourgeois house on the mountain flank, in whichever past the owner preferred.
types.origin_en: Édouard Gohier's Northmount Land Company began subdividing the flank in 1906, and the 1920s and 1930s filled it. The 2005 evaluation makes no attempt to reduce the result to a type: it records a sampling of revival styles on lots whose shape the slope dictated. 728 avenue Pratt, néoclassique, 1937, is one documented example.

siting_landscape: Avenue Bernard between rue Hutchison and avenue McEachran, where 75 % of the buildings date from the 1920s.
Front setbacks of about 3 metres; the front grounds are most often paved rather than planted.
Also on the south side of avenue Willowdale, opened in 1911, and along avenue Van Horne, the working quarter's commercial artery.
massing: Three or four storeys, multi-family.
articulation: On avenue Willowdale, some display a strong Art déco influence.
materials: Half-basements and ground floors generally occupied by shops.

types.origin_en: The conciergerie is what avenue Bernard is made of. The 2005 evaluation attributes the street's harmony to a single fact — three-quarters of its buildings went up in the 1920s — and names the multi-family walk-up with commerce in the half-basement and ground floor as the dominant architectural type. The cinéma Outremont, given municipal heritage status in 2000 and since fully restored, stands on the same street.

canonical_names: Detached or row bourgeois urban house, stone-faced, 2–3 storeys, ornamented

siting_landscape: Front setback that may exceed 5 metres; small side setbacks of 1 to 2 metres.
Oldest examples (1850–1880) on rue Sherbrooke; from the 1900s, rarely, on rue Saint-Hubert, rue Rachel and avenue du Parc-La Fontaine. Many converted to offices or flats.
massing: Centred door; a projecting element may form an oriel or forebody. No sub-variant.
materials: Uniform stone cladding and a higher degree of ornamentation than the duplex (family description).

types.origin_en: Built for the well-to-do west of Saint-Laurent and south of avenue des Pins, then along Sherbrooke, Square Saint-Louis and Saint-Hubert; the family also includes a two-unit superposed variant that differs from the duplex by storeys per dwelling, uniform stone facing and richer ornament.

types.phase_title: The golden age of development
types.name_fr: Le duplex sans marge de recul avant
types.source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, fiche 2.1
canonical_names: Two-storey, two-dwelling brick box, flat roof, superposed units, cornice or parapet

siting_landscape: Party-wall building with no front or side setback.
The base type from which the other duplex variants derive; oldest subdivisions (Ferme Bagg, Courville, Ferme Comte, rue Pontiac, rue Drolet, Village des Carrières).
massing: Rectangular body without projections, two storeys very slightly raised above grade, flat roof.
Possibly a small balcony above the entrance doors (rarely more than one third of the façade width).
Upper dwelling reached by an interior stair.
articulation: Base of the building marked by one or two courses of rusticated stone.
Paired doors at one end of the façade; openings aligned vertically and horizontally; no significant variation in the choice or placement of cladding.
Crown formed by a moulded cornice, more or less elaborate.
openings: Sash or casement windows without muntins, with or without transom.
Doors with or without transom; transom height about one quarter to one fifth of the door.
Lintels of dressed stone or of soldier-course clay brick; on rusticated-stone buildings the surrounds are dressed stone and the lintel is often absorbed into a band running the width of the façade.
materials: Clay brick dominant; occasional rusticated stone cladding.

implantation: Édifice mitoyen sans marge de recul avant ou latérale.
volumetrie: Corps de bâti rectangulaire sans saillies, 2 étages avec une très faible surélévation par rapport au niveau du sol, toit plat, possibilité d'un petit balcon au-dessus des portes d'entrée.
traitement_des_facades: Socle du bâtiment démarqué par un ou deux rangs de pierre à bossage. Portes jumelées à l'une des extrémités de la façade, ouvertures alignées verticalement et horizontalement, aucune variation importante dans le choix ou la disposition des matériaux de revêtement. Couronnement avec corniche moulurée plus ou moins ouvragée, selon le cas.
ouvertures: Fenêtres à guillotine ou à battants sans carreaux avec ou sans imposte. Portes avec ou sans imposte, hauteur de l'imposte : approximativement 1/4 à 1/5 de celle de la porte. Les linteaux des ouvertures sont composés d'un élément de pierre de taille ou d'un appareillage de briques d'argile en soldat. Dans le cas des bâtiments revêtus de pierre à bossage, l'encadrement des ouvertures est formé de pierre de taille; le linteau est alors souvent intégré à un bandeau qui couvre la largeur de la façade.
materiaux: Dominance de la brique d'argile, revêtement occasionnel de pierre à bossage.
sous_variantes: Petit balcon au-dessus du porche d'entrée
Revêtement de pierre à bossage
Porte cochère

types.source_generation: 2004-22 Annexe D
types.blurb_en: The plainest and oldest plex: two superposed flats in a brick box built right on the sidewalk line, paired front doors at one end, an interior stair to the upper flat, and a moulded cornice as the only crown. Its three sub-variants add a small entrance balcony, rusticated stone facing, or a porte cochère.
types.origin_en: The duplex was the first housing type built in the borough under the large speculative subdivisions of the 1880s and belongs to the first construction boom of 1885–1891. It is the developer's product of the pre-1880 regime, before Montréal imposed the front setback: a simple rectangle of two flats, one over the other, that the later duplexes and the triplex all descend from.

types.phase_title: The golden age of development
types.name_fr: Le duplex avec marge de recul avant
types.source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, fiche 2.2
canonical_names: Two-storey, two-dwelling brick box, flat roof, superposed units, cornice or parapet
types.style_label: Montréal faubourg vernacular / Second Empire / mansard / Victorian eclecticism

siting_landscape: Front setback of 1 to 2 metres.
massing: Rectangular body without projections; two storeys with the ground floor raised fewer than 8 risers above grade; flat roof; balcony generally present above the entrance porch.
Occasional front gallery on the ground floor and sometimes the upper floor; small straight entrance stair.
Frequent use of a false-mansard roof.
articulation: Base marked by courses of rusticated stone.
Paired doors at one end of the façade; openings aligned vertically and horizontally.

On flat-roofed buildings, crown marked by a moulded cornice; on false-mansard buildings, pedimented or round-arched dormers generally aligned with the wall plane, the dormer over the balcony often raised to form a stronger crown above the entrance axis.
openings: Sash or casement windows without muntins, with or without transom; proportion 1 width = ½ height.
Doors with or without transom; transom about one quarter of the door height.
Lintels expressed by a dressed-stone band or a soldier course of clay brick.
materials: Clay brick dominant; occasional rusticated stone cladding.

implantation: Marge de recul avant de 1 à 2 mètres.
volumetrie: Corps de bâti rectangulaire sans saillies, 2 étages avec une surélévation du rez-de-chaussée par rapport au niveau du sol inférieure à 8 contremarches, toit plat, balcon généralement présent au-dessus du porche d'entrée.
traitement_des_facades: Socle du bâtiment démarqué par des rangs de pierre à bossage. Portes jumelées à l'une des extrémités de la façade, ouvertures alignées verticalement et horizontalement… Pour les bâtiments à toit plat, couronnement démarqué par une corniche moulurée plus ou moins ouvragée.

Fausse mansarde : lucarnes à fronton ou en arc cintré généralement alignées avec le plan du mur. La lucarne située au-dessus du balcon est souvent surhaussée et forme un couronnement plus marqué pour l'alignement principal des portes d'entrée.
ouvertures: Fenêtres à guillotine ou à battants sans carreaux avec ou sans imposte, proportion de 1 largeur = 1/2 hauteur. Portes avec ou sans imposte, hauteur de l'imposte : environ 1/4 de celle de la porte. Linteaux des ouvertures exprimés par un bandeau de pierre de taille ou par un appareillage de briques d'argile en soldat.
materiaux: Dominance de la brique d'argile, revêtement occasionnel de pierre à bossage.
sous_variantes: Galerie sur toute la largeur (rez-de-chaussée et étage)
Toiture en fausse mansarde avec lucarnes

types.source_generation: 2004-22 Annexe D
types.blurb_en: The same two-flat box pulled back a metre or two from the sidewalk, which is enough to raise the ground floor a few steps, hang a balcony over the porch and, very often, top the façade with a false mansard and dormers. This is the duplex most people picture: the one with the mansard.
types.origin_en: Around 1880 Montréal began applying building by-laws to the new districts: standardised lots and lanes, then a mandatory front setback and stone or brick cladding. The setback produced this variant. Its false-mansard crown is the Second Empire fashion of the 1870s–80s applied to a speculative type; the mansard is decorative (a fausse mansarde), not a full storey.

types.phase_title: The golden age of development
types.source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, fiche 2.3
canonical_names: Two-storey, two-dwelling brick box, flat roof, superposed units, cornice or parapet

siting_landscape: With a front setback.
Mainly in the landscape units of the east and north of the borough.
massing: Rectangular body without projections; two storeys with the ground floor raised 1 to 4 risers; flat roof; upper-floor balcony and exterior stair to reach the upper flat.
articulation: Foundation little marked; cladding may change between ground floor and upper floor.
Horizontal symmetry: an axis of doors at the centre with an axis of windows on each side; openings aligned horizontally.
Crown marked by a moulded cornice or a parapet with or without pediment.
openings: Sash or casement windows without muntins and without transom; proportion 1 width = ½ height; a few square windows with fixed or sliding panels.
Doors with or without transom; transom less than a quarter of the door height.
Lintel of dressed stone or soldier-course clay brick.
materials: Clay brick dominant; occasional stone cladding.

implantation: Avec marge de recul avant.
volumetrie: Corps de bâti rectangulaire sans saillies, 2 étages avec une surélévation du rez-de-chaussée de 1 à 4 contremarches, toit plat, balcon à l'étage et escalier extérieur pour rejoindre l'étage.
traitement_des_facades: Fondation peu démarquée, changement possible de matériaux de revêtement entre le rez-de-chaussée et l'étage. Symétrie horizontale formée d'un alignement de portes au centre et d'un alignement de fenêtres de chaque côté de la façade, ouvertures alignées horizontalement. Couronnement marqué par une corniche moulurée ou un parapet avec ou sans fronton.
ouvertures: Fenêtres à guillotine ou à battants sans carreaux et sans imposte, proportion : 1 largeur = 1/2 hauteur, quelques cas de fenêtres de proportion carrée avec panneaux fixes ou coulissants. Portes avec ou sans imposte, hauteur de l'imposte : moins du quart de celle de la porte. Linteau de pierre de taille ou composé d'un appareillage de briques d'argile en soldat.
materiaux: Dominance de la brique d'argile, revêtement occasionnel en pierre.
sous_variantes: Il n'y a pas de sous-variante.

types.source_generation: 2004-22 Annexe D
types.blurb_en: Two flats, but the upper one now has its own door and its own stair climbing the front of the house. The façade turns symmetrical, doors in the middle, windows either side, and the cornice can give way to a brick parapet. It is the duplex learning the triplex's trick.
types.origin_en: Built from the same moment as the triplex (type 3.2) and the multiplex (3.3), i.e. the second boom of 1904–1914. The exterior stair is the direct consequence of the mandatory front setback: with the building pushed back, the stair to the upper dwelling could be moved outside and the interior floor area given back to the flats.

types.source_ref: PIIA 2004-22 Annexe D, fiche 3.2 (fiche not yet retrieved); Étude typomorphologique 2003; unité de paysage 4.7 fiche
canonical_names: Three-storey, three-dwelling brick building with exterior stair to upper units, flat roof

siting_landscape: Front setback; rectangular plan occupying almost the whole parcel, or an inverted L-plan mirrored from one building to the next; twin buildings on two parcels often read as one.
massing: Three storeys; ground floor raised 0 to 5 risers; flat roof; exterior stair to the upper dwellings.
Occasional narrow balconies on the second and third levels; projecting bay windows are rare.
materials: Clay brick in beige or brown tones; stair and balcony with wood floors and metal railings.

types.profile_note: Fiche 3.2 not yet retrieved; siting, massing and materials taken from the Étude typomorphologique and from the unité de paysage 4.7 fiche, which describe the same type. Articulation and openings left empty rather than inferred. Numbering caveat: the Sud-Ouest borough labels the same form "type 2.6"; codes are document-specific.
types.source_generation: 2004-22 Annexe D
types.blurb_en: The Montréal triplex: three flats stacked in a three-storey brick front, the upper two reached by an outside stair, often the famous curving iron one, with balconies at each level and an L-shaped footprint that leaves a light-well at the back. It is the dominant building of the borough.
types.origin_en: The Étude typomorphologique calls the triplex "la forme architecturale typique de ce secteur de Montréal" and dates it to the second boom, 1904–1914, driven by housing demand and by municipal regulation: standard lots and lanes (1880), then the mandatory front setback and stone or brick cladding, which "amènera la translation de l'escalier d'accès aux logements des étages supérieurs vers l'extérieur". Réjean Legault (1989) is the standard scholarly account.

types.phase_title: Seigneurial côtes and the fur-trade posts
types.name_en: Stone house of the French tradition
types.name_fr: La maison de pierre de tradition française
types.source_ref: Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec, fiches 93274 (site patrimonial Le Ber-Le Moyne, Lachine), 93440 (maison Rangé-dit-Laviolette, Baie-D'Urfé) et 92796 (maison Hyacinthe-Jamme-dit-Carrière, Pointe-Claire); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissements de Lachine, de Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé et de Pointe-Claire (2005)
canonical_names: Urban stone house of French inspiration, one or two levels plus attic, two-slope roof, chimneys in fire-break party walls
types.roofing: cedar shingle at Le Ber-Le Moyne; ribbed copper sheet at Pointe-Claire today, over an original wood shingle

siting_landscape: Each of the three survivors sits on ground that predates the street grid around it. Le Ber-Le Moyne stands on a raised point of land beside lac Saint-Louis at the head of the Lachine rapids, on a slight mound planted with mature trees.

The Baie-D'Urfé house stands at the back of its lot, about a hundred metres from the public road and close to the shore, its main front turned south to the lake and the îles Sainte-Geneviève — RPCQ reads that orientation as evidence that the chemin du Roy once ran between the house and the water.

Pointe-Claire's house stands at the far end of a large treed lot that now isolates it from the postwar subdivision around it, on a censive conceded by the Sulpicians in 1722 along the côte Saint-Jean.
massing: A low stone carré on a near-square or short rectangular plan, one and a half storeys, sitting close to the ground. The Baie-D'Urfé carré measures 9.4 by 9.3 m.

Steep two-slope roof with straight slopes. Eaves are shallow at Lachine, and carried out over a covered gallery at Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire — in both cases a nineteenth-century alteration, not an original feature.
Ancillary buildings belong to the type where they survive - Lachine keeps a stone dépendance of the same date, and an 1781 census records a house, a barn and a stable at Baie-D'Urfé.
articulation: Almost none in the original fabric. What ornament these houses carry — moulded wood chambranles, gable dormers, a neo-Gothic porch, a bell-cast eave — was added between about 1828 and 1874 to bring them up to date.
openings: Openings set out asymmetrically, which RPCQ names as a French-tradition trait at both Baie-D'Urfé and Pointe-Claire.
Casement windows with small panes. At Pointe-Claire the south front is opened up for light while the north wall carries only two windows.
materials: Fieldstone throughout, laid up rubble. Pointe-Claire is left bare, and RPCQ names the absence of crépi as a Montréal-region trait; Baie-D'Urfé is whitewashed on three sides.
Two chimney stacks carried up in the line of the gable walls — the trait RPCQ singles out as belonging "plus particulièrement" to the houses of the island of Montréal and its neighbouring regions.

description: « Les deux bâtiments en pierre de plan rectangulaire s'élèvent sur un étage et sont coiffés d'un toit aigu à deux versants droits aux larmiers peu saillants. »
« Fenêtre(s) : Rectangulaire, À battants, à petits carreaux »

« La partie la plus ancienne présente un plan presque carré, comporte des murs en pierre chaulés sur trois côtés et s'élève sur un étage et demi. Elle est couverte d'un toit à deux versants droits aux larmiers débordants couvrant une galerie du côté sud. Deux cheminées s'élèvent dans la continuité des murs pignon. »

« Construite au tournant du XVIIIe siècle, la maison possède des éléments qui se rattachent à la tradition architecturale d'inspiration française, comme le carré en pierre peu dégagé du sol et la disposition asymétrique des ouvertures. Le plan presque carré et les cheminées qui s'élèvent dans la continuité des murs pignon, plus particulièrement associés aux maisons de l'île de Montréal et des régions environnantes, sont aussi des caractéristiques de l'architecture de cette époque. »
contexte: « La maison LeBer-LeMoyne, dont l'importance patrimoniale est exceptionnelle, a été reconnue par un classement en vertu de la Loi sur les biens culturels en 2001. Elle date du Régime français et est l'une des plus anciennes au Canada. Avec son site, elle rappelle la vocation agricole et commerciale des débuts de Lachine. » (Lachine, 19.E.4)

« Le chemin du Lakeshore regroupe la plus grande densité de bâtiments d'intérêt patrimonial de l'arrondissement. Son parcours comprend d'anciennes maisons de ferme, des maisons bourgeoises et des villas d'été de la fin du XIXe siècle et du début du XXe siècle qui nous sont parvenues avec des degrés d'authenticité divers. » (Beaconsfield–Baie-D'Urfé, 4.I.1)

« … le moulin banal (1709-1710), classé bien archéologique en 1983, la maison Hyacinthe-Jamme dit Carrière (vers 1780), classée monument historique en 1964 par le ministère des Affaires culturelles, ainsi que d'autres maisons des XVIIIe et XIXe siècles. » (Pointe-Claire, 3.1)
elements_caracteristiques: « Elle illustre ce type par son corps de logis bas en pierre, son élévation d'un étage et demi, son toit aigu à deux versants, ses deux cheminées logées dans les murs pignons, ses ouvertures disposées de manière asymétrique et ses fenêtres à battants à petits carreaux. »
« Le plan presque carré et l'absence de crépi sont des éléments fréquemment associés à la maison d'inspiration française de la région de Montréal. »
« Elle est l'une des rares maisons de ferme datant de la fin du XVIIIe siècle à subsister à l'intérieur des terres de Pointe-Claire. »

types.profile_note: A thin record by design, and honest about it. None of the six West Island places has a per-type typology document — no inventory, no thesaurus, no per-type table — so this record is built from the three individual houses that do carry statutory records, plus the three 2005 Ville de Montréal évaluation cahiers, which characterise sectors and not building types. What that leaves empty: `window_proportion` is null because all three RPCQ fiches describe the windows as casements with small panes and none gives a proportion; `roof.pitch_deg` is null because the fiches say "aigu" and "à pente moyenne" and never a figure; `lot_width_m`, `setback_front_m`, `setback_side_m` and `front_yard_green_pct` are null because no source measures a lot or a setback anywhere in the West Island; `sectors` is null because a shared record cannot carry sector codes that exist in only one of its places. `storeys` is entered as 1.5 from the RPCQ "Nombre d'étages" field, which reads 1½ for all three — note that the Le Ber-Le Moyne description text contradicts its own data field, saying the buildings "s'élèvent sur un étage". The canonical is `french-urban-house-stone` rather than `french-rural-house-1st-hip` even though all three are farm or trading-post houses in open country: the discriminant in this vocabulary is fabric and roof, not siting, and all three are stone under a straight two-slope roof with stacks in the gable walls, where the rural canonical is pièce-sur-pièce timber under a hip carried to the wall head with no cellar. RPCQ says as much itself, calling the nearby Sainte-Anne example « la maison rurale d'inspiration urbaine, fréquente dans la région de Montréal et les régions avoisinantes ». The phase is p1 and marked provisional: Lachine's house is 1669–71 and Baie-D'Urfé's about 1700, both inside p1, but Pointe-Claire's classed survivor was built between 1769 and 1791, inside p2 — RPCQ states plainly that this building tradition « se poursuit au-delà de la Conquête (1760) », so the type is filed at its origin and the reader is told the fabric outlives it.
conservation: All three houses are protected individually, and none of the three village or shore ensembles around them is. Lachine's is a classed site patrimonial (2001) covering the exteriors and the land; Pointe-Claire's is a classed immeuble patrimonial (1964-08-12) covering exterior, interior and land; Baie-D'Urfé's is a municipal citation (2001) covering only the exterior envelope of the oldest, eastern section.
types.source_generation: three RPCQ statements of heritage value (valeur patrimoniale + éléments caractéristiques) read against three sector-characterisation cahiers; no source publishes a per-type table for any West Island place, so the five columns are assembled from the three classed or cited houses themselves
types.blurb_en: A low fieldstone box of one and a half storeys under a steep two-slope roof, stacks rising inside the gable walls, openings placed where they were wanted rather than where symmetry asked for them. Three of them survive across three of the six West Island places — a trading post of 1669–71 at Lachine, a farm house of about 1700 at Baie-D'Urfé, and one of 1769–91 at Pointe-Claire — and all three are protected individually while nothing around them is. One record, three municipalities: the photograph on this card is Lachine's, and Baie-D'Urfé's and Pointe-Claire's stand beside it on the type page.
types.origin_en: The Sulpicians became seigneurs of the island of Montréal in 1663 and conceded the côtes that run out to its western end; the houses built on those concessions were stone because stone was what the fields gave up and because fire and raiding made anything else a poor bet. What survives is very little. Lachine's is the oldest and least altered: two rectangular stone buildings put up in 1669–71 as a fur-trade post for Charles Le Moyne and Jacques Le Ber, restored in the 1980s toward their seventeenth-century appearance and now the Musée de Lachine. Baie-D'Urfé's was built about 1700 by Hubert Rangé dit Laviolette on a concession he bought in 1695, and then quietly rebuilt by the Pilon family between 1839 and 1874 — the walls raised, the roof pitch eased off, moulded chambranles and projecting eaves added in what RPCQ calls a taste imported after the Conquest. Pointe-Claire's went up between 1769 and 1791 on a censive conceded in 1722, and was altered again in 1828. Read together the three make the point the West Island pages keep making: the form is one form across three municipalities, the protection is three separate individual instruments granted in 1964, 2001 and 2001, and not one of them protects an ensemble.
