The nine addresses the City names — 11 place Freeman, 1711 boulevard Saint-Louis, 95 boulevard des Estacades, 9350 and 12320 rue Notre-Dame Ouest, 1004-1030 rue Sainte-Cécile, 132 rue Toupin, 1029-1031 rue Saint-Paul, 96 rue Lacroix — return no results on Wikimedia Commons, and the City's own fiche photographs are its property and are not reproduced here. Link out to the fiche instead.
photo.alt: Photograph of Arts & Crafts house houses in Trois-Rivières, from Ville de Trois-Rivières

types.phase_title: The wave: Québec's third city
types.name_fr: L'immeuble de trois étages avec escalier extérieur
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), sector fiches 21.I.2, 21.I.5 and 21.I.6
canonical_names: Three-storey, three-dwelling brick building with exterior stair to upper units, flat roof

siting_landscape: Dense continuous street frontage on lots of conventional width served by back lanes; 21.I.6 records lanes laid out in an "H" and lots of more restricted depth than the Montréal standard.
The 1900–1920 wave filled the ground the dike had made buildable, working outward from the water plant and Vieux-Verdun.
massing: Three storeys, one dwelling to a floor, flat roofed, with the stair to the upper doors climbing the outside of the building. 21.I.5 records the same form at two storeys as well.
articulation: Elaborate cornices and worked masonry detail; alcoves recessed into the façade composition rather than balconies projecting from it.
The cahier's verdict on the whole group is one sentence — « Ces constructions sont typiquement montréalaises. »
openings: Vertical windows carrying stained glass.
materials: Brick, with stone façades on a minority of buildings.

description: « Constitué généralement d'immeubles de trois étages avec escalier extérieur pour l'accès aux étages, il s'est développé au cours de la vague de 1900 à 1920. On y observe surtout des bâtiments en brique avec des corniches élaborées et des détails de maçonnerie. Les fenêtres sont verticales et possèdent des vitraux. Les façades comportent souvent des alcôves dans la composition. Ces constructions sont typiquement montréalaises. » (21.I.2, le voisinage Nord)

« Principalement constitué d'immeubles de trois étages avec escalier extérieur pour l'accès aux étages, il s'est développé à partir du début du XXe siècle sur un lotissement de largeur conventionnelle mais de profondeur plus restreinte et comprenant des ruelles en « H ». Le secteur est dense; il s'agit en général de bâtiments en brique avec des corniches élaborées et des détails de maçonnerie. Quelques immeubles ont des façades de pierre. » (21.I.6, le secteur des Avenues)
volumetrie: « Le cadre bâti, assez hétérogène, est constitué d'immeubles de deux ou trois étages avec escalier extérieur pour l'accès aux étages; il s'est développé au cours de la vague de 1900 à 1920. » (21.I.5)
implantation: « … érigés sur des lots de largeur conventionnelle, assez profonds et dotés de ruelles. » (21.I.5)
ouvertures: « Les fenêtres sont verticales et comportent des vitraux. » (21.I.5, 21.I.6)

types.profile_note: The Évaluation is a sector characterisation, not a type table, so this record is assembled rather than transcribed. Every column is read out of three sector fiches that describe the same building in the same words — 21.I.2 (le voisinage Nord), 21.I.5 (le secteur Rielle et de Verdun) and 21.I.6 (le secteur des Avenues) — plus 21.I.1, which calls the same fabric « le cadre bâti le plus ancien de Verdun … d'une agréable uniformité ». All four are secteurs de valeur intéressante, so `sectors` is left null rather than pointing at an exceptional-value code the type does not belong to; the ten 21.I sectors are Part 10b. Lot width, setback and dwelling count are not given anywhere in the cahier and are left null; "triplex" is entered as the tenure plan because the fiches say three storeys with one access per storey, not because the document uses the word. The cahier never uses "plex", "duplex avec escalier extérieur" or "triplex" at all.
types.source_generation: sector characterisation, three fiches read together
types.blurb_en: Three flats stacked behind a brick front, one to a floor, each reached by its own door and the upper two by a stair climbing the outside. Built through the 1900–1920 wave on lanes laid out in an H, it is what most of northern Verdun is made of, and the cahier disposes of it in five words: typically Montréal.
types.origin_en: Verdun's plex is the Montréal plex, arriving late and all at once. The 2005 cahier dates the fabric to « la vague de 1900 à 1920 » in three separate sector fiches and links it directly to the dike: residential development « prend son envol au début du XXe siècle, après la mise en place de la digue protégeant le territoire des fortes inondations printanières ». The mechanism that puts the stair outside is not explained here — for that see the shared explainer at /topics/escalier-exterieur/ and the Sud-Ouest synthèse, which traces it to the compulsory front setback. What Verdun adds is the counter-case: the cahier's fiche 21.I.7 records that south of avenue Desmarchais « il y a peu d'escaliers extérieurs, mais la présence des balcons avant s'affirme ». One borough, one form, and a line across it where the stair goes back indoors.

photo.credit: Boulevard LaSalle at rue Hickson, Verdun — a continuous brick frontage of plexes with straight iron stairs climbing to the upper doors, elaborate cornices, and the water plant's neighbourhood behind. Photograph by Denis Tremblay for Parcours riverain – Ville de Montréal, CC BY 2.0. Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BoulevardLasalleVerdun.jpg
photo.note: The camera is at rue Hickson, which fiche 21.I.2 names as the boundary of le voisinage Nord — « Ce secteur situé entre l'usine d'alimentation d'eau, la rue Hickson et le Vieux-Verdun ». The buildings in frame are the ones that fiche describes.
photo.alt: Photograph of Three-storey plex with exterior stair houses in Verdun (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: The wave: Québec's third city
types.name_en: Two semi-detached duplexes, or a three-dwelling building, with deep front balconies
types.name_fr: L'ensemble de deux duplex jumelés ou à trois logements
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), sector fiches 21.E.2 and 21.E.3, with 21.I.7
canonical_names: Plex — the Montréal family of two to six stacked dwellings on a narrow lot

siting_landscape: Buildings paired two by two along the street; on avenue Desmarchais a broad landscaped median runs between the two frontages and, in the cahier's words, opens the atmosphere out.
Ground-floor level is held almost constant along the whole avenue, which is what produces the homogeneity the fiche singles out.
massing: Two storeys. Either two duplexes built as a semi-detached pair, or a single building of three dwellings in which the largest is on the ground floor.
Deep balconies across the front. The cahier records no exterior stair here.
articulation: Deep balconies with refined woodwork ("boiseries raffinées") adorning the façades — the phrase is repeated word for word in both sectors.
Elaborate cornices and masonry detail (21.I.7, for the same fabric continuing south).
openings: Tall vertical windows ornamented with stained glass, often combined in groups of two or three.
materials: Brick cladding.

description: « De chaque côté, on trouve des habitations de deux étages de diverses typologies, notamment des ensembles de deux duplex jumelés ou à trois logements dont le plus vaste est au rez-de-chaussée. L'ensemble présente une belle homogénéité. Le niveau du rez-de-chaussée est sensiblement uniforme sur toute l'avenue. » (21.E.2, l'avenue Desmarchais)
« Ce secteur est exceptionnel en raison de sa grande uniformité de typologie et d'état de conservation. Les bâtiments sont, ici aussi, à parement de brique … » (21.E.3, le voisinage Moffat)
revetement: « Les bâtiments sont à parement de brique avec de hautes fenêtres verticales et ornées de vitraux, souvent combinées en groupes de deux ou trois. » (21.E.2; the same sentence recurs at 21.E.3 and 21.I.7)
ornementation: « Des balcons profonds aux boiseries raffinées ornent les façades. » (21.E.2, 21.E.3 and 21.I.7 — three times, unchanged)
contexte: « À partir de l'avenue Desmarchais, le cadre bâti prend une composition différentiée des développements précédents. En évoluant vers le sud, l'espace se dégage et la hauteur des bâtiments se généralise à deux étages. Il y a peu d'escaliers extérieurs, mais la présence des balcons avant s'affirme. » (21.I.7, le secteur Woodland et de Verdun)

types.profile_note: The Évaluation publishes no per-type table, so this record is assembled from sector paragraphs. Its two exceptional-value sectors, 21.E.2 avenue Desmarchais and 21.E.3 le voisinage Moffat, carry one building description between them: 21.E.3 is four lines long and describes the buildings only by back-reference, « ici aussi ». The columns are therefore filled from 21.E.2, checked against 21.E.3, and extended with 21.I.7 (le secteur Woodland et de Verdun), whose fabric the cahier explicitly begins « à partir de l'avenue Desmarchais » and which repeats the balcony sentence verbatim. Dwelling count is deliberately left as the source has it — the fiche allows either two duplexes paired or one building of three dwellings, and gives no way to tell which is commoner — so the canonical link is to the plex family rather than to one of its seven children. Stair position is not stated in either E fiche; 21.I.7 says of the same fabric that exterior stairs are few, and that is recorded as context rather than promoted into the massing column.
types.source_generation: sector characterisation, two exceptional-value fiches read with one interesting-value fiche
types.blurb_en: Two storeys of brick, tall stained-glass windows in twos and threes, and a deep front balcony with carpentry worth describing — either two duplexes built as a pair or one building of three flats with the largest below. It is the form the 2005 evaluation twice calls exceptional, and the only Verdun housing it says that about.
types.origin_en: These are the two residential sectors Verdun's evaluation ranks as exceptional, and they sit in the southern half of the borough, where the cahier says the fabric changes: from avenue Desmarchais southward the space opens up, heights settle at two storeys, exterior stairs become few and the front balcony takes over. That is a genuine typological boundary inside one small borough, and the document draws it in a single sentence. What is protected at Desmarchais and Moffat is not a rare building but an unbroken one: 21.E.3 is judged exceptional « en raison de sa grande uniformité de typologie et d'état de conservation » — the value is in the run, not the unit. Both sectors are inside the territory the 2019– PIIA modernisation brought under review.

photo.credit: « Desmarchais Boulevard, Verdun » — postcard by J. Sykes, Verdun, Que., between 1931 and 1950. Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec, which states « Domaine public au Canada » under the Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0; tagged PD-old-70 on Wikimedia Commons. BAnQ record: https://numerique.banq.qc.ca/patrimoine/details/52327/5130921. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Desmarchais_Boulevard,_Verdun.jpg
photo.licence: Public domain (BAnQ « Domaine public au Canada », CC PDM 1.0; Commons PD-old-70)
photo.note: The avenue as the sector fiche describes it, seventy years before the fiche — the broad landscaped median down the middle, two-storey brick fronts paired two by two on both sides, deep balconies with turned woodwork, and open ground at the far end where the street had not yet been built out. Commons dates it c. 1935; BAnQ's own record gives « entre 1931 et 1950 », which is used here.
photo.alt: Photograph of Two semi-detached duplexes, or a three-dwelling building, with deep front balconies houses in Verdun (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: The wave: Québec's third city
types.name_en: Three-storey commercial block with dwellings above and alcove balconies
types.name_fr: L'immeuble commercial de trois étages avec logements aux étages
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), sector fiches 21.E.1B and 21.E.1C, with 21.I.5
canonical_names: Mixed commercial-residential block, flat roof, shops below and dwellings above

siting_landscape: Built hard to the property line on both sides of the street, with no setback. Rue de l'Église is fifty feet wide, and the cahier says the result « projette une image très urbaine ».
Rue Wellington runs the length of the borough as its commercial axis; rue de l'Église is one of Verdun's two founding routes and carries its oldest commercial buildings.
massing: Three storeys generally — shops at ground level, dwellings above. Ground floors are at street level and entered without steps.
articulation: The commercial storey is separated from the residential storeys by an elaborate cornice.
Because there is no setback to project into, the balconies serving the upper dwellings are cut back into the wall plane instead. The cahier calls this « une typologie originale ».
On rue de l'Église the frontage is deliberately various — « une grande variété de caractéristiques, créant une composition éclectique » — and the façades are generally ornamented.
openings: Tall shopfront windows with a transom over.
materials: Brick, with worked stone inserted at lintels, jambs and sills; stone façades on rue de l'Église.

description: « On y retrouve un ensemble de bâtiments généralement de trois étages, occupés au rez-de-chaussée par des commerces et aux étages par des logements. L'accès aux espaces commerciaux est de plain-pied. » (21.E.1B, la rue Wellington)
traitement_des_facades: « Les vitrines commerciales sont hautes et dotées d'un tympan, et l'étage commercial est démarqué des étages résidentiels par une corniche élaborée. Les immeubles étant construits à la limite de la propriété, une typologie originale s'est développée pour doter les logements de balcons en alcôve. » (21.E.1B)
revetement: « Les façades sont généralement en brique avec des insertions de pierre travaillée aux linteaux, jambages et allèges. » (21.E.1B)

« Les parements de façade sont la brique ou la pierre, et les façades sont généralement ornementées. La hauteur générale des bâtiments est de trois étages et les rez-de-chaussée sont au niveau du sol. » (21.E.1C, la rue de l'Église)
contexte: « La rue de Verdun reprend un peu la typologie commerciale de la rue Wellington, avec ses immeubles de trois étages, ses hautes vitrines de façade, ses corniches et ses balcons en alcôve aux étages supérieurs (résidentiels). » (21.I.5, le secteur Rielle et de Verdun)

types.profile_note: Assembled from sector paragraphs, not from a type table: the Évaluation publishes none. 21.E.1B supplies the massing, the articulation and the materials; 21.E.1C confirms the height, the ground-floor level and the cladding for the second street; 21.E.1A supplies the institutional context and is listed because the three lettered parts are one sector in the document. 21.I.5 is quoted as context because it records the same building repeated on a third street. The record is kept as residential (`is_residential` left at its default) because the cahier defines the type by what is above the shop — « aux étages par des logements » — and because the alcove balcony, the one feature the document calls an original Verdun typology, is a dwelling feature. No dwelling count, lot width or date is given anywhere in the cahier for this form and those fields are left null.
types.source_generation: sector characterisation, two exceptional-value fiches
types.blurb_en: Shops on the ground, flats above, three storeys, built flush to the lot line so there is nowhere for a balcony to project — so the balcony is cut back into the wall instead. The 2005 evaluation calls that alcove balcony an original typology, and it is the one thing in this document that is Verdun's own.
types.origin_en: Two streets meeting at right angles carry the whole of Verdun's commercial fabric: rue Wellington, its commercial axis end to end, and rue de l'Église, one of the two tracés fondateurs — the old chemin de la côte Saint-Paul — with the oldest shops in the borough. Both were built to the property line, which is where the interesting part comes from. The setback that pushed the stair outdoors in the residential streets does not exist here, so there is no room for a projecting balcony; the response was to hollow one out of the wall. The cahier states the causation plainly: « Les immeubles étant construits à la limite de la propriété, une typologie originale s'est développée pour doter les logements de balcons en alcôve. » It spread — fiche 21.I.5 finds the same section repeated on rue de Verdun. Both streets, together with the Pointe-Nord de l'Île-des-Sœurs, are the territory the borough's PIIA singles out for review of new construction, streetward enlargements and signage.

photo.credit: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), p. 26, captions « 21.E.1B Institution bancaire dans le cœur commercial, 4214, rue Wellington » and « 21.E.1B La rue Wellington, vers l'est, du parvis de l'église ». © Ville de Montréal; not reproduced here. No freely licensed photograph of a Wellington or de l'Église block showing the alcove balcony was identified on Commons.
photo.alt: Photograph of Three-storey commercial block with dwellings above and alcove balconies houses in Verdun (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: Depression, the National Housing Act and the war
types.name_en: National Housing Act house — 1½ storeys, brick, to prize-winning plans
types.name_fr: L'habitation unifamiliale de masse « National Housing Act »
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), sector fiche 21.E.5, with 21.I.9 and 21.I.10
canonical_names: Wartime or veterans' house, 1½ storeys, to Wartime Housing Limited or NHA plans

siting_landscape: Detached houses on individual lots, set back behind a planted front yard, on a street layout that abandons the city's orthogonal grid — the cahier's last sentence for the sector is « On abandonne ici la trame de rues orthogonale. »
The homogeneity of the siting mode and of the landscaping is named, alongside the buildings, as a reason the ensemble is of exceptional value.
massing: One and a half storeys throughout. Uniform heights and uniform roof pitches across the whole development.
articulation: Not described. The cahier's interest is in the ensemble, not the elevation, and it names no ornament, no porch and no door treatment.
openings: Not described.
materials: Brick cladding, uniform across the development. 21.I.10 records the same "War Time" typology elsewhere in the borough with brick and/or stone.

description: « Quelques années avant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, le gouvernement promulgue le « National Housing Act ». De nouvelles typologies d'habitation prendront forme dans ce cadre, et plus particulièrement l'habitation unifamiliale de masse. Le voisinage Crawford offre un exemple exceptionnel de ce nouveau type d'intervention urbaine, constitué d'immeubles d'un étage et demi recouverts d'un parement de brique. Ces immeubles ont été construits sur la base de plans d'architecture primés. » (21.E.5, le voisinage Crawford)
elements_caracteristiques: « L'homogénéité des hauteurs, des matériaux, des pentes de toit, du mode d'implantation et du paysagement contribue à la qualité de l'ensemble. On abandonne ici la trame de rues orthogonale. » (21.E.5)
contexte: « Suivant les mêmes typologies que dans le secteur Crawford, ce projet urbain est aménagé autour d'un parc, mais cette fois, inscrit dans la trame de rues orthogonale de la ville. » (21.I.9, un projet « National Housing Act »)

« La typologie « War Time » dans un projet intégré décrite précédemment s'est aussi implantée dans ce secteur, sur des terrains lotis préalablement selon une trame conventionnelle. Les immeubles sont généralement de bonne facture, avec parement de brique et(ou) de pierre et toiture plate avec mansardes ou toit à pignon. » (21.I.10, le voisinage Sud)

types.profile_note: Assembled from sector paragraphs; the Évaluation publishes no type table. 21.E.5 gives storeys, cladding, roof-pitch uniformity, siting and street layout, and is the only place the cahier states the National Housing Act connection. 21.I.9 and 21.I.10 are quoted because they record the same house twice more in the borough and are what allow the roof form to be entered at all: 21.E.5 mentions « pentes de toit » without naming a form, and 21.I.10 says « toiture plate avec mansardes ou toit à pignon » of a mixed fabric that includes the War Time houses among others. `roof.form` is therefore entered as gabled with a null pitch, on 21.E.5's roof-pitch uniformity plus 21.I.10's « toit à pignon », and should be treated as the weakest field in this record. Articulation and openings are left empty rather than inferred from Wartime Housing Limited's standard plans, which the cahier does not cite. The « plans d'architecture primés » are not identified in the document and no architect is named; the Commons uploader of the photograph below attributes the Crawford Park layout to Samuel Gitterman at the NHA, which is not in any municipal source consulted here and is not asserted.
types.source_generation: sector characterisation, one exceptional-value fiche with two interesting-value fiches
types.blurb_en: A storey and a half, brick, detached on its own lot, one of several hundred built to the same handful of award-winning plans on streets that curve away from Verdun's grid. The 2005 evaluation ranks the result among the borough's seven sectors of exceptional value — for the ensemble, not for the house.
types.origin_en: Crawford Park is Verdun's one piece of planned suburb, and the cahier treats it as an event in the history of housing policy rather than as architecture: the federal National Housing Act « quelques années avant la Seconde Guerre mondiale » produced « de nouvelles typologies d'habitation … et plus particulièrement l'habitation unifamiliale de masse », and Crawford is « un exemple exceptionnel de ce nouveau type d'intervention urbaine ». What is exceptional, in the document's own reasoning, is uniformity plus the abandoned grid — heights, materials, roof pitches, siting and landscaping all held constant on curving streets, in a borough otherwise laid out in blocks. The same house recurs twice more in Verdun and the cahier separates the three occurrences by street plan alone: 21.I.9 puts it back on the orthogonal grid around a park, and 21.I.10 finds it dropped onto conventionally subdivided lots in the south. This is the same form as the Lévis wartime housing and the Sud-Ouest's maison de vétérans, and it is also the only house type anywhere on this site that a municipal fee schedule names: Verdun's 2020 tariff by-law sets a PIIA study fee reserved for enlarging the roof volume of a "wartime"-type house to add habitable space.

photo.credit: A line of 1½-storey brick houses on rue LeClair in Crawford Park, Verdun — uniform heights, uniform roof pitches, planted front yards. Photograph by Commons user A611662, CC BY-SA 4.0. Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Crawford_Park_Extension.jpg
photo.note: Not `address`: the cahier illustrates 21.E.5 with rue Fayolle and rue Truman, and this photograph is of rue LeClair, which Commons places inside Crawford Park but which the cahier does not name and whose position relative to the sector boundary has not been verified. The buildings are what 21.E.5 describes. The identical file is also on Commons as Crawford Park Extension at Verdun.jpg — byte-for-byte the same photograph uploaded twice.
photo.alt: Photograph of National Housing Act house — 1½ storeys, brick, to prize-winning plans houses in Verdun (borough of Montréal), from Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: Build-out, île des Sœurs and the Mies plan
types.name_fr: La tour d'habitation de l'île des Sœurs
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), sector fiche 21.E.6 and §3.2.2 D, les immeubles de valeur patrimoniale exceptionnelle
canonical_names: Postwar modernist residential tower or slab

siting_landscape: Free-standing on open ground, oriented so that views through to the river are kept open. Building tall is the means, not the end — the plan builds up in order to free ground for parks and community space.
Pedestrian and vehicle circulation separated; the shoreline developed as public space.
massing: Slab blocks. Three of them by Mies van der Rohe, at 100 and 200 rue De Gaspé and 201 rue Corot.
articulation: Not described by the cahier, which treats the sector as an urban-planning object and says so — « Ce sont ces éléments urbains qui caractérisent ce secteur. »

description: « La planification urbaine de ce secteur de l'île des Sœurs a été élaborée en collaboration avec l'architecte de réputation internationale Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. On y retrouve aussi trois tours d'habitation de l'architecte ainsi que la station d'essence de la pétrolière Esso. Van der Rohe est aussi l'auteur, à Montréal, du complexe Westmount Square et du Centre Saidye Bronfman. » (21.E.6)
implantation: « La planification urbaine de l'île des Sœurs repose sur la construction en hauteur dégageant de plus grands espaces au sol (parcs, espaces communautaires, etc.), l'aménagement public de la berge, une séparation entre la circulation piétonne et la circulation automobile, et une orientation des bâtiments permettant les percées visuelles sur le fleuve. Ce sont ces éléments urbains qui caractérisent ce secteur. » (21.E.6)
contexte: « En 1956, l'île des Sœurs jusque là exclusivement agricole est définitivement annexée à la ville de Verdun. Les Sœurs de la Congrégation de Notre-Dame quittent les lieux. » (ch. 2, Historique)

« Les années 1960 transformeront l'île, jusqu'alors vouée à l'agriculture, en un vaste projet de développement urbain planifié. Sous l'influence de l'architecte Mies van de Rohe et d'urbanistes, une nouvelle ville sera planifiée selon des règles strictes dont l'influence est encore ressentie et dont l'esprit supporte les orientations actuelles. » (§3.1, Mise en situation — the source's own spelling « van de Rohe » is reproduced here and corrected everywhere else on this page)

types.profile_note: The thinnest record on this page, and deliberately so. The Évaluation characterises 21.E.6 as an urban-planning proposition and describes no building: it gives no storey count, no structural or cladding description, no dates and no dimensions for the three towers. Storeys, window proportion, openings and materials, garage and setbacks are therefore null or empty. `principal_cladding` is the one field entered from the photographs rather than from the text — continuous glazed bands with spandrel panels, visible in both — and should be read as observation, not source. What the cahier does give with certainty is identity and address, from its own list of immeubles de valeur patrimoniale exceptionnelle — « 201, rue Corot — Habitations multiples – Mies van der Rohe » and « 100 et 200, rue De Gaspé — Habitations multiples – Mies van der Rohe » — and those are recorded as example_addresses. The filling station at 201 rue Berlioz is in related_buildings, not here, because it is not housing.
types.source_generation: sector characterisation plus the cahier's own list of exceptional buildings
types.blurb_en: Three residential slabs on an island that was farmland until 1956, set on open ground so the river stays visible between them, in a plan Mies van der Rohe worked on. The evaluation ranks the sector exceptional for the plan rather than for the buildings, and describes no building at all.
types.origin_en: Île des Sœurs belonged to the Congrégation de Notre-Dame from 1769 and was farmed until the Sainte-Famille farm was abandoned in 1957; the island was annexed to the ville de Verdun in 1956 and the sisters left. What replaced the farm is the only planned town on this site laid out on modernist principles rather than garden-city ones — building tall in order to free the ground, the shoreline made public, pedestrians separated from cars, and the blocks turned so the river shows between them. The cahier is unusually candid that this, and not the architecture, is what it is protecting: « Ce sont ces éléments urbains qui caractérisent ce secteur. » It also records that the plan's authority outlasted its authors — « une nouvelle ville sera planifiée selon des règles strictes dont l'influence est encore ressentie et dont l'esprit supporte les orientations actuelles » — which is why the Pointe-Nord de l'Île-des-Sœurs is one of the three territories Verdun's PIIA singles out for review of new construction. Set this beside the Westmount modern tower and the Outremont apartment blocks: same decade, same idiom, three different reasons for being there.

types.phase_title: Build-out, île des Sœurs and the Mies plan
types.source_ref: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), sector fiche 21.I.8, with 21.I.10
canonical_names: Plex — the Montréal family of two to six stacked dwellings on a narrow lot

siting_landscape: In rows, on the last buildable ground in the borough — between the aqueduct canal and rue Bannantyne — filled in mainly after 1950.
Some blocks keep the shape of the original subdivision, and the cahier credits that shape with having forced public green space into the plan.
massing: Two dwellings stacked, built in a row rather than paired or free-standing. The cahier says the row works « quelques modèles originaux » — a small number of repeated designs.
materials: The cahier's stated reason for the sector's interest is the quality of the original materials and the general harmony, not any particular feature.

description: « Ce secteur situé entre le canal de l'aqueduc et la rue Bannantyne s'est construit principalement après 1950. Ce sont majoritairement des duplex en rangée reprenant quelques modèles originaux. L'intérêt de ce secteur découle de la qualité des matériaux d'origine et de l'harmonie générale. Certains îlots bénéficient aussi de la morphologie des lotissements d'origine, qui ont entraîné la planification d'espaces verts publics. » (21.I.8, le voisinage Ouest)
contexte: « De l'Hôpital Douglas à la limite de la municipalité, on retrouve un cadre bâti assez hétérogène de basse densité. … Le secteur est essentiellement résidentiel (unifamilial ou bifamilial), avec des immeubles majoritairement détachés sur des terrains individuels. … Ce sont des constructions un peu plus récentes que celles du reste de l'arrondissement. » (21.I.10, le voisinage Sud)

types.profile_note: The most sparsely evidenced record on this page, and included because it closes Verdun's plex sequence rather than because the source says much. Everything comes from one four-sentence fiche, 21.I.8, which is a secteur de valeur intéressante — hence `sectors: null`, since the ten 21.I codes are not encoded in this part. That fiche gives the date, the row form, the dwelling count implied by "duplex", and a judgement about materials; it gives no storey count, no roof form, no cladding, no opening description and no ornament. `storeys: 2`, `roof.form: flat` and `principal_cladding` are entered from the word "duplex" and from the borough's uniform practice as the cahier describes it elsewhere, not from this fiche, and are the fields to distrust. Articulation and openings are left empty. The canonical link is to the plex family as a whole rather than to one of its seven children, because nothing in the source says where the stair to the upper dwelling is.
types.source_generation: sector characterisation, one interesting-value fiche
types.blurb_en: Two flats stacked and built in a row, on the strip between the aqueduct canal and rue Bannantyne that was the last ground left. Post-1950, from a handful of repeated designs, and valued by the evaluation for the quality of what it was originally made of.
types.origin_en: Verdun ran out of land in the late 1950s — the cahier says the development « se poursuivra de façon constante pour atteindre les limites du territoire à la fin des années 1950 », after which « l'expansion se poursuivra alors sur le seul territoire encore vierge, l'île des Sœurs ». The voisinage Ouest is the end of that sequence on the mainland, and it shows the plex having quietly changed shape: no longer three storeys with a stair on the front, but two stacked dwellings repeated in a row from a short catalogue of models. Nothing about the transition is explained by the document, which is the honest state of the record; what it does say is that the value lies in the materials and in the harmony, and that where the original subdivision survived it produced public green space. Read alongside the exterior-stair plex of the 1900–1920 wave and the balcony duplex of the south, it completes the borough's three-stage plex sequence within one small territory.

photo.credit: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — arrondissement de Verdun (2005), p. 32; the page's only photograph is captioned « 21.I.8 L'école Riverview », which is the school, not the housing. © Ville de Montréal; not reproduced here. No freely licensed photograph of the voisinage Ouest row duplexes was identified on Commons.

types.phase_title: The walled town of New France
types.name_fr: Maison de pierre du Régime français
types.source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
canonical_names: Urban stone house of French inspiration, one or two levels plus attic, two-slope roof, chimneys in fire-break party walls

siting_landscape: Built to the street line inside the walled town, on the narrow lots of Dollier de Casson's 1672 tracé; the RPCQ's characteristic elements list the alignment of buildings on the public way, the high density of ground occupation and party-wall construction as the site's defining relation.
Interior courts and courettes in some sectors, reached from the street.
The surviving concentration is in sector 24.E.45, the quartier Bonsecours, which the cahier says is the one part of Vieux-Montréal that kept its residential vocation after 1850.
massing: Generally low — one or two storeys.
Two-slope or hipped roof of medium pitch.
Chimneys carried up in the plane of the gable walls, and firebreak walls between houses.
articulation: Not stated by either source beyond the masonry itself. The RPCQ describes this family in one sentence and does not treat its ornament.
openings: Wooden casement windows with small panes.
materials: Rubble masonry of roughly squared stone.
Grey limestone predominates in the site as a whole until 1850, after which a wide variety of stone types appears.

elements_caracteristiques: « La présence de bâtiments du Régime français présentant des structures généralement basses (un ou deux étages), des toitures à deux versants ou à croupes de pente moyenne, des murs de moellons grossièrement équarris, des cheminées dans la continuité des murs pignons, des murs coupe-feu et des fenêtres en bois à battants et à petits carreaux. »
« L’utilisation de matériaux traditionnels marquée par une prédominance de la pierre calcaire grise jusqu’en 1850, puis par une grande variété de types de pierre. »
description: « Les immeubles les plus anciens - habitations et édifices conventuels - qui datent de l’époque de la Nouvelle-France présentent une maçonnerie en pierre et des toits à pignon. »

types.profile_note: Roof pitch in degrees, roofing material, window proportion, lot width, setbacks and green front yard are all null because neither source states them. The RPCQ gives the roof only as « de pente moyenne » and the windows only as « à battants et à petits carreaux », with no dimension attached to either; the 2005 cahier characterises sectors, not buildings, and prints no dimensional table at all. There is no per-type document for Ville-Marie, and there will not be one until the plan de conservation for the site patrimonial is produced — this record is a reconstruction from a site fiche's statement of value, and its five columns carry only what that fiche and the cahier say.
types.source_generation: RPCQ fiche 93528, sections « Valeur patrimoniale » and « Éléments caractéristiques » (fiche source: Ministère de la Culture et des Communications du Québec, 2004), read 17 August 2026; cross-read against the cahier's sector fiches 24.E.41, 24.E.45 and 24.E.46.
types.blurb_en: The oldest domestic form on this site and the one that recurs in six places: low walls of roughly squared rubble, a two-slope or hipped roof of medium pitch, chimneys rising in the plane of the gable walls, firebreak walls between neighbours, and small-paned wooden casements. In Vieux-Montréal it is an urban house — built to the street line, party-walled, on a narrow lot — rather than the freestanding rural house of the Île d'Orléans or the côtes.
types.origin_en: Ville-Marie was founded in 1642 as a missionary settlement and became the bridgehead of the fur trade. The Sulpicians became seigneurs of the island in 1663, and their superior François Dollier de Casson traced the first streets in 1672 with the notary-surveyor Bénigne Basset Des Lauriers: three streets parallel to the river and seven perpendicular to it. Between 1685 and 1800 the town was walled, and the wall fixed its form. The intendants' ordonnances then fixed the relation between street and building, including the alignment of construction; stone became the preferred material for new building, which is why so little of the wooden town survives. The form is the same one recorded on this site at Île d'Orléans, Charlesbourg, Québec, Terrebonne and Lachine — the same walls, the same roof, the same chimneys — with the difference that here it is packed against its neighbours.

photo.credit: Maison Du Calvet, rue Saint-Paul at rue Bonsecours, Vieux-Montréal — rubble stone walls, a steep two-slope roof, chimneys carried up in the plane of the gable walls and firebreak walls stepping above the roof. Photograph by Mathieu BROSSAIS, 7 August 2008, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maison_Du_Calvet_%C3%A0_Montr%C3%A9al.jpg — licence, author and file URL read through the Commons API before download; the photograph was opened and checked against its description.

types.phase_title: British regime — classical stone
types.name_en: Classical house of the British regime
types.name_fr: Édifice d’inspiration classique du Régime britannique
types.source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
canonical_names: Opulent village house (maison cossue) in stone or brick with elaborate ornamentation, deep setback and ornamental fence

siting_landscape: Built on the public alignment, at high density, party-walled, like everything else inside the old town; the RPCQ lists the setting-back of certain administrative and public buildings as the exception that proves it.

The Plan des commissaires of 1804 gave the quarter a terrace along the river, an enlarged Champ-de-Mars and wider streets, and the three principal arteries bounding the site — rues de la Commune, Saint-Antoine and McGill — descend from it.
massing: Not stated. The RPCQ says only that the site's gauges are heterogeneous and very variable, particularly in height.
articulation: Symmetrical composition of the façade.
The classical orders recalled — Doric, Ionic, Corinthian.
Pediments and quoined angles.
openings: Not stated by either source for this family.

The RPCQ does record, as a characteristic of the site, the relation between lot and street "manifested by steps, carriage doors, railings, rights of way and several entrances — one on each façade giving on the street".
materials: Cut stone (pierre de taille).
Grey limestone predominant until 1850, then a wide variety of stone types.

elements_caracteristiques: « La forte proportion de bâtiments du Régime britannique d’inspiration classique se distinguant par l’emploi de la pierre de taille, la composition symétrique des façades, le rappel des ordres classiques (dorique, ionique, corinthien), les frontons et les chaînages d’angle. »
« L’utilisation de matériaux traditionnels marquée par une prédominance de la pierre calcaire grise jusqu’en 1850, puis par une grande variété de types de pierre. »

« La relation entre le lot et la rue se manifestant par la présence de marches, de portes cochères, de grilles, de servitudes de passage et de plusieurs entrées, à savoir une sur chaque façade donnant sur la rue. »
description: « Les nombreux édifices d’inspiration classique du Régime britannique sont caractérisés, entre autres, par la pierre calcaire grise. »

types.profile_note: Storeys, roof form and pitch, roofing, window proportion, lot width, setbacks and green front yard are null because neither source states them. The RPCQ's sentence on this family is a sentence about façades — stone, symmetry, orders, pediments, quoins — and says nothing about section or roof; the site's massing it describes only as heterogeneous. Tenure plan is given as row because the RPCQ's characteristic elements record party-wall construction and alignment on the street as general to the site, not because either source classes this family by plan. This is a reconstruction from a site fiche, not a type record from a typology document.
types.source_generation: RPCQ fiche 93528, sections « Valeur patrimoniale » and « Éléments caractéristiques » (fiche source: Ministère de la Culture et des Communications du Québec, 2004), read 17 August 2026; cross-read against the cahier's sector fiches 24.E.36, 24.E.39 and 24.E.43.
types.blurb_en: What the British regime built when the walls came down: cut grey limestone, a symmetrical street front, an order recalled rather than reproduced, a pediment, quoined angles. The RPCQ treats it as the most numerous family in the site — « la forte proportion de bâtiments du Régime britannique d'inspiration classique » — and, because a site fiche describes a landscape rather than a house, it describes the family entirely in terms of the façade.
types.origin_en: From 1800 Montréal became the principal city of the two Canadas. The political upheavals of the 18th century, the Conquest and American independence among them, drove population growth and immigration, and dynamic import-export merchants replaced the magnates of the fur trade. The RPCQ's account of the change is architectural in one line: « Les maisons en bois des artisans font place aux résidences et édifices en pierre d'inspiration néoclassique. » The fortifications were demolished between 1801 and 1817 and three commissioners were appointed to plan the freed ground; their terrace along the river, enlarged Champ-de-Mars and wider streets are still the frame of the quarter. Grey limestone stayed the predominant material until 1850. The two great fires of 9 and 10 July 1852, which destroyed some 1 200 dwellings and left about 10 000 people homeless, ended wooden construction in the city outright and made stone the rule rather than the preference.

photo.credit: Maison Papineau, 440 rue de Bonsecours, Vieux-Montréal — a symmetrically composed street front with quoined angles, a carriage arch and a dormered roof. Photograph by Jeangagnon, 24 July 2011, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maison_Papineau_01.jpg — licence, author and file URL read through the Commons API before download; the photograph was opened and checked against its description. Shown as an example of the classical street front the RPCQ describes, not as a building either source attributes to this family by name.

types.phase_title: Warehouses, maisons-magasins and the faubourgs
types.name_en: Maison-magasin and warehouse with dwellings above
types.source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
canonical_names: Maison-magasin / warehouse with dwellings above, flat roof, heavy projecting cornice

siting_landscape: Built to the street line in a continuous run, party-walled, on the blocks between rue de la Commune and rue Saint-Paul and along rues des Récollets, Sainte-Hélène, Saint-Pierre and Le Moyne.
Two-faced by design where the block runs through: the cahier records a relatively plain elevation on the goods-handling side and a far more elaborate one on the commercial side, on rue Saint-Paul.
massing: Flat roof.
Thick, projecting and often very ornamented cornice.
articulation: Heavy projecting cornice as the crowning element.
Ornament concentrated on the commercial elevation; showrooms for retail selling behind the ground-floor bays in the sector of the Bourses.
openings: Wide bays (« larges baies »).
materials: Mixed structure of timber, cast iron and stone.
Red brick.
Grey limestone on the older runs, in a site where grey limestone predominates until 1850 and a wide variety of stone types after it.

elements_caracteristiques: « L’empreinte de l’architecture éclectique du XIXe siècle, visible notamment dans les bâtiments commerciaux, industriels, institutionnels et les édifices à bureaux, reconnaissables à leur structure mixte de bois, de fonte et de pierres, leurs larges baies, leur toit plat, leur corniche épaisse, débordante et souvent très ornementée et l’emploi de la brique rouge. »
traitement_des_facades: « Plusieurs de ces bâtiments ont une façade relativement sobre du côté où se fait la manutention des marchandises, tandis que la facture architecturale est plus élaborée du côté commercial, sur la rue Saint-Paul. »

types.profile_note: Storeys, roof pitch, roofing, window proportion, lot width, setbacks and green front yard are null because neither source states them. Note also what the two sources are doing: the RPCQ describes this as a commercial, industrial and institutional family — « les bâtiments commerciaux, industriels, institutionnels et les édifices à bureaux » — and the residential content of the type is a fact of its second life, not of its first. It is carried on a residential site because the conversion of these buildings to dwellings is what repopulated Vieux-Montréal, and because the cahier says so. Tenure plan is recorded as mixed for the same reason.
types.source_generation: RPCQ fiche 93528, section « Éléments caractéristiques » (fiche source: Ministère de la Culture et des Communications du Québec, 2004), read 17 August 2026; with the cahier's sector fiches 24.E.38, 24.E.40 and 24.E.42 and its historical chapter, printed pp. 34–35.
types.blurb_en: The building that made the port quarter and then, a century later, repopulated it. A mixed structure of timber, cast iron and stone; wide bays; a flat roof; a thick, projecting, often very ornamented cornice; red brick. In the runs between rue de la Commune and rue Saint-Paul it is frankly two-faced — sober where the goods came in, elaborate where they were sold. From the 1970s these are the buildings that were recycled into dwellings, which is how a quarter with a few hundred residents in the 1950s came to hold several thousand.
types.origin_en: Montréal became the undisputed metropolis of Canada in the second half of the 19th century, at the centre of a road, maritime and transcontinental rail network, and the old town turned into a financial and administrative city — the shop window of Canadian capitalism, in the RPCQ's phrase. Offices, banks, insurance head offices, warehouses and courthouses went up with great stylistic eclecticism. Then the fall: after 1945 Montréal lost the metropolitan role to Toronto, the economic centre moved north-west, and by the 1950s, the cahier records, retail had practically vanished from the old town and its residents numbered only a few hundred. Serious proposals for an expressway through Vieux-Montréal followed, and the protests against them led to the Québec government decreeing the quarter an arrondissement historique in 1964. Survival then meant new uses for empty floors, and the cahier states the mechanism plainly: « On y a recyclé plusieurs de ces bâtiments en condos, dont le premier exemple est celui des Cours Le Royer, posant ainsi le premier jalon d'un repeuplement du Vieux-Montréal. » The loft conversions of rue Saint-Paul and the faubourg des Récollets follow the same line.

photo.credit: Magasin-entrepôt Jean-Leclaire, 28-30 rue Saint-Paul Est with its secondary façade at 29 rue de la Commune Est, and its neighbours — grey stone, wide bays in regular tiers, flat roofs and heavy cornices, with commercial ground floors. Photograph by Jeangagnon, 19 May 2014, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Magasin-entrepot_Jean-Leclaire.JPG — licence, author and file URL read through the Commons API before download; the photograph was opened and checked against its description.

types.phase_title: The Mille carré doré and the Victorian terrace
types.name_fr: Demeure bourgeoise isolée du Mille carré doré
types.source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
canonical_names: Freestanding greystone mansion on landscaped grounds, 2½–3 storeys, eclectic revival

siting_landscape: Freestanding, often surrounded by gardens and outbuildings, on the south flank of the mountain.
The cahier values the sector as much for what the houses leave open as for the houses — « le dégagement qu'elle assure à la montagne ».
Only the part north of avenue du Docteur-Penfield falls inside the site patrimonial du Mont-Royal; sector 24.E.30, south of Sherbrooke, is explicitly outside it.
massing: Not stated for this sector. The neighbouring croissant Redpath, 24.E.28, is described as mostly three storeys under a two-slope roof — that is the cahier's figure for that sector, not for this one.
articulation: Not stated. The cahier calls the sector remarkable for « la qualité architecturale des bâtiments qui le composent » without describing that architecture.
openings: Not stated.
materials: Not stated for the sector. The cahier's neighbouring fiche 24.E.28 gives clay brick or stone for the Redpath crescent, and the site as a whole is characterised by grey limestone to 1850 and a wide variety of stone types after it.

description: « Compris dans l’arrondissement historique et naturel du mont Royal, ce secteur résidentiel est urbanisé entre 1860 et 1935. C’est un quartier de résidences bourgeoises souvent entourées de jardins et de dépendances. »

« On y retrouve un grand nombre de demeures bourgeoises exceptionnelles, dont certaines sont classées monuments historiques. On y voit notamment des résidences unifamiliales isolées, de luxueuses maisons en rangée et de riches immeubles de logements. »

« Certaines des villas sont aujourd’hui occupées par des bureaux, ambassades, consulats et délégations commerciales. Cette zone est caractérisée par la présence de bâtiments d’influence française et anglaise. »

types.profile_note: Storeys, roof, openings, articulation, materials, lot width, setbacks and green front yard are all null, and the reason is the point of this record. Ville-Marie's own heritage document grades the Mille carré doré exceptionnelle and then describes it in six sentences, none of which describes a building: it gives the dates, the siting in gardens, the present institutional uses and the view of the mountain. There is no per-type table, no inventory fiche and no plan de conservation for this quarter, because it has no ensemble protection to generate one. The richest domestic architecture on the island is also the worst documented at type level of anything on this site, and the empty cells below are that fact rendered as data. Style list is the range of currents the named examples carry, attributed building by building in the list of buildings, not a characterisation either source makes of the sector.
types.source_generation: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005), sector fiches 24.E.29, 24.E.30, 24.E.28 and 24.E.3, and the historical chapter printed p. 30; with Héritage Montréal, Memento, « McGill and Golden Square Mile Houses », read 17 August 2026. The RPCQ fiche 93528 covers the declared site only and does not reach this quarter.
types.blurb_en: The richest domestic architecture on the island of Montréal, and the least protected. A freestanding house of two and a half or three storeys standing in its own garden with its own outbuildings, on the slope between Sherbrooke and the mountain, built between about 1860 and 1935 in whichever revival was current — Italianate, Second Empire, Romanesque, Queen Anne, Beaux-Arts. The Ville grades the two sectors that hold them exceptionnelle. Neither carries an ensemble designation, and the columns below are empty because no document describes these houses as a type.
types.origin_en: The cahier's historical chapter puts it plainly: the north-west of the quartier Saint-Antoine, part of it running up the flank of the mountain, went on attracting the great Montréal bourgeoisie, which in the wake of the McTavishes and the McGills had sumptuous residences built by well-known architects — « On y compte les Allan, les Van Horne, les Forget » — and the sector would later be called the Square Mile. Héritage Montréal dates the golden age 1840–1930 and the buildings principally 1850–1930, and describes a commercial aristocracy that controlled two-thirds of the country's wealth. After the 1929 crash the families moved west to Westmount and the Town of Mount Royal, apartment and office buildings were put up in their gardens, and the quarter went, in Héritage Montréal's phrase, from golden age to urban decay in fifty years. Attrition, as English Wikipedia states it citing Rémillard and Merrett's Mansions of the Golden Square Mile (1987): "By 1983, only 30% of the mansions in the northern half of the Square Mile had survived demolition; and only 5% survived south of Sherbrooke Street." Héritage Montréal's own page carries a more cautious version — "Only about 30% of the bourgeois homes survived, north of Sherbrooke Street" — with neither the year nor the 5%. Whichever figure is right, the surviving stock is a remnant, and Héritage Montréal states that the ensemble "does not have a designation or specific strategy to protect and promote its heritage over current urban development considerations".

photo.credit: Ravenscrag, 835-1025 avenue des Pins Ouest — the Allan house, freestanding on its wooded ground below the mountain, with the belvedere tower of its Italianate composition. Photograph by Thomas1313, 7 August 2013, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maison_Hugh_Allan,_dite_Ravenscrag_16.jpg — licence, author and file URL read through the Commons API before download; the photograph was opened and checked against its description.
photo.alt: Photograph of Freestanding greystone mansion houses in Ville-Marie (Montréal), from RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: The Mille carré doré and the Victorian terrace
types.name_fr: Maison en rangée de pierre grise
types.source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
canonical_names: Party-wall greystone row house, 2–3 storeys, flat roof or false mansard, runs of up to eight units

siting_landscape: Contiguous, in series, on the streets around the villas rather than on the villa streets themselves — the cahier is explicit that these were built for the middle class, on the streets neighbouring the Shaughnessy villas.
Very dense fabric in the Village Lincoln, where the cahier says it is the terraces and the individual heritage houses together that make the sector exceptional.
massing: Two and a half storeys.
articulation: Not stated for the Village Shaughnessy terraces beyond their Second Empire inspiration.

In the Milton Park half the Plateau cahier records decoration that is often elaborate, and Héritage Montréal describes great architectural diversity, with large single-family Victorian houses standing cheek by jowl with duplexes, triplexes and apartment houses.
openings: Not stated by any of the three sources.
materials: Stone, or sometimes brick, on the principal façade.
In Milton Park, grey stone or red sandstone.

description: « Entre 1870 et 1910, de nombreuses maisons unifamiliales en rangée destinées à la classe moyenne ont été construites sur les rues avoisinantes; ce sont généralement des maisons de deux étages et demi, avec revêtement de pierre ou parfois de brique sur la façade principale. La plupart d’entre elles sont d’inspiration Second Empire. On retrouve aussi dans le secteur de bons exemples de maisons de rapport érigées dans les années 1920. »

« Le type architectural dominant est le bâtiment uni- ou bifamilial contigu en pierre grise ou en grès rouge au décor souvent élaboré, construit entre 1875 et 1900 et subdivisé ultérieurement en deux logements ou plus. »

types.profile_note: Roof form and pitch, roofing, window proportion, articulation, lot width, setbacks and green front yard are null because none of the three sources states them. The « inspiration Second Empire » the cahier records for the Village Shaughnessy terraces is a style attribution, not a statement about roof form, and it has not been converted into one here. One further thing this record makes visible: two of its three sectors are in Ville-Marie and the third, Milton Park, is not — it is 25.E.12 in the Plateau-Mont-Royal cahier, north of rue Sherbrooke. The form runs across the boundary; the documents stop at it. The same form is recorded on this site in Westmount, and the cross-link on the canonical page is the useful one.
types.source_generation: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005), sector fiches 24.E.9 and 24.E.7; Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Plateau-Mont-Royal (2005), sector fiche 25.E.12, for the Milton Park half of the same form; Héritage Montréal, Memento, « Milton Parc Neighbourhood », read 17 August 2026.
types.blurb_en: The middle-class counterpart to the mansion, and the form this project has already recorded in Westmount: contiguous single-family houses in series, two and a half storeys, stone — sometimes brick — on the principal façade, mostly Second Empire in inspiration, built between 1870 and 1910 on the streets around the Shaughnessy villas and between 1875 and 1900 in Milton Park north of Sherbrooke. Many were later subdivided into two dwellings or more, which is why so much of this stock now reads as plex without ever having been built as one.
types.origin_en: Two halves of one form, on either side of a borough boundary that did not exist when it was built. South of Sherbrooke, the Village Shaughnessy: John Ostell's 1842 master plan turned development north-west, rues Chomedey and Lambert-Closse were cut about 1880, and between 1870 and 1910 the streets around the surviving villas filled with row houses for the middle class, with good maisons de rapport of the 1920s among them. North of Sherbrooke, Milton Park, which the Plateau cahier reads as the same building repeated — the contiguous one- or two-family house in grey stone or red sandstone, 1875–1900, later subdivided. The two halves went in opposite directions after 1945. Shaughnessy Village lost its villas one by one and was renamed a quartier; Milton Park was bought up by a single developer, threatened with total demolition, and bought back by its residents. See the notes at the foot of this page.

photo.credit: Rue Pierce seen from rue Sainte-Catherine — the maisons en rangée William D. Stroud, 1419 to 1441, built 1889–1890 by the architect Robert Findlay, in a run of contiguous houses with gabled dormers, bays and front stairs. Photograph by Jeangagnon, 15 October 2012, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maisons_en_rangee_William_D.-Stroud_12.jpg — licence, author and file URL read through the Commons API before download; the photograph was opened and checked against its description. The dating and attribution are the 2005 cahier's, fiche 24.E.7.

types.phase_title: Warehouses, maisons-magasins and the faubourgs
types.source_ref: RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005)
canonical_names: Flat-roofed faubourg house, party-wall multi-unit filling the full lot width, porte cochère, ornamented crown

siting_landscape: Small lots on blocks laid out without a ruelle, which is the whole of the type's logic: with no service lane, access to the rear of the lot has to be taken through the building.
The carriage gate gives on to houses standing at the back of the yard and to fuel storage.
Deep lots, in 24.I.6 and 24.I.9, with rear-yard annexes since demolished; front yards where the ground floor stands clear of the ground.
The quarters that grew round the Molson brewery, the Canadian Rubber and the MacDonald Tobacco works.
massing: Two or three storeys.
Fine cornices, and in 24.I.5 false cornices.
articulation: Elaborate cornices, carriage gates and exterior stairs, in the cahier's own list for 24.I.6.
Elaborate crownings, slate roofs and dormers with worked joinery on the brick and grey-stone ensembles near rue Ontario (24.I.4).
openings: Vertical windows.
The carriage gate itself — a full-height arched opening in the street front, still visible throughout the sector.
Access to the ground floor fixes the front setback: none where the access is internal, set back where a stair on the façade has to be accommodated (24.I.4).
materials: Brick as the principal facing.
Grey stone or brick on the finer ensembles.

description: « Les quartiers qui entourent ces usines se composent de petits lots, et les quadrilatères (îlots) sont sans ruelle. Dans ce type de lotissement, c’est la porte cochère, toujours visible dans ce secteur, qui donne accès aux maisons en fond de cour ainsi qu’à l’entreposage de combustibles. »

« Construit essentiellement sur le lotissement ancien, sans ruelle, mais pourvu de terrains très profonds, le cadre bâti offre une gamme de typologies d’habitation. […] La brique est le parement principal et la porte cochère est à l’honneur. »
elements_caracteristiques: « La relation entre le lot et la rue se manifestant par la présence de marches, de portes cochères, de grilles, de servitudes de passage et de plusieurs entrées, à savoir une sur chaque façade donnant sur la rue. »
ouvertures: « L’accès au rez-de-chaussée fixe la marge avant : nulle si l’accès se fait de l’intérieur, ou en recul pour accommoder un escalier en façade. »

types.profile_note: Roof form and pitch, roofing, lot width, setbacks and green front yard are null because the cahier states none of them. Roof form in particular is left empty on purpose: the I-sector fiches describe crownings and cornices rather than roofs, 24.I.4 records slate roofs with dormers on the finer ensembles, and 24.I.9 records a few surviving faubourg houses « avec toit à pignon » — three different roofs in one family, and no source that says which is the type's. The canonical form is given as the flat-roofed faubourg house because that is what the cornice-and-crowning descriptions imply, and it is the one inference in this record; it is flagged here rather than buried. No count, no dimension and no dated example is published for this type anywhere in the cahier.
types.source_generation: Ville de Montréal, Évaluation du patrimoine urbain — Ville-Marie (2005), historical chapter printed pp. 29–30, and sector fiches 24.I.1, 24.I.5, 24.I.6, 24.I.9, 24.I.10, 24.I.11 and 24.I.12; with RPCQ fiche 93528, which lists the porte cochère among the characteristic elements of the declared site.
types.blurb_en: The eastern alternative to the ruelle, and the one detail in this borough that exists nowhere else on this site. Where the blocks around the Molson brewery, the Canadian Rubber and the MacDonald Tobacco works were cut into small lots with no service lane behind them, the only way to the back of the lot is through the building — so a full-height carriage gate is driven through the street front. Behind it are houses standing at the back of the yard and the coal and wood store. Two or three storeys, brick, vertical windows, elaborate cornices; the front setback is decided by nothing more than whether the stair to the upper dwellings is inside or out.
types.origin_en: The cahier gives the mechanism in the middle of its historical chapter, describing the dense population that gathered round the Molson brewery — in the quarter since the 18th century — the Canadian Rubber and the MacDonald Tobacco works: « Les quartiers qui entourent ces usines se composent de petits lots, et les quadrilatères (îlots) sont sans ruelle. Dans ce type de lotissement, c'est la porte cochère, toujours visible dans ce secteur, qui donne accès aux maisons en fond de cour ainsi qu'à l'entreposage de combustibles. » Set that against the Sud-Ouest, where Montréal's regulation of residential construction from about 1880 produced blocks with ruelles first in an « I » and then in an « H », and where the same regulation pushed the stair to the upper dwellings out of the building and into the front yard. Two solutions to one problem — how to reach the back of a deep, narrow lot — separated by a generation of by-laws and four kilometres of city. The carriage gate is the older answer, and Centre-Sud is where it survives; the RPCQ lists it among the characteristic elements of the declared site as well.

photo.credit: Photograph pending. RPCQ imagery for the site patrimonial de Montréal (rpcq_bien_93528_*) is © Gouvernement du Québec and is not reproduced: permission required. The 2005 cahier's own photographs of the I sectors — 24.I.7 at 1221-1229 rue Plessis and 24.I.9 at 1834-1848 rue Plessis, credited to the Ville de Montréal and its named photographers — are likewise not reproduced. A search of Wikimedia Commons on 17 August 2026 for a freely-licensed photograph of a Centre-Sud porte cochère returned nothing whose description survived inspection, and no substitute has been invented.
photo.alt: Photograph of Workers' house with carriage gate houses in Ville-Marie (Montréal), from RPCQ id 93528 (MCC); Ville de Montréal

types.phase_title: Côtes, farms and quarries
types.source_ref: Règlement 01-283-124, Annexe F, fiche 1.1
canonical_names: Small-gabarit village house of an 18th–19th-century bourg, wood or brick, tin roof, minimal setback

siting_landscape: Built on large lots that were later cut down by cadastral resubdivision, so the house often now stands on a parcel far smaller than the one it was set out on.
Set back from the street with a medium to large front margin — the opposite of every other type in this by-law except the post-war ones.
massing: Square or rectangular plan, compact, one storey above ground with the habitable space carried up into the attic.
Mansard roof with dormers; the ridge runs parallel to the street.
One or more chimneys, placed on the side walls.
articulation: Modest houses, clad in wood clapboard.
The front door is reached by a covered gallery running the full width of the façade.
openings: Windows may have shutters.
Openings are of vertical proportion and of similar dimensions to one another.
materials: Wood clapboard in the base typology; variant B is built in stone or brick instead.

contexte: Comme son nom l’indique, cette typologie est associée à une occupation agricole ou villageoise du territoire. Bien que la majorité de ces maisons n’aient pas résisté au passage du temps, on en trouve encore quelques exemples dans les secteurs les plus anciens de Villeray et de l’ancienne Cité de Saint-Michel.
implantation: Ce type d’habitation a généralement été construit sur des terrains de grandes dimensions, qui ont ensuite été réduits lors de redécoupages cadastraux. La maison est implantée en recul par rapport à la rue, avec une marge avant de moyenne à importante.
volumetrie: La maison rurale possède un plan carré ou rectangulaire. Elle est habituellement de volumétrie compacte avec un étage hors sol et un espace habitable situé dans les combles. Le toit est mansardé et agrémenté de lucarnes. La ligne faîtière de la toiture est parallèle à la rue. Le bâtiment peut comporter une ou plusieurs cheminées, positionnées sur les murs latéraux.
traitement_des_facades: Ces maisons sont modestes et revêtues d’un clin en bois. Les fenêtres peuvent être équipées de volets. La porte d’entrée est accessible par une galerie couverte faisant la pleine largeur de la façade.
ouvertures: Les ouvertures présentent des proportions verticales de dimensions similaires.
sous_variantes: A — MAISON RURALE OU VILLAGEOISE À TOITURE À DEUX VERSANTS. La particularité de cette variante est que son toit n’est pas mansardé, mais plutôt à deux versants.
B — MAISON RURALE OU VILLAGEOISE À PAREMENT DE BRIQUE OU DE PIERRE. Ces maisons sont construites avec un revêtement de pierre ou de brique.

types.profile_note: The oldest and rarest of the thirteen types, and the only one whose fiche opens by admitting that most examples are gone. The by-law makes the mansard the base form and the two-slope roof the variant — the reverse of how most Québec sources file the pair, and worth noting beside Charlesbourg and Île d'Orléans, where the straight two-slope roof is the parent and the mansard a later courant. The sector link is to 14.A.1, the archaeological record of the ancien village de Villeray, because that is where the cahier says traces of the village survive; it is not a claim that any surviving house of this type stands inside that perimeter.
types.source_generation: By-law Annexe F, fiche 1.1, pp. 1.1.1 to 1.1.5 — the fiche d'accompagnement, the three headings of the typologie de base, and the two lettered variants, transcribed verbatim
types.blurb_en: What the borough looked like before the tramway: a compact wood-clad house on a big lot, set back from the road, one storey under a mansard with the bedrooms in the attic and a covered gallery running the whole width of the front. The by-law keeps it because a few survive in the oldest parts of Villeray and of the former Cité de Saint-Michel, not because it is common.
types.origin_en: This is the borough's link to the rural Québec forms catalogued elsewhere on this site — the small village house of Charlesbourg's Trait-Carré, of Île d'Orléans, of Lévis. Here it is a survivor inside a twentieth-century street grid rather than the parent of what came after: nothing in Villeray's plex or shoebox descends from it. The by-law's ordering makes the point by putting it first and then never referring back to it.

photo.credit: Règlement 01-283-124, Annexe F, p. 1.1.2 — elevation drawing of the typologie de base, with further elevations of variants A and B at pp. 1.1.4–1.1.5. © Ville de Montréal. Not reproduced.
